In the trespass case of Waterhouse vs. Gibson & al., the plaintiff sued the defendants for removing a barn and blacksmith’s shop from his land. The land had previously been set off by an execution to a creditor, Cotton B. Brooks, from one of the defendants, James Jack, and was later purchased by the plaintiff. The execution returns contained no exception or reservation regarding the buildings. 

During the trial, the defendants attempted to introduce parol evidence showing that the buildings stood on blocks without foundations sunk in the ground, and that the creditor's attorney had excluded them from the appraisal, verbally leaving them for Jack to remove, and only accidentally omitted this exception from the written returns. The trial judge rejected this evidence, resulting in a verdict for the plaintiff.

Upon review, the court affirmed the verdict, ruling that a conveyance by extent is governed by the same rules of construction as a conveyance by deed. Consequently, an execution on a debtor’s land conveys all of the debtor's buildings standing on it, regardless of whether their foundations are sunk into the ground. While exceptions exist for leased land where tenants erect buildings for trade, buildings owned by the landowner pass as real estate when the land is conveyed. Finally, the court held that parol evidence is inadmissible to modify written returns to show that the buildings were verbally excepted from the appraisal.

To establish the precise relationship between isotacticity and mechanical properties, the team tested polypropylene film samples with varying degrees of isotacticity (from 25 to over 95 percent) that were either quenched in ice water or cooled slowly. Obtaining experimentally representative atomistic structures for disordered materials is challenging, requiring both scalable and accurate simulation methods. Standard Monte Carlo (MC) and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations do not guarantee experimental agreement. While reverse MC (RMC) and hybrid RMC (HRMC) methods improve agreement, they can produce unphysical structures or suffer from poor computational efficiency, restricting simulations to a few thousand atoms. Previous attempts to use more scalable MD methods for inverse structure optimization also faced scaling and accuracy issues, inaccurate gradients, and omitted thermal broadening effects. 

To address this, this article details the theory of molecular augmented dynamics (MAD), an $O(N)$ modified MD method that finds low-energy, ab-initio accurate atomistic structures matching experimental data. The MAD Hamiltonian combines kinetic energy, interatomic potential, and an experimental potential—which measures deviations between predicted observables and experimental data—resulting in a multi-objective optimization of experimental agreement and system energy. To ensure scalability and efficiency, the method uses analytical forces derived from the negative gradients of the potentials, accounting for thermal broadening and generating smooth gradients for X-ray diffraction, neutron diffraction, pair distribution functions, and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy.

Azerbaijan aims to increase its honey and beekeeping product exports to meet a projected global demand of 2–2.5 million tonnes in 2020–2022, according to Agriculture Minister Heydar Asadov. Because Azerbaijani honey is organic, it has easier access to premium markets, and the ministry plans to propose increased state support for beekeeping.

The Housing Authority of the City of Santa Barbara won a Gold Nugget Award for Best Affordable Project at the Pacific Coast Builders Conference for Bradley Studios. Built by McGillivray Construction and designed by Peikert Group Architects LLP in 2012, this 54-unit development replaced blighted buildings. The environmentally responsible, California Craftsman-style project houses low-income residents with special needs and provides on-site amenities, including recreation rooms and social service offices for counseling, job training, and mental health treatment.

Acting CDC Director Jim O’Neill and President Trump have called for the combined MMR (measles, mumps, and rubella) vaccine to be replaced by three separate monovalent shots administered at different medical appointments. However, the passage notes there is no evidence that separating the vaccine improves safety or effectiveness, as the current MMR shot has been safely administered for over fifty years with minimal side effects. 

Outside experts warn that splitting the vaccine is logistically infeasible because monovalent versions are no longer available in the U.S., and developing and approving new ones would take years. Furthermore, past research indicates that children receiving single-antigen shots are less likely to complete their recommended vaccine series compared to those receiving the combination shot. A Stanford University physician stated that proposing to separate the vaccines could lead parents to question the current schedule, resulting in lower vaccination rates and more preventable illness in children.

In 1976, Kent Howerton won the opening AMA 500cc National Motocross Championship, which featured six different brands in the top six. In 1982, Ricky Johnson won the High Point 250 National, Darrell Shultz won the 500 Class, and Mark Barnett won the Toronto Supercross. Also in 1982, Yamaha cut budgets, dropped coach Gary Bailey, and saw riders favor lucrative international races over the Trans-USA Championship. Additionally, Ross Pederson won the 1987 Montreal Supercross.

This study explores the empathic profile of 206 education faculty teachers at University G in Spain, as well as the relationship between their empathy levels and socio-demographic and occupational profiles. Using the Spanish adaptation of the Interpersonal Reactivity Index (IRI), researchers measured four dimensions: Perspective Taking (PT), Fantasy (FS), Empathic Concern (EC), and Personal Distress (PD). 

Results revealed a high overall level of empathy among the educators, with optimal levels in PT, FS, and EC, and moderate scores in PD, suggesting a protective balance against emotional overinvolvement. Female participants scored significantly higher across the total scale and all individual dimensions. While prior non-university teaching experience did not significantly affect the total IRI score, teachers with such experience scored higher in PT, FS, and EC, whereas those with only university experience scored higher in PD. No significant differences in empathy were found regarding the degree programme taught, campus location, contractual status, or overall years of teaching experience. 

Because students develop empathy by observing teachers as empathetic models, the study highlights the need for university educators to possess these skills, though a limited sample size and potential social desirability bias caution against broad generalisations.

The Texas Instruments MSPM0C1105 and MSPM0C1106 are ultra-low-power, 32-bit microcontrollers based on the Arm Cortex-M0+ core, operating at up to 32MHz. They operate with supply voltages from 1.62V to 3.6V across a temperature range of -40°C to 125°C. The devices feature up to 64KB of embedded flash memory, 8KB of zero-wait-state SRAM, and a 3-channel DMA controller.

To balance performance and power consumption, the MCUs utilize two power domains (PD0 and PD1) and five operating modes: RUN, SLEEP, STOP, STANDBY, and SHUTDOWN. The Power Management Unit (PMU) regulates core supplies and monitors external supply, while the Clock Module (CKM) provides various internal and external oscillator options. An event manager transfers digital events between peripherals, the DMA, and the CPU.

Integrated analog peripherals include a 12-bit 1.6Msps ADC, a configurable voltage reference (VREF) offering 1.4V and 2.5V internal references, a comparator with an 8-bit reference DAC, and a linear temperature sensor. Digital and communication peripherals include up to 45 GPIOs controlled via an IOMUX, one 16-bit advanced timer, four 16-bit general-purpose timers, an independent watchdog timer (IWDT), a windowed watchdog timer (WWDT), a real-time clock (RTC_B), a 16-bit CRC module, flexible firewalls, three UARTs, two I2Cs, and one SPI. Debugging is supported via a two-wire Serial Wire Debug (SWD) interface and a Debug Subsystem (DEBUGSS). Read-only device identification and factory trim constants are stored in a memory-mapped FACTORY region. 

For hardware implementation, TI recommends placing 10µF and 0.1µF decoupling capacitors near the VDD and VSS pins, a 47kΩ pullup resistor with a 1000pF pulldown capacitor on the NRST pin, external bypass capacitors for crystal oscillators, and pullup resistors for 5V-tolerant open-drain IOs. TI provides various development tools, software, and documentation, such as the TI Resource Explorer, SysConfig, and GUI Composer. Device nomenclature uses the "X" prefix for experimental prototypes and "MSP" for fully qualified production devices. The document also provides revision histories, mechanical and packaging specifications, solder paste guidelines, and legal disclaimers.

The Department advises postponing discussions of decentralizing the international organization or dividing its General Assembly until the organization is firmly established, to ensure its effectiveness. 

For the upcoming Mexico City Conference on February 21, the Government aims to discuss the Dumbarton Oaks proposals without making conflicting commitments, and may address the Argentine problem. Similar discussions were held with Latin American Ambassadors in Washington to gather views and support for the proposals.

The Dumbarton Oaks proposals also call for establishing an International Court of Justice with a statute annexed to the Charter, either modifying or replacing the existing Permanent Court of International Justice Statute. Because the existing Court involves states that will not be initial members (including enemy and neutral states), complex problems arise. Since no final agreements were reached regarding a preliminary meeting of jurists to draft the statute, it is recommended that the US, UK, Soviet Union, and China agree to convene about fifteen jurists once United Nations Conference invitations are issued. These jurists should draft a statute based on the current one and propose implementation procedures, leaving the final decision of whether the statute is a revision or new to the Conference.

The NVIDIA A100 Tensor Core GPU, based on the NVIDIA Ampere architecture (GA100) and fabricated on TSMC’s 7nm N7 process, is designed to accelerate AI, high-performance computing (HPC), and data analytics workloads in cloud data centers, servers, and supercomputers. It includes 54.2 billion transistors, 108 Streaming Multiprocessors (SMs), 6,912 FP32 CUDA Cores, and 432 third-generation Tensor Cores. 

Key architectural advancements in the A100 include:
* **Third-Generation Tensor Cores:** These support FP16, INT8, INT4, and Binary data types, while introducing TensorFloat-32 (TF32), Bfloat16 (BF16), and IEEE-compliant FP64 for HPC. TF32 accelerates FP32 data by 10x over the prior Tesla V100 without code changes. A new Fine-Grained Structured Sparsity feature uses a 2:4 sparse matrix definition to skip zero-value computations, doubling Tensor Core compute throughput.
* **Memory Enhancements:** The A100 features 40 GB of HBM2 memory delivering 1555 GB/sec of bandwidth (1.7x higher than V100), a 192 KB combined L1 data cache and shared memory per SM, and a 40 MB L2 cache (nearly 7x larger than V100) with 2.3x the read bandwidth. Compute Data Compression further improves DRAM and L2 bandwidth by up to 4x and L2 capacity by up to 2x.
* **Multi-Instance GPU (MIG):** For optimal utilization and multi-tenant use cases, MIG allows a single physical A100 to be securely partitioned into up to seven isolated GPU Instances, each with dedicated SMs, L2 cache banks, memory controllers, and DRAM address busses to ensure predictable throughput and fault isolation.
* **Interconnects and Hardware Accelerators:** The third-generation NVLink doubles data rates to provide 600 GB/sec of total GPU-to-GPU bandwidth. The A100 also supports PCIe Gen 4 (31.5 GB/sec), SR-IOV, Mellanox InfiniBand/Ethernet, and Magnum IO. Additionally, it features a 5-core hardware JPEG decode engine (NVJPG), an Optical Flow Accelerator, and five NVDEC video decode units.

To support this hardware, CUDA 11 introduces programming advances that reduce latency and software complexity. These include Task Graph Acceleration for faster workflow launches, an Asynchronous Copy instruction that transfers data directly from global to shared memory (bypassing L1 and register files), hardware-accelerated Asynchronous Barriers, L2 Cache Residency Controls for managing persistent data, and hardware-accelerated warp-wide reductions via Cooperative Groups. 

Finally, the NVIDIA DGX A100 system integrates eight A100 GPUs connected via six NVSwitches, eight Mellanox ConnectX-6 HDR InfiniBand adapters, and an optimized software stack. It delivers 5 PFLOPS of AI performance and can be partitioned into up to 56 discrete accelerators using MIG.

Cutaneous leishmaniasis (CL) is caused by intracellular protozoan parasites of the genus *Leishmania*. While immune checkpoints (ICs) like IDO1 and PD-L1 (CD274) regulate T cell function and disease outcomes, their spatial regulation in chronic tissue pathology remains poorly understood. This study combined spatial transcriptomics (10x Visium and Nanostring CosMx) and quantitative immunohistochemistry to define the cellular and transcriptomic niches of IDO1+ and PD-L1+ myeloid cells in tissue biopsies from patients with Sri Lankan CL, Brazilian *L. braziliensis* CL, and Indian post kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis (PKDL). 

In Sri Lankan CL lesions, *IDO1* and *CD274* transcripts localized to the lesion core and deeper T cell-rich dermal regions, predominantly within mature dendritic cells (DC3) and *CCL18*+ macrophages. These niches were enriched with specific cytokines and chemokines, including *CCL18*, *IL24*, *IL1B*, *TNFRSF6B*, *IFNGR2*, *CXCL9*, and *IL32*. Single-cell neighbourhood and image analyses revealed that *IDO1*+ and *CD274*+ myeloid cells closely interact with other myeloid cells, *CD274*-*IDO1*- *CCL18*+ macrophages, regulatory T cells (Tregs), and CD8+ memory T cells, with the majority of CD8+ T cells located within 25 micrometers. CD8+ memory T cells and Tregs were the primary sources of the cytokine *IL32* (specifically the upregulated *IL32γ* and *IL32β* isoforms), while source and neighbouring myeloid cells primarily expressed *CXCL9*, *CCL18*, *IL24*, *IFNGR2*, and *IL1B*. 

Across the Sri Lankan, Brazilian, and Indian cohorts, *IDO1* and *CD274* expression consistently correlated with a core signature of five genes: *IL32*, *LYZ*, *GBP1*, *IFI30*, and *FTH1*. Furthermore, in Sri Lankan CL patients treated with sodium stibogluconate, a low abundance of dermal IL-32+ cells and CD8+IL-32+ T cells was significantly associated with a faster rate of cure, whereas FoxP3+IL-32+ Treg abundance showed no significant difference. The authors propose a model where *CCL18*+ macrophages recruit IL-32+ Tregs and IL-32+ CD8+ T cells, which induce IDO1 and PD-L1 expression on myeloid cells to inhibit effector T cell function and restrain chemotherapy efficacy. Study limitations include restricted biopsy sampling, lack of matched single-cell reference datasets, and the inability to isolate lesional cells for *ex vivo* analysis.

The University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill placed Professor Dwayne Dixon on leave while investigating his alleged advocacy of politically motivated violence, which could lead to his termination. The investigation follows social media posts by Turning Point USA spokesperson Andrew Kolvet. After sharing a photo of a Georgetown University flier for the John Brown Gun Club—an affiliate of the now-disbanded political group Redneck Revolt—that referenced the late Charlie Kirk's suspected killer, Kolvet linked to an article citing Dixon’s past involvement in a Redneck Revolt chapter and called for his firing. 

Dixon, who previously remained employed at UNC despite past blowback and a dismissed arrest related to his armed counterprotest activism, stated he left his Redneck Revolt chapter in 2018. A petition to reinstate Dixon has over 900 signatures, and the local American Association of University Professors condemned UNC's actions as capitulating to right-wing activists. Dixon is among dozens of faculty members investigated, disciplined, or fired after being identified on social media by right-wing personalities following Kirk's shooting death.

Coach Quenneville and Stan Bowman discuss their hockey team's progress, consistency, and upcoming playoff series. Quenneville notes the maturity of his core group, the impact of young players, and the productive playoff performance of "Sharpie." Regarding their opponents, Quenneville highlights their strong positioning, big point shooters, a patient and quick goalie, and the defensive challenge posed by Chara. He also briefly recalls playing for the expansion Spitfires in Windsor and commends Claude's career.

After recently beating Los Angeles, Bowman emphasizes that playoff success relies on incremental improvements, roster continuity, and a total organizational effort. The Bearish Engulfing candlestick pattern is a technical analysis tool that appears in an uptrend and indicates a potential reversal to a downtrend, suggesting sellers have taken control. It consists of a bullish (white) candlestick followed by a larger bearish (black) candlestick whose body completely engulfs the first. In contrast, a bullish engulfing pattern reverses a downtrend with a white candlestick following a black one. Other bearish reversal patterns—like the dark cloud cover, evening star, and bearish harami—indicate weaker bearish sentiment because the black candlestick does not fully engulf the white one.

Traders use this pattern to close long positions, adjust stop-loss orders, or enter short positions (placing a stop-loss above the white candlestick's high). Because the pattern can be subjective and carries risks like false signals, varying market conditions, volatility, and leverage, traders should incorporate risk management. This includes using stop-loss orders, risk/reward ratios, position sizing, diversification, hedging, and a clear risk management plan. 

The pattern is the third most frequent of all 75 candlesticks, appearing 311 times in the S&P 500 since 1993, and has a 55% to 65% win rate in the stock market. Despite its name, the pattern is fairly bullish and often acts as a continuation pattern in the stock market. Traders are advised to backtest strategies and confirm the pattern's validity using market context, momentum changes, and indicators like the RSI or MACD. For example, backtesting shows that filtering S&P trades with a 5-day RSI above 60 increases the average gain per trade from 0.73% to 0.88%.

The 50-day Exponential Moving Average (EMA) strategy is a popular, simple trend-following method used in technical analysis to capture medium-term market trends and generate buy and sell signals. Typically applied to 4-hour or daily charts, an upward-sloping 50 EMA with prices above it indicates an uptrend (prompting long positions), while a downward-sloping line with prices below it signals a downtrend (prompting short positions). Traders often combine the 50 EMA with oscillators and momentum indicators like the RSI or MACD to confirm signals, and may use stop-loss and take-profit orders for risk management, though backtesting shows stop-losses rarely improve strategies. 

Proper backtesting on platforms like Tradestation or Amibroker is necessary to validate the strategy. Backtests of a basic 50 EMA crossover system show poor performance on gold, stocks, bonds, and commodities, though on the S&P 500 it yielded a 6.8% annual return with a lower maximum drawdown (32%) than buy-and-hold (56%). However, using the 50 EMA as a filter alongside a second indicator significantly improves results for stocks. This modified strategy yielded an 11.5% annual return and a 22% maximum drawdown on the QQQ ETF, and an 8.9% annual return with a 16% maximum drawdown on the SPY ETF, despite being invested less than 30% of the time. The same rules also performed decently on long-term Treasury bonds (TLT), averaging a 0.18% gain per trade.

This study examines the characteristics, regulations, and employment patterns of Hungarian higher education lecturers since 1990. Initially, Hungarian higher education expanded, and non-state institutions emerged. However, after 2010, the government reduced state funding, increased tuition, and tightened admission requirements, which decreased student enrollment, froze social mobility, and stagnated the proportion of young graduates well below the EU's 40% target. 

Between 1990 and 2022, lecturer numbers fluctuated. The student-teacher ratio rose from 5.9 in 1990 to 17.9 in 2006, before falling to 10.4 in 2022. Hungary’s teaching staff is older than the developed-country average, though in the middle range internationally, and the share of female lecturers (41.5% in 2020) ranks 80th out of 144 countries.

Historically, a 1951 decree centralized scientific qualifications under the Hungarian Academy of Sciences. Although the 1993 Higher Education Act restored universities' rights to award PhDs and set specific qualification requirements for academic ranks, the Academy still retains its "Doctor of Sciences" degree. Subsequent laws in 2005 and 2011 tightened employment and publication requirements, regulated working hours, and reduced institutional autonomy by introducing government-appointed chancellors. In 2020, the government reorganized 22 state institutions into public foundations run by boards of trustees. This eliminated university autonomy and ended civil service status for employees, though it brought a 70–80% salary increase linked to performance evaluations.

Between 2005 and 2020, the number of university and college professors fell by two-thirds due to retirements, 2011 funding cuts, stricter legal requirements, and low civil servant salaries. Economic analyses show that the lifetime earnings of PhD graduates in Hungarian public academia are significantly lower than those of graduates in the business sector and the national economy average, making academic careers financially unappealing. Finally, Hungary ranks worse than 40th internationally in the number of doctoral students, threatening the future supply of higher education faculty and research performance.

The AMD Secure RNG library provides an easy-to-use API interface to access hardware-generated random numbers found in AMD Zen processors. While hardware RNGs offer more secure and robust values than software generators, accessing them directly via low-level x86 instructions (RDRAND and RDSEED) and memory-mapped I/O (MMIO) can be cumbersome and relatively slow. 

The library abstracts this low-level programming, manages hardware failure checks, allows specified retry attempts, and enables applications to verify hardware support using the CPUID instruction. It exposes various APIs to fetch single 16-bit, 32-bit, or 64-bit random values, arrays of 32-bit or 64-bit values, or arrays of random bytes. 

These random numbers are vital for high-performance computing, gaming, and cryptography. Because reading directly from the cryptographic co-processor via MMIO is slower than software-based pseudo-random number generators (PRNGs), latency-sensitive applications can use a hybrid approach by seeding a software PRNG with a hardware-generated value to improve performance while maintaining higher security.

New research from Emory University suggests that probiotics, already known to benefit the gut, may also protect the liver from drug- and alcohol-induced damage. In a study, mice fed a diet rich in the common probiotic Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG (LGG) for two weeks were given high doses of acetaminophen, which can cause liver-damaging free radicals and oxidative stress. Researchers found that the LGG-fed mice had an improved liver antioxidant response, protecting them from oxidative damage, with a protein called Nrf2 playing a pivotal role in this defense. While these findings show that the benefits of probiotics extend beyond the gastrointestinal tract, further studies are needed to see if the results can be replicated in humans. Probiotics are not a substitute for medicine, and individuals should consult a doctor before taking new supplements.

The 1-2-2 Zone is a strong defense against outside shooting teams, for initiating fast breaks, and for protecting late-game leads. In the basic alignment, the point (X1) is at the top of the circle, wings (X2, X3) are at the elbows, and baseline players (X4, X5) are above the blocks. Defenders must shift while passes are in the air, with baseline players moving in unison and wings working opposite each other. If the ball enters the middle, all defenders collapse on it. 

Variations of the 1-2-2 zone include having the wing either deny the return pass or help on the low post when the ball is in the corner. Other adjustments include trapping the ball handler in the corner, switching to a 2-1-2 zone on the first pass to match a two-guard offensive front, and extending the defense into a half or full-court press.

In resource-limited countries, patients often bypass lower-level health facilities and self-refer to tertiary hospitals, causing overcrowding and inefficiency. At Kenyatta National Hospital (KNH) in Kenya, high bed occupancy in orthopaedic wards and a low nurse-patient ratio have compromised care. To address this and focus on complex medical conditions, KNH enforced the 2014 Kenya Health Sector Referral Guidelines on July 1, 2021, requiring official referral letters and prior concurrence before patient admission. 

A pre-posttest study analyzed 468 orthopaedic and trauma facility referrals to KNH in 2021, comparing five months before (220 referrals) and five months after (248 referrals) the enforcement. Results showed that over four-fifths of referrals originated from Nairobi and its neighboring counties, and about three-fifths came from government facilities. Following enforcement, there was a statistically significant reduction in direct referrals from lower-level (Tier II and III) facilities and an increase in referrals from higher-level (Tier IV, V, and VI) facilities. Additionally, 43 health facilities—over two-thirds of which were private and over four-fifths of which were Tiers II to IV—stopped referring patients to KNH altogether. 

The primary factors driving referrals to KNH across both public and private facilities were inadequate human resource capacity, lack of medical supplies and orthopaedic equipment, financial considerations, and infrastructure limitations. Patient preference was also a major factor for private facility referrals. The study concludes that enforcing referral guidelines successfully reduces lower-tier referrals. It recommends that policymakers, KNH, and health facilities strengthen human resource capacity, develop standard operating procedures, and continuously sensitize staff and facilities to adhere to the national referral guidelines.

New NVIDIA shading advancements include Mesh Shading, VRS, Texture-Space Shading, and Multi-View Rendering (MVR). Mesh shading moves object list processing from the CPU to the GPU, supporting more objects and new algorithms. VRS dynamically controls shading rates to improve efficiency and frame rates. Texture-space shading caches results in memory to eliminate duplicate work or improve quality. Finally, MVR extends Single Pass Stereo by rendering multiple views from different origins or directions in a single pass.

This paper reflects on how the changing context caused by the COVID-19 pandemic can reposition and reinvigorate the field of Comparative and International Education in 2023. The United Nations' 2015 Sustainable Development Goals (specifically Goal 4) and the Incheon Declaration established a global vision for inclusive, equitable, quality education by 2030. However, even before 2020, global education showed massive shortfalls in quantitative participation, quality (input, process, output, and product), and equality. 

The 2020 COVID-19 outbreak caused further deterioration. School closures affected 91% of the global student population, and the shift to online distance learning ended educational opportunities for many, negatively impacted quality, and exacerbated existing inequalities, particularly for disadvantaged learners. Conversely, the pandemic forced the conservative education sector to embrace technology. 

Because educational strategies must fit their societal contexts to succeed, scholars of Comparative and International Education should assess how different systems used technology to address pandemic disruptions. This effort can generate recommendations for achieving the 2030 goals while also addressing the field's own deficiencies, which include unresponsiveness to new vistas, the "black box syndrome," a lack of autochthonous theory, inadequate university presence, Northern Hegemony, and a lack of demonstrable impact. Ultimately, the field is pivotal in helping education recover and build better systems toward the 2030 goals.

Texas Tech University officials recently posted and then removed a frequently asked questions page after three days without explanation. The FAQ was the first written clarification regarding new policies prohibiting faculty from speaking or teaching about transgender identity. The guidance, which applied only to the flagship campus, stated that the directives affect instruction rather than independent research. It advised faculty against mentioning personal pronouns or LGBTQ allyship on syllabi, though preferred name policies and neutral classroom discussions on gender views were permitted. 

The American Association of University Professors has pushed back against these policies. Meanwhile, faculty at the Texas Tech University Health Sciences Center received no written guidance, only conflicting verbal instructions to avoid terms like "transgender" and "gender-affirming care." Health-care instructors are concerned because caring for transgender patients is required for student certification exams, and they remain unsure how to address student questions on the topic.

In *Closson v. Billman et al.*, the appellant sought to foreclose a material man’s lien for $863.35 worth of lumber furnished to a contractor, Levi A. Worley, for the construction of a house on a lot owned by appellee Marie E. Billman. The appellees defended by showing that Worley was contractually obligated to furnish and pay for the materials, and that the appellant had co-signed a $1,500 bond guaranteeing Worley's performance of the contract. Because Worley breached the contract by failing to pay for the lumber and permitting a lien to be filed, the appellant became liable on the bond for the unpaid amount. 

The court affirmed the lower court's judgment for the appellees, ruling that the bond and contract must be construed together and required the contractor to deliver the house free of material liens. By signing the bond, the appellant acted as a guarantor and was liable for the contractor's default. To avoid a circuity of action, the appellant's liability on the bond served as a sufficient defense against his suit to foreclose the lien. Furthermore, notice of acceptance of the guaranty was unnecessary because it was executed contemporaneously with the contract, and the burden was on the guarantor to plead and prove any damages resulting from a lack of notice of default.

This passage is the June 7, 2001 issue of the VentureWire newsletter, sent to jdasovic@enron.com, detailing venture capital, technology, and business news. 

**Top Stories:**
* FreeMarkets and Adexa terminated their $340M acquisition agreement; FreeMarkets will instead take a $6M, 3% stake in Adexa.
* inVentures and Redwood Partners merged to form Redwood Partners International, which is raising a $100M fund.
* ChipData closed a $23M second round of funding.

The present disclosure relates to systems, methods, devices, and computer-readable media for route planning for transportation vehicles, such as automated guided vehicles (AGVs), based on a map (e.g., a topological map). Conventional route planning can be negatively affected in accuracy and efficiency when the motion of other vehicles impacts node information. To address this and prevent collisions, the disclosed systems and methods incorporate motion status information of other vehicles.

The route planning system (or scheduling system) may include a server, a network, vehicles, terminal devices, and a storage device. A processing device within the system includes modules for obtaining locations, maps, and motion statuses, as well as a route determination module. The system can also allocate specified or unspecified tasks to vehicles based on whether they are in an idle (schedulable) or non-idle (non-schedulable) state.

The route planning method involves obtaining a map of a target region containing a plurality of nodes and their associated node information (e.g., location, barcode, serial number, weight value, passability, turn capability, count of adjacent nodes, and connectivity). The system obtains a start location and a destination for a target vehicle, along with the motion status information (static or moving status) and occupied nodes of other vehicles in the region. 

The system preprocesses the map by modifying the node information based on the other vehicles' motion statuses to generate a modified (or target) map. This preprocessing can be performed in two stages, either separately or collectively:
1. First preprocessing: For static vehicles, the system modifies the node information of nodes within a preset region centered on each static vehicle (e.g., by assigning high weight values and setting them as incapable of turning) to generate a first modified map. 
2. Second preprocessing: If a planned route based on the first modified map overlaps with the route of a moving vehicle (indicating a potential collision), the system performs a second preprocessing. This modifies the node information for static vehicles (e.g., setting nodes within the preset region as impassable barriers) and for moving vehicles (e.g., assigning high weight values to unpassed nodes on their planned routes) to generate a second modified map.

Using the modified map, the system determines a start node and a destination node (selecting the nearest available nodes that are not barriers or occupied by other vehicles). If the start or destination node is determined to be a barrier, the route planning fails, or a next-nearest available node may be selected. 

To determine the target route, the system iteratively calculates the total costs of nodes between the start and destination nodes using a route planning algorithm (such as A-star, Dijkstra, or others) and open/closed sets with a binary heap structure. The total cost of a node is the sum of the cost from the start/current node to the node and the cost from the node to the destination node (calculated using Manhattan or Euclidean distance). The cost from the current/parent node to the node is determined using the node's weight value, the parent node's cost, the distance cost between the parent node and the node, and the turn cost between them. The system sequentially selects nodes with the minimum total cost until the destination node is reached, thereby establishing a collision-free route.

Prior to being adjudged a voluntary bankrupt in November 1915, W. T. Hay conveyed real estate to his brother, who then conveyed an interest in it to Hay's wife, Matilda M. Hay. At the time, Hay was indebted to the Deposit National Bank, which entered a judgment against him in July 1915. Following Hay’s discharge from his debts in June 1916, the bank issued an execution on its prior judgment and directed the sheriff to levy upon the real estate conveyed to Hay's wife, alleging the conveyance was made to defraud creditors. Hay petitioned to permanently stay the writ of execution due to his bankruptcy discharge. The lower court stayed the writ personally against Hay, except as to the real estate levied upon. Hay appealed this refusal. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal at the appellant's costs, ruling that because Hay does not own or claim the property, his rights are entirely unaffected by the sheriff's sale, leaving him with no standing to appeal or raise questions regarding the bank's right to proceed.

Following the failures of two previous U.S. women’s professional soccer leagues, the Women’s United Soccer Association (WUSA) and the Women’s Professional Soccer League (WPS), the National Women’s Soccer League (NWSL) was established in 2012. To ensure stability, it was structured as a single entity and initially backed by the United States Soccer Federation (U.S. Soccer), which managed the front office and paid the salaries of allocated U.S. Women’s National Team (USWNT) players. The Canadian Soccer Association and Mexican Football Federation also initially funded allocated players. Despite the USWNT's international success and a high-profile equal pay lawsuit against U.S. Soccer, the NWSL faced ongoing challenges, including low media coverage, varied game attendance, and low compensation for non-allocated players, who formed a union (NWSLPA) in 2017. However, the league possessed a passionate, online-oriented fan base and secured new broadcast and streaming agreements with CBS and Twitch in March 2020.

On March 10, 2020, Lisa Baird, a marketing executive with experience at the NFL and the United States Olympic and Paralympic Committee, began her tenure as NWSL commissioner. Just two days into her role, the COVID-19 pandemic forced the cancellation of NWSL preseason matches. Concerned that canceling the entire season would threaten the eight-year-old league's survival, Baird organized specialized workstreams involving staff, owners, medical professionals, and the NWSLPA to safely return to play. The league secured a Paycheck Protection Program loan to cover player salaries and added Google, Verizon, and P&G/Secret as new sponsors, joining existing sponsors Nike and Budweiser.

Consequently, the NWSL became the first U.S. professional team sport to return to play by hosting the Challenge Cup from June 27 to July 26, 2020, in a quarantined "bubble" in Utah. Eight of the nine teams participated, as the Orlando Pride withdrew due to COVID-19 cases. During the tournament, the league supported players' social justice initiatives, including supporting the Black Lives Matter movement and kneeling during the national anthem. The Challenge Cup cost $1.8 million, resulted in zero positive COVID-19 tests out of over 2,000 conducted, and set league television viewership records on CBS. Following this success, Baird capitalized on postponed college football broadcast slots to organize a regional "Fall Series" from September to October 2020, though several USWNT and non-allocated players opted out or went to play in Europe. Overall, the NWSL's 2020 television viewership increased by 493% over 2019, and social and traditional media mentions rose significantly.

Entering 2021, Baird and the NWSL faced several strategic priorities and challenges:
*   **Fan Engagement and Exposure:** Converting casual viewers into avid fans, expanding international reach, and securing consistent mainstream media coverage.
*   **Expansion and Investment:** Integrating new teams in Louisville, Kansas City, Los Angeles (Angel City FC), and Sacramento, alongside an influx of high-profile female investors.
*   **Governance:** Defining a new relationship with U.S. Soccer following the federation's official management separation from the league in December 2020.
*   **Compensation and Labor:** Managing increased allocation money—which allowed teams like the Portland Thorns to sign USWNT players directly—and negotiating a collective bargaining agreement with the NWSLPA.
*   **Rebranding and Social Justice:** Developing a new league brand for its 10th anniversary in 2022 and continuing to lead on social justice issues.

This study investigates the structural, optical, and electrical properties of undoped and copper-doped nickel oxide (NiO:Cu) thin films synthesized on ITO-coated glass substrates via an ultra-fast spray pyrolysis technique at 450 °C with a 1.5-minute deposition time. The gas sensing performance of the films was evaluated using approximately 1 vol% liquefied petroleum gas (LPG). 

X-ray diffraction (XRD) confirmed a cubic crystal structure for both films and indicated successful Cu incorporation without changing the crystal structure. Due to the larger ionic radius of Cu2+ compared to Ni2+, doping caused the lattice parameter to expand from 4.18 to 4.20 Å, interplanar spacing to increase from 2.41 to 2.42 Å, and crystallite size to decrease from 21 to 20 nm. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) of the NiO film showed well-dispersed cuboidal or polyhedral crystalline grains alongside some smoother, potentially amorphous regions.

Optically, UV-Vis spectroscopy showed that Cu doping enhanced visible spectrum absorbance (400–800 nm) and reduced the direct optical bandgap from 3.70 eV to 3.65 eV. Raman spectroscopy further confirmed lattice distortion and defect formation, evidenced by the disappearance of the TO mode and red shifts in the LO, 2TO, and 2LO vibrational modes. Photoluminescence (PL) spectra showed strong emission bands for both films, including a near-infrared peak at 881 nm attributed to deep-level defect transitions, as well as bands associated with nickel and oxygen vacancies. However, NiO:Cu exhibited significant PL intensity quenching, peak broadening, and red shifts, indicating increased defect density and non-radiative recombination centers.

Electrically, both films demonstrated p-type semiconducting behavior. Upon exposure to LPG at a 5 V bias, the current increased from 249 to 327 mA for pure NiO, and from 265 to 480 mA for NiO:Cu. Resistance decreased upon gas exposure, with ∆R values of 4 Ω for NiO and 8 Ω for NiO:Cu. The NiO:Cu film outperformed undoped NiO in gas sensitivity across all applied voltages above 1 V, achieving a sensitivity of 1.8 at 5 V compared to 1.3 for pure NiO. Overall, the structural disorder, narrowed bandgap, and increased defect density induced by Cu doping improved charge transport, surface reactivity, and adsorption sites, making NiO:Cu an effective material for gas sensor applications.

This passage details the technical specifications, build environments, and execution procedures for AMD's AGESA software.

**Modules and Build Environment**
Various PPIs, PEIMs, HOBs, and DXE drivers manage processor core, memory, and late initialization, warm resets, data tables, and iGPU VGA decoding. Building AGESA core files uses either Binary Modules or Source Integration. It requires specific reference and control files (e.g., `<Plat>Options.c`, `.inf` files) and setting environment variables like `AGESA_ROOT` and `AGESA_OptsDir` for targeted platform solutions.

**Stack Procedures**
Native assembly macros establish or remove the pre-memory Cache-As-Ram (CAR) stack for x86-64 APUs (AARCH64 APUs with PSP initialize DRAM via PSP instead). Key macros include `AMD_RESET_ENABLEMENT` for early critical settings, `AMD_ENABLE_UEFI_STACK` to allocate core stack regions, and a procedure to disable CAR mode once main memory is available.

**Service Procedures**
Helper functions assist the host environment. These include `AmdCreateStruct` and `AmdReleaseStruct` for parameter block storage allocation, `AmdReadEventLog` for reading circular buffer error logs, and routines to obtain DIMM data eye bitmaps, APIC addresses, pre-memory execution cache sizes, base PCI addresses, current core IDs, FRU memory device IDs, and MMIO address mappings.

**Entry Procedures**
Executed in time-point order by the BSP and APs:
*   **AmdInitReset:** Performs minimal processor initialization and sets up to three flash ROM execution cache regions after reset.
*   **AmdInitEarly:** Performs full processor, HyperTransport, power management, VRM, and PCIe/GNB initialization before main memory setup.
*   **AmdInitPost:** Locates, trains, and initializes main system memory, transitioning from pre-memory to post-memory phase and disabling the pre-memory stack.
*   **AmdInitEnv:** Closes pre-memory operations, configures display/LVDS and FCH settings, and moves temporary HOB artifact data into permanent memory buffers.
*   **Graphics Configuration:** Configures display hardware after PCI enumeration.
*   **AmdInitLate:** Generates OS informational data tables (DMI, ACPI PState, WHEA, ALIB, IVRS, CRAT, CDIT) before OS boot.
*   **Suspend and Resume:** `AmdInitRtb` saves critical registers to volatile and non-volatile storage for S3 suspend. `AmdInitResume` and subsequent restoration procedures re-initialize silicon and memory and reload registers prior to OS restart.

**Required Call-Outs**
The host environment must implement specific call-out functions for AGESA to operate: `AgesaAllocateBuffer`, `AgesaDeallocateBuffer`, and a buffer locator for post-memory buffer management; a function to initiate cold or warm system resets; `AgesaReadSpd` to read 256-byte DIMM SPD data over the SMBus (not used by newer PSP-equipped APUs); and a dispatcher to execute code on specific or all Application Processors.

Academic achievement in postsecondary health professions education (HPE), including occupational therapy (OT), is often negatively impacted by students' previous or ongoing exposure to trauma and adverse childhood experiences (ACEs). Trauma can impair cognitive, social, and behavioral functioning, disrupting daily routines, attendance, and academic performance, and increasing dropout risks. Furthermore, healthcare students face risks of secondary traumatic stress and vicarious trauma during their training. 

To support students and prevent re-traumatization, HPE and OT programs can adopt the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration’s (SAMHSA) Trauma-Informed Care (TIC) framework. This approach relies on four foundational assumptions (realization, recognition, responding, and resisting re-traumatization), six core principles (safety, trustworthiness/transparency, peer support, collaboration, empowerment, and cultural/historical/gender sensitivity), and ten implementation domains. 

Implementing TIC in higher education requires engagement from leadership, faculty, staff, and students. Effective strategies and interventions include:
*   **Faculty Development:** Pursuing trauma-informed training and utilizing reflection tools or validated scales (like the ARTIC) to assess TIC knowledge and attitudes.
*   **Classroom and Pedagogical Practices:** Providing advance notice of triggering content, conducting emotional check-ins, teaching and modeling self-care, utilizing constructivist pedagogies, maintaining predictable routines, and ensuring culturally inclusive, safe environments.
*   **Curricular Integration:** Embedding TIC and ACEs education early and throughout programs. Simulation-based training, such as the PATH model, has been shown to significantly increase OT students' knowledge and self-efficacy regarding ACEs and TIC.
*   **Student Support Services:** Offering peer-led support groups, trauma-informed referral networks, and peer health and wellness coaching to build resilience and healthy coping strategies.

Although fields like nursing and social work have established TIC competencies, OT education currently lags in including trauma content in its curricula. Adopting TIC strategies in OT programs can make students feel supported and engaged in the short term, while improving retention, graduation rates, and compassionate, client-centered care in the long term.

Researchers created human egg cells from adult skin cells in a proof-of-concept study that could eventually help treat infertility or allow same-sex male couples to have genetically related children. The team replaced a human egg cell's nucleus with a fibroblast skin cell nucleus. Because the resulting cell already contained 46 chromosomes instead of the 23 needed for an egg, researchers fertilized it and added the molecule roscovitine to coax the cell into expelling half its chromosomes. 

While some fertilized eggs developed into early embryos, none were allowed to grow past six days. Ultimately, none of the embryos were viable because random chromosome pairing resulted in abnormal chromosome sets. Additionally, the method requires donor eggs, is currently too risky and inefficient for clinical use, and is at least a decade away from clinical trials. However, it marks a significant breakthrough in halving the human genome.

The expanded use of malaria rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) detecting *Plasmodium falciparum* histidine-rich proteins 2 and 3 (PfHRP2/3) is threatened by an increase in *pfhrp2/3* gene deletions, which cause false-negative results. Because alternative RDTs have lower sensitivity or lack WHO prequalification for specific combination needs, most countries rely on PfHRP2-based RDTs, making the spread of deleted strains a growing public health crisis. 

This study uses an individual-based mathematical model and recent data to assess the global risk and predict the spread of *pfhrp2/3* deletions, focusing on sub-Saharan Africa. The model incorporates multiple risk factors, including malaria prevalence, microscopy use, treatment-seeking rates, private sector care, diagnostic test usage, RDT nonadherence, RDT brands, PfHRP3 cross-reactivity, and parasite fitness costs. Using WHO Malaria Threat Maps data, the authors estimated that 63.5% of *pfhrp2*-deleted samples globally (and 61.2% in Africa) also had *pfhrp3* deletions, indicating strong positive linkage. By fitting the model to data from Eritrea and Ethiopia, the relative fitness of *pfhrp2*-deleted parasites was estimated at 96.4%, and the probability of HRP3 cross-reactivity yielding a positive test in *pfhrp2*-deleted/*pfhrp3*-intact infections was estimated at 29.0%. Across simulations, malaria prevalence was the most important determinant of selection, with lower prevalence increasing selection pressure. 

The authors developed two risk metrics based on the WHO threshold for switching RDTs (when 5% of clinically relevant infections are misdiagnosed due to deletions):
1. **Innate Risk Score:** Evaluates the time for misdiagnosed clinical cases to rise from 1% to 5%, assuming exclusive use of HRP2-based RDTs. Globally, 73 of 106 modelled countries have at least one region predicted to reach the 5% threshold within 20 years. Twenty countries (17 in Africa) have a majority of regions classified as High Innate Risk (reaching 5% within 6 years). The highest-risk areas have very low transmission, while high-prevalence regions in Central and Western Africa face low risk (exceeding 40 years to reach 5%).
2. **Prospective Risk Score:** Models the continued spread of deletions across Africa based on current WHO prevalence estimates (assuming 0% in unsurveyed countries), current RDT types used, and parasite movement between neighbouring regions once prevalence hits 25%. This model predicts 29 of 49 African countries will have at least one region reach the 5% threshold within 20 years, spreading south from the Horn of Africa through East Africa, and increasing in West Africa (notably Senegal and Mali). 

Countries identified as majority High Risk across both scores include Djibouti, Eritrea, Ethiopia, Senegal, Zambia, and Kenya. Study limitations include simplistic modelling of geographic spread, high parameter uncertainty (especially regarding malaria prevalence), assumptions that prevalence, treatment, and genetic linkage remain constant, and an inability to capture non-RDT-driven emergence, as seen in South America. Nevertheless, these risk maps and the accompanying interactive tool can help policymakers prioritize surveillance and deploy alternative RDTs.

A new study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences suggests that the brain chemical dopamine plays a key role in the mother-child bond. Researchers studied 19 mothers and their babies by video-recording their interactions and performing brain scans on the mothers as they watched videos of their own and other infants. 

The results showed that mothers secreted more dopamine when watching their own babies. Mothers with higher dopamine secretion were more sensitive to their infants' needs and provided better care, whereas less responsive mothers secreted less dopamine. Researchers believe this process likely continues as children grow, supports other close relationships, and aids infant brain development. However, further research is needed to see if non-biological caregivers experience similar dopamine boosts. This lecture explores the mechanics of protein folding by modeling protein backbones as fixed-angle linkages, where edge lengths and angles remain static, and movement is restricted to spinning around edges. The professor examines four main mathematical problems related to these models:

1. **Span:** Determining the minimum and maximum distance between a chain's endpoints. Finding the min or max span for a flat state (2D) is NP-hard, proven by reducing from the partition problem. In 3D, the general problem remains open, though the maximum span for orthogonal chains (90-degree angles) can be solved in linear time.
2. **Flattening:** Determining whether a fixed-angle chain can be configured in a 2D plane without self-intersection. This problem is also proven to be NP-hard.
3. **Flat State Connectivity:** Determining if all flat states of a chain are in a single connected component, allowing transformation from one flat state to another via 3D motions without self-intersection. While the general problem for open chains is open, chains with orthogonal, obtuse, or equal acute angles are proven to be flat state connected. Conversely, certain partially rigid fixed-angle trees are flat state disconnected, which can be proven using knot theory. 
4. **Locked Chains:** Determining if a chain is stuck in a disconnected configuration. While equilateral and equiangular fixed-angle chains can be locked, it remains an open problem whether a chain that is simultaneously equilateral, equiangular, and obtuse—properties closely matching real proteins—can be locked. 

Finally, the lecture introduces "producible protein chains," which models how the ribosome creates proteins link-by-link. By treating the ribosome as a giant obstacle (modeled geometrically as a cone with a half-angle $\alpha$), the chain is restricted from intersecting itself or the cone as it emerges. Using this constraint, any producible configuration can be folded backward into a helix-like canonical configuration inside a smaller cone of half-angle $\alpha/2$. Because all flat states are also producible from this cone, all producible configurations and flat states exist within one connected component. This proves that producible chains are flat state connected and cannot be locked, offering a candidate mechanical algorithm for how nature folds proteins.

Gas colic is a common equine condition that occurs when gas—a normal byproduct of hindgut plant fermentation—fails to pass through the large colon, potentially causing complications like colon displacement or twisting. Primary causes include stress, dehydration, ulcers, inflammation, sudden feed changes, limited forage, and stall confinement. Restricting forage disrupts digestion, alters hormones, causes ulcers, and prompts horses to gorge, leading to undigested feed and excess gas. Confinement reduces the hindgut motility needed to expel gas, while stress increases inflammation and colic risk. 

To prevent gas colic, horses require 24-hour forage access, which can be managed using constantly full slow feeders to help them self-regulate. Pasture or outdoor turnout is recommended to reduce stress and improve blood circulation and motility. Any hay or feed changes should be made gradually over one to three weeks, and inconsistent meals like weekly bran mashes should be avoided. Owners should also avoid inflammatory commercial feed ingredients like sugar, soy, and preservatives. Additionally, supplements such as prebiotics, B vitamins, yeast, and colostrum can support digestive health, heal ulcers, and reduce stress.

The NVIDIA Turing GPU architecture (including the TU102, TU104, and TU106 GPUs) introduces major advancements in memory, display, rendering, and AI capabilities compared to the prior Pascal generation. 

**Memory, Display, and Connectivity**
Turing is the first GPU architecture to use GDDR6 memory, delivering 14 Gbps signaling rates and a 20% power efficiency improvement over GDDR5X. Combined with larger L2 caches and improved lossless memory compression, Turing achieves a 50% increase in effective bandwidth over Pascal. The new display engine supports DisplayPort 1.4a, native HDR with tone mapping, and dual 8K displays at 60 Hz. Updated NVENC and NVDEC units improve video encoding and decoding, enabling 4K streaming and 8K HEVC encoding. For VR headsets, Turing introduces hardware support for USB Type-C and VirtualLink, consolidating power, display, and data into a single cable. Additionally, TU102 and TU104 GPUs replace the traditional SLI bridge with second-generation NVLink for faster GPU-to-GPU data transfers (TU106 does not support NVLink or SLI).

**Real-Time Ray Tracing and Hybrid Rendering**
Historically, real-time rendering relied on rasterization because ray tracing was too computationally intensive for a single GPU. Turing enables real-time ray tracing through a "Hybrid Rendering" model that combines rasterization, ray tracing, and AI. Each Streaming Multiprocessor (SM) includes a dedicated RT Core that autonomously accelerates Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH) tree traversal and ray-triangle intersection testing. This offloads the SM and allows Turing to process ray tracing 10 times faster than Pascal. Combined with AI and non-AI denoising filters—which reduce the number of rays required per pixel—Turing renders physically accurate shadows, ambient occlusion, and reflections in real time. 

**AI and Neural Graphics Acceleration (NGX)**
Turing utilizes Tensor Cores to power NVIDIA NGX, a deep learning technology stack exclusive to Turing. NGX features include:
*   **Deep Learning Super-Sampling (DLSS):** Trained on 64x supersampled reference images, DLSS infers high-quality images from lower input sample counts with half the shading work of Temporal Anti-Aliasing (TAA), helping the RTX 2080 Ti achieve twice the performance of the GTX 1080 Ti. A "DLSS 2X" mode is also available for higher fidelity.
*   **InPainting:** Removes unwanted objects from images and synthesizes new content to fill the gap.
*   **AI Slow-Mo:** Inserts interpolated frames into video streams for smooth slow-motion.
*   **AI Super Rez:** Upscales images or videos by 2x, 4x, or 8x by intelligently creating new pixels.

**Advanced Shading Technologies**
Turing introduces several new shading capabilities to optimize compute workloads and support VR:
*   **Mesh Shading:** Introduces cooperative Task and Mesh Shaders to process object lists in parallel, eliminating CPU draw-call bottlenecks and managing Levels of Detail (LOD).
*   **Variable Rate Shading (VRS):** Allows developers to dynamically adjust shading rates in 16x16 pixel regions. It supports Content Adaptive Shading (lowering rates in low-detail areas), Motion Adaptive Shading (lowering rates on fast-moving objects), and Foveated Rendering (lowering rates in the viewer's peripheral vision).
*   **Texture Space Shading (TSS):** Decouples visibility and appearance sampling by shading in a separate texture space, allowing shaded texels to be reused across frames or stereo VR views.
*   **Multi-View Rendering (MVR):** Expands Pascal's Simultaneous Multi-Projection to support up to four views per pass, improving efficiency for wide-FOV and canted VR headsets. 

**GPU Implementations and Metrics**
The TU104 GPU (3,072 CUDA Cores, 368 Tensor Cores, 48 RT Cores) powers the GeForce RTX 2080, Quadro RTX 5000, and the data-center-focused Tesla T4 (which uses a 40-SM configuration). The TU106 GPU (2,304 CUDA Cores, 288 Tensor Cores, 36 RT Cores) powers the GeForce RTX 2070. To measure performance across Turing's varied workloads (Tensor, FP32, RT, and concurrent INT32 operations), NVIDIA introduced the RTX-OPS metric, which weights peak operations based on their percentage of use during a frame time. The document concludes with standard legal disclaimers, warranty limitations, and trademark notices from NVIDIA.

In *People v Helzer*, the defendant was convicted by the same jury of two counts of gross indecency and of being a sexually delinquent person, which carries a potential sentence of one day to life imprisonment. At trial, the defendant was allowed five peremptory challenges—the number appropriate for the gross indecency charge—and was denied his request for 20 challenges based on the potential life sentence. The Court of Appeals reversed and ordered a new trial on all charges, finding the defendant was entitled to 20 challenges.

Upon appeal, the Court ruled that sexual delinquency is not merely a penalty enhancement, but a separate, alternate sentencing provision originally tied to a broader statutory scheme of mental health rehabilitation. Because the sexual delinquency hearing involves broad jury discretion, psychiatric testimony, and a high risk of prejudice if heard by the original jury, the Court held that a separate second jury must be empaneled immediately after conviction on the principal charge, unless waived by the defendant. 

For the initial jury hearing the principal charge, a defendant is only entitled to the peremptory challenges appropriate for that offense. Furthermore, the first jury must not learn of the sexual delinquency charge; if it does, it is grounds for a mistrial or reversible error. For the second jury deciding sexual delinquency, the defendant is entitled to 20 peremptory challenges due to the possible life sentence. Additionally, the prosecutor must bring the sexual delinquency charge in the original indictment or by amendment prior to the start of the trial on the principal charge, or the opportunity is waived.

Finding no error in the trial of the principal charge, the Court affirmed the defendant's gross indecency convictions, reversed the order for an entirely new trial, and remanded the case for a hearing on the sexual delinquency charge before a separately empaneled jury where the defendant is accorded 20 peremptory challenges. The Court declined to consider the defendant's constitutional claims at this time. Chief Justice Kavanagh dissented, stating the sexual delinquency statute is unconstitutional and void for vagueness.

Quantum spin relaxation in chemical systems, particularly radical pair spin relaxation dynamics, is central to applications in quantum computing, spintronics, and quantum biophysics. A typical radical pair consists of two unpaired electrons interacting with surrounding nuclear spins under external magnetic fields. Modelling these systems presents three main computational challenges: ensemble averaging for randomly oriented initial nuclear spins, the exponential growth of Hilbert and Liouville space dimensions, and long-time propagation for relaxation processes (1 ns to 1 µs). While various classical and stochastic approaches exist to address these issues, quantitative accuracy across diverse systems requires a full quantum-mechanical treatment, which tensor network methods can provide by tackling exponential complexity. 

This work aims to introduce recent tensor-network methods to spin chemistry, clarify the radical-pair problem's challenges for the physics community, and showcase avian magnetoreception. The radical pair Hamiltonian includes Zeeman, hyperfine, exchange, dipolar, and Haberkorn relaxation terms, with electronic state populations serving as typical observables. To model radical pair mixed states, three tensor network methods are introduced. First, stochastic matrix product states (MPS) reduce wavefunction elements from exponential scale to $O(Ndm^2)$ and use spin-coherent state sampling for Monte Carlo integration. Second, the matrix product density operator (MPDO) formalism deterministically evaluates observables without stochastic sampling, reducing matrix elements to $O(Nd^2\chi^2)$. This is explored via a locally purified MPS representation (LPMPS) and a direct vectorisation (vMPDO), which reshapes the MPDO into an MPS-like structure in twin space.

The American Cancer Society (ACS) has updated its guidelines to recommend that average-risk adults begin regular colorectal cancer (CRC) screening at age 45 instead of 50. This update stems from a 51% increase in CRC incidence among adults under 50 since 1994, rising mortality rates in younger populations, and modeling that demonstrates a favorable benefit-to-burden ratio when starting at age 45. 

Screening for ages 45 to 49 is a "qualified recommendation" due to less direct evidence in this group, whereas screening for ages 50 and older is a "strong recommendation." Healthy adults with a life expectancy over 10 years should continue screening through age 75. Clinicians should individualize decisions for ages 76 to 85 and discourage screening for those over 85. 

To improve screening rates and accommodate patient preferences, the ACS endorses six stool-based or visual test options (FIT, HSgFOBT, mt-sDNA, colonoscopy, CTC, and FS) at intervals ranging from one to ten years without prioritizing any specific test. All positive non-colonoscopy results require a timely follow-up colonoscopy. Lowering the starting age addresses persistent elevated risks in younger cohorts and is expected to benefit both average-risk adults and disproportionately affected groups, including blacks, Alaska Natives, and American Indians.

Standard diagnosis for intracranial space occupying lesions (ICSOL) relies on invasive tissue biopsies, which carry procedural risks. Since approximately 70% of ICSOLs are benign, a non-invasive diagnostic method is beneficial. This study evaluates a minimally invasive, blood-based test to detect primary glial malignancies (GLI-M) and differentiate them from benign brain tumors (BBT), non-glial central nervous system malignancies (NGCM), and epithelial malignancies (EPI-M) with brain metastases. 

The test uses a proprietary medium to enrich circulating glial cells (CGCs) from peripheral blood, identifying them via immunocytochemistry (ICC) profiling based on GFAP and OLIG2 co-expression. Analytical validation using spiked blood samples established that samples can be stored for up to 48 hours at 2°C–8°C with ≤15% cell loss. The test demonstrated a limit of detection of 1 cell/5 mL, an overall limit of quantitation of 6 cells/5 mL, and was unaffected by interfering substances. Analytical sensitivity was 92.5% for GFAP and 95.0% for OLIG2, with 100% specificity. 

Clinical performance was evaluated across four studies:
* **Case Control Study-1 (189 samples):** The test Set achieved 100% sensitivity and 100% specificity in differentiating GLI-M from BBT.
* **Case Control Study-2 (586 samples):** Using GFAP, OLIG2, and PanCK markers, the test differentiated GLI-M, BBT, EPI-M, and healthy individuals with 100% sensitivity and 100% specificity for CGC detection.
* **Prospective Study-1 (68 ICSOL patients):** The test showed 100% sensitivity and 100% specificity in differentiating GLI-M from BBT.
* **Prospective Study-2 (31 intra-axial ICSOL patients):** Evaluating GLI-M, BBT, and NGCM, the test achieved 92.9% sensitivity and 100% specificity.

Additionally, orthogonal verification using FISH on 44 matched blood and tissue samples showed 100% concordance for EGFR gene amplification. 

Overall, the clinical validation demonstrated >99% sensitivity and 100% specificity for GLI-M detection. While the test detects common subtypes accounting for 97% of GLI-M, it does not detect rarer subtypes like CNS lymphoma and gliosarcoma, nor does it differentiate tumor grade or subtype. The study was funded by Datar Cancer Genetics Private Limited, which employs several of the authors.

Panic disorder affects two to three percent of Americans. Unlike persistent anxiety, a panic attack is an intense burst of fear typically peaking at 10 minutes and lasting under 30 minutes. Anyone can experience a triggered panic attack, whereas panic disorder attacks occur without an obvious environmental cause. 

Mental health professionals recommend several techniques to manage panic attacks:
* **Know the signs:** Learn the physiological and psychological symptoms—such as a pounding heart, shortness of breath, dizziness, and fear of dying—and get a physical exam to rule out other issues.
* **Keep written reminders:** Carry an index card or phone note stating that panic attacks are not life-threatening, along with positive mantras to counter catastrophic thoughts.
* **Visualize a wave:** Picture panic sensations as temporary waves that will crest and pass.
* **Use smartphone distractions:** Play word games, listen to relaxing music, or use guided relaxation sessions to distract from unpleasant symptoms.
* **Practice deep breathing:** Practice daily full-body breathing—inhaling deeply through the nose and exhaling slowly through the mouth—to effectively slow your heart rate and calm down during an attack.

Using data from a subsample of 1,190 households in the 2019 National Survey of Early Care and Education (NSECE) Household Survey, this study explores Child Care and Early Education (CCEE) search patterns for children under age 6 not yet in kindergarten. The analytic sample included households that conducted a CCEE search within the past 24 months and considered more than one provider. Compared to the overall population, the analytic sample had higher incomes, was more likely to have two working parents, and was more likely to speak only English. 

Researchers used Latent Class Analysis (LCA) to identify distinct search types based on families' reported use of up to two information sources out of five potential options. About half of the sample reported using one source, and half used two. Five common search types emerged, categorized by their top two sources: 
1. Search Type 1: Child Care Resource & Referral (CCR&R) agencies or friends/family.
2. Search Type 2: Internet search or social media.
3. Search Type 3: Known providers or friends/family.
4. Search Type 4: Social media or friends/family.
5. Search Type 5: Friends/family or internet search.

Using logistic and multinomial logistic regression analyses, researchers examined whether search types varied by the specific information sought (out of seven options) and by family or child characteristics. Most variables showed no relationship to search types, with three statistically significant exceptions:
* Information Sought: Search Type 1 was more likely, and Search Type 2 was less likely, to include families looking for information on "type of care" compared to Search Type 5.
* Child Condition: Search Types 1 and 3 were more likely than other types to be used for a child with a physical, emotional, developmental, or behavioral condition affecting care provision (19% each, compared to 5-10% in other types).
* Geographic Region: Search Type 5 was more likely to include Northeastern families compared to Search Types 1, 2, and 3. Search Type 3 was more likely than any other type to include Western families.

Study limitations include recording only the first two information sources mentioned by families and excluding 79% of the overall NSECE sample (who did not conduct a recent search or considered only one provider). Excluded households had lower incomes, more children under age 13 on average, and were more likely to speak Spanish exclusively, meaning findings may not reflect their experiences. Overall, search types were more similar than different regarding family and child characteristics.

The NVIDIA Ampere architecture-based A100 Tensor Core GPU is designed for AI, deep learning, and high-performance computing (HPC) workloads in data centers. L2 cache residency controls and Compute Data Compression further improve bandwidth and capacity.

The A100 includes 108 SMs with third-generation Tensor Cores that support peak mixed-precision compute performance 16x higher than standard FP32 FMA operations. To target strong scaling in deep learning, the architecture introduces thread data-sharing improvements, a maximum SMEM allocation of 164 KB per SM, and an asynchronous copy instruction that loads data directly from global memory to SM shared memory, bypassing the L1 cache and register file. The A100 also supports fine-grained structured sparsity, which prunes neural networks to increase compute throughput and reduce memory usage without compromising accuracy.

A new Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) capability allows a single A100 to be partitioned into up to seven isolated GPU Instances, each with dedicated SMs, L2 cache slices, memory controllers, and Sys Pipes. MIG provides quality of service (QoS) and fault isolation for multi-tenant environments, allowing multiple virtual machines or containers to run simultaneously, and supports vGPU migration.

For interconnectivity, the A100 implements third-generation NVLink, providing 600 GB/sec total bandwidth per GPU, alongside PCIe Gen 4 with SR-IOV support. Additional hardware features include enhanced error detection and containment, a 5-core NVJPG hardware JPEG decode engine, an Optical Flow Accelerator, improved FP16 and FP32 atomic operations, and five NVDEC video decode units.

CUDA 11 supports the A100’s new Compute Capability 8.0 features. It accelerates CUDA Task Graphs through launch and execution dependency optimizations, exposes APIs for asynchronous copy and hardware-accelerated asynchronous barriers, manages L2 cache residency for persisting data, and expands Cooperative Groups with asynchronous copies and a hardware-accelerated warp reduce API.

The A100 powers the NVIDIA DGX A100 system, which combines eight A100 GPUs interconnected via NVSwitch, Mellanox ConnectX-6 HDR InfiniBand adapters, and the Magnum IO SDK to deliver 5 PFLOPS of AI performance. The system is supported by a fully optimized DGX software stack—featuring the NGC Private Registry, CUDA 11, and the NVIDIA Container Toolkit—and can be partitioned into up to 56 MIG instances or scaled into large clusters like the DGX SuperPOD.

In this 2013 opinion, the Supreme Court of Arizona addressed whether A.R.S. § 13-4033(B) prohibits a defendant in a noncapital case from directly appealing a contested post-judgment restitution order entered pursuant to a plea agreement. 

Following a traffic accident, Frank Hoffman pleaded no contest to driving under the influence and agreed to pay restitution up to a capped amount of $53,653.45. After the court later ordered him to pay $40,933.45, Hoffman directly appealed. The superior court dismissed the appeal, ruling that Hoffman waived his direct appeal rights via the plea agreement and could only challenge the order through Rule 32 post-conviction relief proceedings.

Hoffman argued that A.R.S. § 13-4033(A)(3) permitted his appeal as a post-judgment order affecting substantial rights. However, the Supreme Court held that a post-judgment restitution order contemplated by a plea agreement and within the agreed-upon cap is part of a defendant's "sentence." Therefore, § 13-4033(B)—which bars direct appeals of judgments or sentences entered pursuant to plea agreements—applies as an exception to subsection (A)(3). The Court reasoned this interpretation furthers the legislative goal of reducing appellate burdens, prevents a hybrid review system, and recognizes that mandatory restitution is typically part of sentencing. 

Consequently, the Court affirmed the dismissal of Hoffman's direct appeal, holding that defendants in such situations must pursue their constitutional right to appellate review through Rule 32 post-conviction relief proceedings. To the extent earlier appellate cases (*State v. Foy* and *State v. Unkefer*) conflicted with this interpretation, the Court disapproved them.
