The ADS9803 is an eight-channel, 20-bit, 2MSPS data acquisition (DAQ) system featuring a built-in analog front-end. Each analog input channel includes an internal clamp protection circuit (allowing up to ±18V swing), a Programmable Gain Amplifier (PGA) supporting single-ended and differential inputs, a programmable antialiasing low-pass filter (LPF) with low-noise (up to 22.7kHz) and wide-bandwidth (up to 700kHz) modes, and a common-mode rejection circuit supporting up to ±12V. The device features an internal precision voltage reference and also supports an external reference at the REFIO pin.

Normal operation requires a free-running continuous differential or single-ended sampling clock. Multiple devices can be synchronized using the SMPL_SYNC signal. The ADC outputs 20-bit conversion data in straight-binary or binary two's-complement formats over a source-synchronous data interface supporting 2-lane and 4-lane modes with SDR or DDR. Additional features include a data output randomizer (using bit-wise XOR), simple and moving data averaging to improve SNR, and digital test patterns (fixed, digital ramp, and alternating) for interface debugging. A speed-boost mode allows a sampling rate up to 8MSPS for a single user-selected channel pair while the other six channels remain idle.

The device can be powered down or reset via hardware pins or register writes, and it requires a specific register write initialization sequence after power-up or reset. Its 16-bit configuration registers are organized into three banks accessed via 24-bit SPI frames for read and write operations. Multiple ADS9803 devices can be connected in an SPI daisy-chain topology. The passage details specific register addresses and field descriptions across the register banks for configuring device modes, test patterns, gain error correction, and channel settings.

For ATE applications, the ADS9803 achieves a post-calibration total unadjusted error (TUE) of 0.0015% at 25°C ±5°C and settles to 99.95% FS in 7.5µs in wide-bandwidth mode when sampling multiplexed PMU signals. The device uses three power supplies (AVDD_5V, VDD_1V8, and IOVDD) with no required power-up sequence, though separate 0.1µF bypass capacitors and careful board layout separating analog and digital lines are recommended. The passage concludes with information on Texas Instruments support resources, ESD cautions, mechanical and packaging details, and legal disclaimers.

Extrapulmonary tuberculosis (EPTB) affects organs outside the lungs, most commonly the lymph nodes and pleura, and accounts for about 16% of reported TB cases. Despite its prevalence, EPTB therapy is less studied than pulmonary TB and uses the same standard four-drug regimen: rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol. To evaluate EPTB treatment, the authors developed a whole-body physiologically-based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) model consisting of 17 tissue compartments, uniquely incorporating the pleural space and a consolidated lymph node compartment. The model simulates the time-dependent tissue concentrations of all four primary anti-TB drugs in adults, considering slow and fast acetylators of isoniazid as discrete cases. 

The model was parameterized using literature values, calculated tissue:plasma partition coefficients, and pharmacokinetic parameters estimated by fitting the model to reported plasma and lung concentration data. Separate datasets were used for independent validation, which showed good agreement with reported plasma, lung, and pleural concentrations for most drugs. 

Simulated drug concentrations at various EPTB sites were compared to WHO-prescribed critical concentrations. Results indicated that rifampicin and isoniazid achieved peak concentrations above their critical thresholds in all compartments. However, rapid metabolizers of isoniazid quickly eliminated the drug, suggesting a benefit to customizing dosages based on acetylator status. Furthermore, the model over-predicted rifampicin concentrations in the pleura and brain. Ethambutol failed to reach its critical concentration in the brain, kidney, bone, and skin compartments, and remained below the threshold in the lungs for a large fraction of time. Pyrazinamide failed to reach its critical concentration or lowered MIC in any simulated organ. 

Model limitations include using a single consolidated lymph node compartment and assuming no drug-drug interactions, no rifampicin autoinduction, and no age- or disease-dependent pharmacokinetic variations. Because the model does not account for drug synergy or host immune responses, the authors suggest this PBPK model serves as a starting point for optimizing EPTB dosing regimens.

Because East Asian and elderly populations are underrepresented in endovascular thrombectomy (EVT) trials for acute ischemic stroke, researchers integrated the Korean (CRCS-K) and Taiwanese (TREAT-AIS) stroke registries. This formed the K-T collaborative EVT registry, comprising 9,941 EVT-treated patients (7,835 from Korea and 2,106 from Taiwan) with roughly 200 common data fields. 

Analyses revealed differences between the two cohorts. Taiwanese patients were older on average, had a higher prevalence of vascular risk factors (hypertension, diabetes, dyslipidemia, and atrial fibrillation), presented with more severe strokes, and had longer arrival and treatment timelines. While successful recanalization and symptomatic intracerebral hemorrhage (SICH) rates were similar between the countries, 90-day functional independence was lower in the Taiwanese cohort, whereas 90-day mortality was higher in the Korean cohort.

The study also evaluated the impact of age on EVT outcomes. Nearly a quarter (24.9%) of the patients were aged 80 or older. Compared to younger patients, elderly patients arrived later, had more severe neurological deficits, and were less likely to receive IV thrombolysis. Advanced age—particularly between 75 and 85 years—strongly influenced outcomes, resulting in lower rates of favorable functional recovery, lower successful recanalization, and higher mortality. However, SICH incidence did not significantly differ by age. 

Despite worse overall outcomes, elderly patients could still benefit from EVT, as favorable recovery in those aged 80 and older was predicted by factors such as pre-stroke functional independence, lower baseline stroke severity, and bridging thrombolysis. Therefore, age alone should not exclude patients from EVT. Study limitations include retrospective analysis, differing inclusion periods, and a lack of detailed imaging and post-discharge data.

This lecture introduces Probabilistically Checkable Proofs (PCPs) and demonstrates how to construct one from the GKR protocol. A PCP converts a classical proof or witness into a polynomially larger string, allowing a probabilistic polynomial-time verifier to check its validity by reading only a few randomly chosen bits nonadaptively, rather than the entire proof. 

The complexity class PCP is defined by four parameters: completeness ($c$), soundness ($s$), randomness complexity ($r$), and query complexity ($q$). While it is known that any NP witness can be verified by reading just 3 bits, this lecture proves that all of NP (focusing on 3SAT) has a PCP with completeness 1, soundness 1/2, and $\text{polylog}(n)$ randomness and query complexity. 

The PCP is constructed by "unraveling" the GKR protocol, which consists of $2d$ sumcheck protocols over a bounded-depth verification circuit. Because the verifier lacks the witness $w$, the prover includes the low-degree extension of $w$ and the low-degree extensions of the values of every layer in the circuit within the PCP. The prover also writes out a tree of all possible partial transcripts for the sumcheck protocols corresponding to every layer, point, and verifier randomness. 

To maintain a polynomial-sized PCP despite $\text{polylog}(s)$ randomness, the construction relies on specific parameter settings ($H = \log s$, $m = \log s / \log \log s$, and field $F = \text{polylog}(s)$) and the "memoryless" property of GKR, which avoids repeating the entire transcript tree for every round. The verifier acts as an honest GKR verifier, querying the PCP oracle for sumcheck answers. Soundness is guaranteed via a union bound over the $2d$ sumchecks, though the verifier must also perform one low-degree test on the input layer's extension to prevent a prover from cheating on the witness.

This study investigated the impact of pupil dilation (mydriasis) on retinal image gradability and artificial intelligence (AI) model performance for diabetic retinopathy (DR) screening using portable cameras, which are vital for resource-limited settings. Researchers analyzed retinal images from 327 patients captured with a Phelcom Eyer portable camera before and after mydriasis, using a convolutional neural network trained on the mBRSET dataset for DR classification. 

Results showed a statistically significant difference in image gradability: 82.1% of mydriatic images were gradable compared to 55.6% of non-mydriatic images. In the non-mydriatic group, systemic hypertension, older age, longer diabetes duration, male gender, and Indigenous race were significantly associated with lower image quality. 

Analyzing 597 pairs of gradable images, the AI model achieved higher accuracy (82.91% vs. 79.23%), F1 score (0.83 vs. 0.79), and AUC (0.94 vs. 0.93) in the mydriatic group compared to the non-mydriatic group. Mydriasis resulted in fewer false positives (13.9% vs. 17.8%) and slightly more false negatives (3.2% vs. 3.0%), though overall performance differences between the groups were not statistically significant (P=0.3279). While mydriasis improves image quality and reduces false positives, study limitations include selection bias, a learning curve for handheld cameras, and using a single dataset and camera model.

In this lecture, Markus Klute examines a higher-order Feynman diagram with a self-energy correction loop. Calculating the amplitude requires integrating from zero to infinity, which diverges and results in infinity. This problem stalled the theory's progress because scattering cross-sections should not be infinite and lifetimes should not be zero. 

The solution is introducing a cutoff scale to keep calculations sensible under Lorentz transformation, and re-normalizing the physical objects so they appear as bare masses and couplings plus a correction. Because experiments are performed at specific scales, infinite-scale corrections are not a problem when comparing theoretical predictions to experiments. 

Observed physical masses and couplings for electromagnetic, weak, and strong interactions depend on and run as a function of a specific energy scale. While they do not converge at a very high mass scale, introducing new particles along the scale changes the couplings' running behavior. A concept for new physics suggests that introducing new particles could combine all three couplings at a specific scale, creating a unified theory for nuclear and particle physics.

Robert Pearl Bryson was convicted by a Stephens County jury of two counts of aggravated sodomy, four counts of aggravated child molestation, one count of child molestation, and two counts of failure to register as a sex offender. On appeal, the court affirmed the judgment, finding no error in the proceedings.

First, the court determined that the evidence was sufficient to support Bryson's convictions:
* **Aggravated Sodomy:** Video interviews and trial testimonies from victims B. S. and K. S. established contact between Bryson's sex organs and mouth with those of the children. Under Georgia law, contact, rather than penetration, is sufficient to establish sodomy.
* **Child Molestation:** A witness saw the 51-year-old Bryson kiss 10-year-old K. S. on the lips while swimming. Given the surrounding circumstances and other acts of molestation, the jury could rationally infer the kiss was intended to satisfy Bryson's sexual desires.
* **Failure to Register as a Sex Offender:** Previously convicted of a sex offense in North Carolina, Bryson registered in Stephens County in February 2003. However, in July 2003, he fled when an officer attempted to question him, remaining out of state for over a year until his apprehension in Tennessee. Because the relevant statute pertains to "residence" rather than "domicile," his failure to report his change of residence within ten days to the sheriff supported the conviction.

Second, the court upheld several procedural rulings by the trial court:
* **Motions to Quash:** The trial court properly denied Bryson's motions to quash the indictment. A county sheriff's wife serving on the grand jury did not make it illegally constituted, and Bryson's challenge to the dates on Count 8 was waived because it was not raised prior to his not guilty plea.
* **Motion to Withdraw:** The trial court did not abuse its discretion in denying trial counsel's motion to withdraw filed four days before trial, as granting it would have delayed the proceedings and counsel stated he was prepared for trial.
* **Motion to Sever:** Severing the failure to register counts from the remaining charges was not required because the offenses were a connected series of acts. Bryson's flight and failure to report constituted evasive conduct relevant as circumstantial evidence of guilt regarding the molestation charges.
* **No Contest Plea:** Bryson waived his objection to the admission of his North Carolina no contest plea by failing to object at trial. Additionally, the plea was legally admissible to establish a prior conviction for sex offender registration requirements, and the jury was properly instructed not to use it as an admission of guilt for the current offenses.

Finally, the court ruled that Bryson waived his claim of ineffective assistance of trial counsel. Despite warnings from the trial court, Bryson instructed his post-trial counsel not to pursue the issue during the hearing on his motion for a new trial, thereby barring appellate consideration.

Image registration aligns a moving image to a fixed image via coordinate transforms. While essential in biomedical sciences, current algorithms run out of memory on ultra-high-resolution images due to high computational and memory demands. To address this, the authors identify key bottlenecks—grid sampling, Local Normalized Cross-Correlation (LNCC), and Mattes Mutual Information (MI)—and propose fused CUDA kernels to reduce High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) usage on a single GPU. These include a composite implicit grid sampler and implicit Parzen windowing for MI, both reducing memory overhead from O(N) to O(1), alongside an efficient fused LNCC kernel that reduces memory by up to 76.5%. 

To scale to an arbitrary number of GPUs, the authors introduce Flash Fused Distributed Primitives (FFDP). FFDP utilizes "Grid Parallel" (GP) to shard tensors with boundary synchronization for convolutions, a distributed Ring Sampler to interpolate sharded moving images without memory-expensive allgather operations, and distributed loss functions (MSE, LNCC, MI). 

In experiments, FFDP accelerates traditional registration pipelines by up to 7.48× (reducing memory by up to 59%) and deep learning pipelines by up to 6.14× (using up to 24% less memory). Notably, FFDP aligned a 250µm in-vivo MRI to a 100µm ex-vivo human brain volume (over 11.8B parameters) in about one minute using 8 A6000 GPUs. On the simulated 250µm faux-OASIS dataset, existing methods ran out of memory, and modified patch-based or downsampled baselines degraded in accuracy at higher resolutions. Conversely, the proposed method improved in accuracy—increasing Dice by 18.1 points, InvDice by 31.6 points, and reducing AvgHD90 by 62.1%—while requiring up to 500× fewer GPU-hours. Ablations confirm the Ring Sampler keeps peak memory independent of GPU count, and GP prevents boundary artifacts.

NeoWorld is a deep learning framework that constructs an infinitely expandable, interactive virtual world from a single input image. Unlike prior 2D and 2.5D methods that primarily support static rendering or basic visual navigation, NeoWorld balances computational efficiency with 3D realism to enable 3D-consistent scene exploration, user-driven object manipulation, and physics-based dynamic simulation.

The framework operates through three core components:
* **Object-Centric Scene Representation:** Using panoptic segmentation, the input image is decomposed into 2.5D foreground and background Gaussian layers. Each Gaussian primitive is bound to a learnable attribute coefficient using a compact codebook to efficiently encode instance-level semantics, while cross-scene alignment ensures continuity across views.
* **Progressive 2.5D-to-3D Unfolding:** Based on camera proximity or user prompts, interaction-relevant foreground objects are converted into full 3D representations using an image-to-3D module (Amodal3R). A two-stage coarse and fine alignment process integrates the 3D objects into the scene. If reconstruction fidelity falls below a similarity threshold, a fallback strategy reverts the object to 2.5D.
* **Intuitive User-World Interaction:** A Large Language Model (Gemini-2.5pro) interprets natural language commands to identify target objects and predict manipulation attributes, allowing users to translate, rotate, or animate entities.

In experimental evaluations, NeoWorld outperformed existing 3D world generation, video diffusion, and 3D segmentation baselines in 3D consistency, scene quality, segmentation accuracy (IoU), and text-motion alignment, while achieving the second-fastest rendering speed among 3D unbounded methods. However, because NeoWorld relies on a cascade of external, pre-trained modules, its end-to-end robustness is vulnerable to upstream errors such as alignment failures, LLM misinterpretations, segmentation errors, and 3D reconstruction issues under heavy occlusion.

This March 2006 specification update from Advanced Micro Devices, Inc. (AMD) details issues, implications, and resolutions for the AMD Geode CS5535 Companion Device Silicon Revision A3:

* **SSMI & Interrupts:** Simultaneous IRQ and SSMI events prevent reliable SSMI generation; use the Geode GX processor instead.
* **IDE, UDMA, & ATAC:** Enabling the IDE bus master before sending a PIO command fails; use normal UDMA procedures. An unexpected IDE device interrupt resets the bus master (resolved via drive firmware). The tACK bits do not affect UDMA timing, which is fixed at 30 ns (no resolution needed). WORD-aligned PRDs can hang the ATAC; use DWORD alignment.
* **Power, Wake, & Sleep:** GPIO[27:24] transitions do not wake the system from ACPI S3; use PWRBTN# with external circuitry. The LOWBAT_FLAG fails to set after exiting standby (no resolution). Premature counter resets keep SLEEP_X, SLEEP_Y, and PCI/IDE inputs non-functional when exiting Sleep; program their delay counters below the PM_SED counter value.
* **Memory & Buses:** Reading legacy RTC CMOS RAM immediately after writing to extended RAM returns the extended data (no resolution). Block/demand mode legacy DMA blocks LPC I/Os; use single transfer mode. LPC controllers may abort transactions with LPC-to-ISA bridges; use a PLD workaround. The GLPCI retry counter counts all PCI bus retries; disable it or adjust MSR 51000010h[51:49].
* **Controllers & GPIO:** USB Controller reads fail when idle if clock gating is enabled; disable clock gating. Reading Port 60h clears the KEL AuxOutputFull bit; use interrupts for PS/2 emulation on USB. The SMB controller's NEGACK bit behaves incorrectly; write twice to register SMB_STS to clear it. The SMBus minimum data hold time is also noted as too short. Atomic writes to GPIO High Bank Feature Bit Registers after a suspend clear non-selected bits; use Read-Modify-Write transactions instead.

The document concludes with AMD's standard legal disclaimers, product use restrictions, and trademark notices.

This paper by Sergey A. Yablonsky investigates the relationship and value of Artificial Intelligence (AI), Big Data (BD), and Advanced Analytics (AA) within digital business platforms. Addressing a lack of systematic empirical analysis in AI management research, the study takes a managerial perspective to examine how BD and AA engage with AI to transform traditional business strategies, products, and services. 

Using an iterative combination of conceptual-to-empirical and empirical-to-conceptual approaches, the author collected qualitative data through a literature review (spanning 2010 to 2019) and 50-minute semi-structured interviews with members, founders, and CTOs of the Russian National Technology Initiative. This data was used to develop a taxonomy of data-driven AI platform innovation containing seven dimensions and twenty characteristics. 

The study notes that business platforms are infused with data and analytics and are supported by seven overlapping technology platforms: Information Systems, Customer Experience, Data and Analytics, IoT, Ecosystems, Trust (blockchain), and Integration platforms. Furthermore, the field of analytics is broken down into five categories: descriptive, diagnostic, predictive, prescriptive, and augmented analytics.

The paper adds several key results to the current knowledge base on AI innovation:
1. It creates an AI/BD/AA micro-level value chain to model high-level enterprise activities, identifying four main dimensions: AI Awareness/BD Acquisition, Measurement of AI/BD Curation, AI Reporting and Interpretation/BD Storage, and AI Decision-making/BD Usage.
2. It develops a multidimensional BD-driven AI enterprise maturity framework with five levels of maturity that correspond to the value chain: Human Led/Initial Analytics; Human Led, Machine Supported/Advanced Analytics I; Machine Led, Human Supported/Advanced Analytics II; Machine Led, Human Governed/Advanced Analytics III; and Machine Controlled/Advanced Analytics IV.
3. It creates and tests BD-driven AI innovation value chains as end-to-end processes for each maturity level.

Ultimately, this multidimensional framework focuses on data-driven human-machine relationships. It provides a pragmatic tool for managers, owners, and investors to evaluate AI innovation, guide strategic planning and investment decisions, identify automation use cases, and manage intellectual and informational assets while considering legal, ethical, and societal norms.

Researchers led by Joshua Caldwell at Vanderbilt University, alongside contributors from several other institutions, have improved the imaging capability of hexagonal boron nitride (hBN), a crystal used in hyperlensing, by a factor of ten. By creating hBN crystals with 99 percent isotopically purified boron, the team overcame efficiency limitations caused by natural boron isotopes. This purification reduced optical losses and tripled the lifetime and travel distance of surface phonon polaritons, which allow hBN to surpass the typical optical diffraction limit. Consequently, lenses made from this purified crystal can theoretically resolve objects as small as 30 nanometers, such as small viruses. Unlike electron-based or atomic-force microscopes that require conditions lethal to living organisms, hyperlenses use harmless, low-energy infrared light. This advancement could allow scientists to observe living cells in their natural environments and gather spectroscopic information, potentially impacting biology, medicine, communications, and nanoscale optical components.

Ulysses S. Gandy appealed to the Supreme Court of Mississippi following his second manslaughter conviction and ten-year sentence stemming from a June 1976 two-car collision that killed Daniel Palmer and two passengers. Gandy raised four assignments of error: that the verdict was against the overwhelming weight of the evidence, the refusal of Instruction D-13, the admission of State's Exhibits 1, 5, and 7, and the failure to give the jury a recess for food or refreshments during deliberations.

Despite conflicting witness testimony regarding Gandy's intoxication and the post-impact positions of the vehicles, the Supreme Court found sufficient evidence to support the jury's finding of culpable negligence. Specifically, evidence showed Gandy was intoxicated and drove into the wrong lane of traffic on a straight, unobstructed stretch of road. 

The Court also rejected Gandy’s remaining claims of error. It ruled that refusing Instruction D-13 was not a reversible error because other instructions properly presented the issue of intoxication, and D-13 offered no guidance beyond common judgment. The admission of the State's exhibits—sketches made by three witnesses—was upheld as appropriate and relevant because they illustrated the witnesses' personal observations after the crash rather than attempting to reconstruct the impact. Finally, the Court found no merit in the argument regarding the lack of a jury recess during the nearly three-hour deliberation, noting the jury could have requested one and Gandy cited no supporting authority. The trial court's judgment was affirmed.
In the appeal of People v. Roldán, the judgment was reversed and the defendant was acquitted based on the court's decision in the nearly identical case No. 2037.

In soccer, defenders execute an offside trap by moving up to place strikers in an offside position. To beat this trap, attackers must stay onside just as the ball is passed. Through scouting and effective coaching, players must recognize the trap, adjust their play to avoid being called offside, and utilize the space behind the defenders. This requires patience to avoid running into offside positions, not interfering with play if forced offside, and executing specific tactics. 

Players ahead of the defenders or behind the ball can use several methods to beat the trap: dribbling through after faking a pass, using timed through passes, or making horizontal, lateral, checking, deep-lying, bending, or delayed runs. Teams can also use short passes, back-passes, square passes to delay for time, or a designated "non-runner" during free kicks. 

Additionally, attackers can use fakes before free kicks to expose the trap, capitalize immediately if a defender fails to move up, and prepare for a one-on-one with the goalkeeper once the trap is beaten. Successfully beating the trap once often makes the opponent less likely to use it again.

Grief is a unique, personal emotional reaction to losing someone or something you care about. Beyond bereavement, people can grieve major life changes, such as losing personal freedom when becoming a carer, retiring, experiencing declining health, or moving out of a longtime family home. Because moving after a partner's death creates a double loss and can increase loneliness, major housing decisions should be deferred if possible. Grief can also be anticipatory, occurring when someone is diagnosed with a terminal illness, affecting both the ill person and their loved ones. 

Rather than following sequential stages, the grieving process is complex and variable, with emotions shifting rapidly depending on personality, life experience, and the circumstances of the loss. Common reactions to a loved one's death include:
*   **Numbness and shock**, particularly after traumatic or unexpected deaths.
*   **Denial and disbelief**, which may manifest subconsciously.
*   **Acceptance and relief**, often felt when a loved one's long, degenerative illness ends.
*   **Yearning and searching**, where the longing feels physical, such as thinking you see or hear the deceased.
*   **Repeating the event** mentally or aloud to process the reality of the death.
*   **Restlessness and disturbed sleep**, causing daytime concentration issues.
*   **Loss of confidence**, especially when adjusting to life as a single person after a partner dies.
*   **Guilt and regret** over things said, unsaid, or not done.
*   **Anger** directed at the deceased, relatives, or doctors.
*   **Profound sadness and depression**, which may cause lethargy and neglect of daily tasks long after initial external support fades.

There is no set timeline for grief, and it can be especially difficult for older people. While the deceased will always be missed, the intense pain eventually subsides, allowing good days to outnumber the bad. Those struggling with depression or needing extra help should reach out to family, friends, a GP, or specialist bereavement organisations.

This study investigates the relationship between Google Community Mobility Reports (GCMR) and SARS-CoV-2 transmission dynamics. The authors developed a discrete-time, age-structured SIR meta-population model and fitted it to weekly hospitalization counts in 11 Norwegian and 21 Swedish regions from February 2020 to July 2021, and in two German regions (Bavaria and Berlin) from February to December 2020. 

The model assumes an additive, linear relationship between contact frequencies and four GCMR settings: Retail and recreation, Grocery and pharmacy, Transit stations, and Workplaces. The Residential and Parks settings were excluded. Unexplained transmissions are captured by a region- and week-specific parameter. The model also accounts for vaccination roll-outs and incorporates multiplicative effects on infection probability from temperature (representing seasonality) and the Alpha and Delta Variants of Concern (VoCs).

Results show that the four GCMR settings accounted for 60.0% of infections in Sweden, 38.7% in Norway, and 65.2% in the German regions. At pre-pandemic baseline levels, Transit stations and Workplaces contributed the most to infectious contacts in Norway and Sweden, whereas Retail and recreation contributed the most in the German regions. 

Across all regions, a 20-degree Celsius temperature increase reduced transmissibility by approximately 40% to 50%. Compared to the wildtype virus, the Delta VoC approximately doubled transmissibility in Norway and Sweden, while the Alpha VoC increased transmissibility by about 20% in Norway, with no clear increase in Sweden. Both VoCs were assumed to increase hospitalization risk by a factor of 1.9.

The study concludes that GCMR data reflect behavioral changes directly related to SARS-CoV-2 spread. However, the model is limited by strong assumptions, such as constant linear relationships between mobility and contacts, an all-or-nothing vaccine effect, and potential GCMR measurement errors.

The ADS9803 is an eight-channel, 20-bit, 2MSPS data acquisition system with a built-in analog front-end. It features two data averaging modes to improve SNR: simple average (which halves the output data rate) and moving average. For debugging the data interface, it supports fixed, digital ramp, and alternating test patterns across two channel groups (CH[4:1] and CH[8:5]). The device can be powered down or reset via pins or registers and requires a free-running sampling clock and register write sequences for initialization. It also offers a speed-boost mode allowing up to an 8MSPS sampling rate for a single user-selected channel pair while other channels remain idle. 

The ADS9803 uses 16-bit configuration registers grouped into three banks, which are read and written via SPI frames. Multiple devices can be connected in a daisy-chain topology for SPI configuration. The passage details specific register addresses, offsets, and bit fields for configuring modes, error correction, common-mode ranges, and output data lanes. 

For Automatic Test Equipment (ATE) applications, the ADS9803 achieves a post-calibration total unadjusted error (TUE) of 0.0015% at 25°C ±5°C. It offers low-noise (up to 22.7kHz) and wide-bandwidth (up to 700kHz) modes, the latter allowing multiplexed signals to settle to 99.95% full-scale in 7.5µs. The device uses three power supplies (AVDD_5V, VDD_1V8, and IOVDD) with no required power-up sequence, and requires specific board layout practices, such as placing 0.1μF ceramic bypass capacitors near power pins and isolating analog signals from digital lines. Finally, Texas Instruments provides support resources, ESD precautions, packaging definitions, and legal disclaimers regarding product use and warranties.

The NAAIM Exposure Index, compiled by the National Association of Active Investment Managers, measures the average US Equity market exposure of its members based on weekly Wednesday surveys. The indicator line represents a two-week moving average of these responses, showing the adjustments active managers have made to client accounts. 

The index is widely used to track investor sentiment and act as a contrarian indicator, where high readings suggest bullishness (a potential market top) and low readings suggest bearishness (a potential market bottom). However, the index is not predictive of future stock market movements. 

Several backtests using NAAIM data—such as investing $10,000 in July 2006 when the weekly reading was below or above its 10-week moving average—yielded poor performance, resulting in CAGRs of 4.4% and 2.5% excluding dividends. Altering the moving average length or using extreme readings did not significantly improve results. Ultimately, the backtests demonstrate that the NAAIM index is not an effective contrarian trading indicator, and better alternatives like the VIX indicator exist.

This study used electroencephalography (EEG) to investigate whether Tourette syndrome (TS) is associated with increased sensorimotor neural noise, defined as increased trial-by-trial variability in response to single-pulse median nerve electrical stimulation (MNS). Data were analysed from 19 right-handed adults with TS and 19 age- and sex-matched healthy controls (HC). 

Key findings from the CP3 electrode include:
* **Somatosensory Evoked Potentials (SEPs):** The spatial topographies, timing, and timing variability of early- and mid-latency SEP components generally did not differ between groups, except for a 1ms delay in P1 timing and reduced N2 timing variability in the TS group. However, the TS group exhibited substantially increased amplitudes in the P1, P2 (P100), and P3 components.
* **Trial-by-Trial Variability:** Standard deviation (SD) was higher in the TS group throughout the entire epoch, not just post-stimulation. When standardised (z-score) or measured using the coefficient of variation (CV), variability changed at comparable rates in both groups following stimulation onset, with CV decreasing substantially post-stimulation for both groups.
* **Power Spectral Density (PSD):** Mean spectral power was increased in the TS group at high-beta (>25Hz) and gamma (>30Hz) frequencies, resulting in a flatter 1/f noise slope compared to controls.
* **Inter-Trial Phase Coherence:** Phase coherence increased in both groups after stimulation across theta, alpha, beta, and low-gamma bands. However, the TS group showed a shallower early rate of rise (~0–40ms) across alpha, beta, and gamma bands, a shorter duration of sustained high alpha coherence, and increased beta coherence ~100ms post-stimulation (coinciding with the P2 component).
* **Clinical Correlations:** In the TS group, P2 amplitude was positively predicted by YGTSS-impairment scores, and pre-post stimulation alpha coherence changes were predicted by YGTSS-motor scores. PUTS-R scores predicted changes in gamma coherence and CV, while WASI (IQ) scores negatively predicted mean SEP variability (SD) and PSD (25–45Hz).

The authors conclude that while conscious tactile perception processing (P100) is heightened in TS, the recruitment of neuronal sensorimotor populations is less stable at rest in individuals with TS compared to controls, but normalises in response to somatosensory stimulation.

In an October 2001 email, Toby Kuehl shares a *Texas Monthly* article by Mimi Swartz detailing the rise and decline of Enron. 

Formed in 1985 through a merger engineered by Ken Lay, Enron initially struggled with debt and gas industry deregulation. Lay hired consultant Jeff Skilling, who created the "Gas Bank," transforming Enron from a traditional pipeline company into a dominant energy trader and financier. Between 1985 and 2000, Enron's revenues grew from $40 billion to $100 billion, and its stock price increased 1,700 percent. 

Skilling, who joined Enron in 1990 and became president and COO in 1997, cultivated an aggressive, high-pressure corporate culture. He recruited top graduates, offered uncapped bonuses, and instituted the Performance Review Committee, a forced ranking system that replaced 15 percent of his division's workforce annually. This fostered fierce internal competition, paranoia, and a focus on short-term gains. Enron expanded into trading electricity, coal, steel, weather, online commodities, and broadband capacity. To maximize immediate profits, Enron used "mark-to-market" accounting to book multi-year profits up-front. Skilling also spurned tangible assets, eventually sidelining rival executive Rebecca Mark—who led Enron's asset-heavy international division and a troubled power plant in India—by placing her in charge of a water utility, Azurix, which faltered and led to her resignation.

Skilling succeeded Lay as CEO in February 2001, just as Enron's fortunes reversed. The company faced severe public backlash over California's energy crisis, and its heavily hyped telecommunications division collapsed when the tech bubble burst, alongside a failed Blockbuster deal. As the business press and Wall Street analysts began questioning Enron's accounting practices and executives' stock option sales, the stock price dropped from $80 in January to around $35. 

Frustrated by the unyielding stock drop and citing personal sacrifices and a desire for family time, Skilling abruptly resigned after six months as CEO. Lay returned as CEO, promising to calm investors, focus on core businesses, and soften the company's harsh culture. In July 2021, Public Health Wales investigated a Salmonella Typhimurium outbreak linked to an Eid al-Adha celebration barbecue and lunches in a Cardiff North African community. A total of 22 symptomatic cases were identified from a social network of 43 people. Over half of the cases (12/22) sought emergency hospital care, and six were admitted overnight.

Researchers conducted a cohort study of 36 attendees and a nested case-control study using Firth logistic regression. Statistical analysis identified a traditional raw sheep's liver dish, "marrara" (or "marara"), consumed at the barbecue as the primary vehicle of infection. Those who ate the raw liver were 50 times more likely to become cases. While all barbecue cases also ate lamb, multivariable analysis showed lamb and spicy sauce confounded the raw liver effect, though cross-contamination and undercooking likely occurred. 

Whole genome sequencing of human stool samples, leftover raw lamb, and samples from the two local butchers and the supplying abattoir yielded genetically indistinguishable sequences (0 SNP difference). These cases were also linked to a wider, ongoing UK-wide cluster dating back to 2018.

In response, Public Health Wales collaborated with community liaisons to deliver culturally sensitive food safety education. This included an in-person session and a two-phase multilingual social media campaign sharing food hygiene infographics for World Food Safety Day and ahead of the 2022 Eid al-Adha festival. The outbreak highlights the ongoing public health risks of consuming raw meat and offal and the need for future outbreak investigations to consider culturally specific dishes beyond those on routine questionnaires.

Introduced in 1965 by economist E.S.C. Coppock for the Episcopal Church, the Coppock Curve Strategy (or Coppock Guide) is a smoothed momentum indicator designed for long-term stock market investments. It captures uptrends and filters out downtrends on a monthly time frame. The indicator is calculated using a 10-month Weighted Moving Average (WMA) of the sum of 14-month and 11-month Rate of Change (ROC) values— timeframes Coppock based on the estimated months required to mourn a loved one's death. 

A long entry is triggered when the curve crosses above zero, and an exit occurs when it crosses below zero. Backtesting the S&P 500 index since 1960 yielded 12 trades over 63 years, all of which were winners, including two recent trades netting roughly 80% and 65% profits. Compared to a Buy & Hold strategy, the Coppock Curve offers a higher risk-adjusted return, substantial drawdown reduction, and about 25% less time spent in the market. The blog also offers this strategy's code and logic in a purchasable compilation of trading ideas.

In an interview with STAT’s “First Opinion Podcast” editor Torie Bosch, Morgan McSweeney (known on social media as “Dr. Noc”) discusses his work as a science communicator. McSweeney, who has a Ph.D. in pharmaceutical sciences and immunology and works full-time in biotech developing monoclonal antibody-based therapeutics, has 4 million followers across platforms. He started making content during Covid using an old video game handle, and though initially embarrassed, he now embraces “edutainment”—turning complex public health and academic science topics into engaging, digestible formats. 

McSweeney creates various types of videos, such as reacting to incorrect health claims with research papers or explaining how food impacts the gut microbiome. Rather than arguing with strongly anti-science individuals or riling up those who already agree with him, he targets the confused middle ground. He draws audiences in with non-polarizing topics, which then exposes them to his other evidence-based videos. He selects topics by browsing recent comments, messages, and news, often waiting briefly on high-profile stories to see what questions arise so he can provide the specific details and nuance audiences want. 

Because he cannot reach everyone, McSweeney believes a greater diversity of science communicators is needed so audiences can find messengers they relate to and trust. He notes that misinformation and wellness content vastly out-reach factual content online. Major health institutions like the WHO, NIH, and CDC struggle to compete because they lack resources dedicated to influencer-style communication, have slow review processes, and face the inherent difficulty of making hundreds of videos to get good at it. Furthermore, many healthcare providers avoid making content due to fear of employer backlash. McSweeney keeps his supportive small biotech employer separate from his videos to avoid perceived conflicts of interest, and he handles hostile comments by hiding, blocking, or deleting them rather than engaging and boosting their visibility. 

Finally, McSweeney learned that audiences care as much about the messenger's humanity as the data. Sharing small personal details, like cooking dinner for his wife or showing his dog, builds a parasocial relationship that fosters trust. While he hasn't taught his own course on science communication, he frequently gives guest seminars to students.

The TILER includes an extra 4-GBytes of addressing range to access rotated and mirrored frame buffer views, fully accessible only to the HDVPSS and ISS subsystems, while other masters can access a single view via a 512-MB region. 

Additionally, the text explains that terminal function tables identify external signal names, pin numbers, pin types, internal pullup/pulldown resistors, supply voltages, and pin multiplexing controlled by PINCNTLx registers. At reset, these pins are sampled to determine configurations such as GPMC wait enable, address/data multiplexing, data bus width, reset output, XIP (NOR), Ethernet PHY mode, and ARM boot modes. After reset, these pins function as GPMC multiplexed data/address pins.

This lecture covers asset-level sustainable real estate finance, focusing on the broader sustainable finance landscape, debt (mortgages), and private equity. 

The sustainable finance field largely began in 2020 when BlackRock CEO Larry Fink highlighted that climate risk is a financial risk, emphasizing a fiduciary responsibility to manage it. In a real estate context, individuals act as both end-users who can pay higher rents for green buildings and investors whose pension and insurance funds drive institutional capital toward sustainable assets.

Investors evaluate real estate using a weighted average cost of capital from debt and equity sources, proceeding only if the return exceeds this cost (or yields a positive Net Present Value). In portfolio theory, sustainable finance incorporates externalities. Green buildings provide positive externalities—avoiding regulatory penalties, attracting tenant preferences, and lowering investor risk—which increase Net Operating Income, lower the discount rate, and raise asset value. Conversely, "brown" buildings face negative externalities that decrease their value. Consequently, green buildings offer higher returns and lower risk, shifting the portfolio's efficient frontier and absorbing capital, though high demand eventually lowers expected returns toward a new equilibrium.

In the private debt market, climate risks like wildfires and floods lower property values. If a property’s value drops below the loan amount, borrowers rationally choose to default. This threatens government-backed entities like Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, and the National Flood Insurance Program. While researchers are working to incorporate climate risk into mortgage appraisal models, charging higher interest rates in risky areas creates a social and political dilemma, as it burdens marginalized, low-income households living in those locations. 

Conversely, banks offer "green mortgages" with lower interest rates or higher loan-to-value ratios for energy-efficient properties. Because green buildings have higher values and lower monthly utility bills, borrowers have more disposable income, which reduces default risk—an effect particularly strong among low-income households and also present in commercial real estate. Furthermore, banks can lend extra money upfront for green renovations, knowing the property's value will appreciate.

Finally, on the private equity side, commingled funds (managed by General Partners with capital from passive Limited Partners) are increasingly integrating ESG into their investment memos and management processes, aligning social value with business value to achieve higher returns and reduce physical and transition risks.

In football, a "blitz" is a defensive play where five to eight defenders—more than the typical four—rush the offensive backfield to attack the ball carrier and disrupt the offense. Called by the defensive coordinator, the goal is to quickly get the defense off the field by forcing bad passes, sacking the quarterback, or stopping the run. However, blitzing carries risk because sending extra rushers leaves fewer defenders to cover receivers, and mobile quarterbacks can evade the pressure. 

Different types of blitzes include:
* **Conventional blitz:** Five or more defenders rush while defensive backs play man coverage.
* **Zone blitz:** A linebacker rushes while a lineman drops into coverage to confuse the offense.
* **Safety and Cornerback blitzes:** Defensive backs rush to surprise the offense, though this leaves open gaps.
* **Zero blitz:** A high-risk play leaving no deep safety coverage, usually used when anticipating a run.
* **Run blitz:** Designed specifically to stop the run game early.

Offenses can beat the blitz by identifying weak points and executing quick passes (often to the running back), utilizing a mobile quarterback to dodge defenders and run, or using "max protection" schemes where extra players stay back to block.

Market sentiment measures the aggregate mood of traders and investors, indicating whether they are bullish, neutral, or bearish. A sentiment indicator is an oscillating measure of this crowd psychology. While popular indicators include the VIX and Investors Intelligence Bulls & Bears, the American Association of Individual Investors (AAII) sentiment index is among the most used. Published weekly since the 1980s, the AAII index surveys members on the direction they feel the stock market will take in the next six months. 

These indicators work because extreme sentiment signals potential reversals; when the majority is already positioned as bullish or bearish, little is needed to reverse the market's direction. 

Backtesting the AAII index since 1987 by holding trades for four weeks yielded the following average returns per trade:
* Buying when the bull-bear spread turns negative: 0.68% (70% cumulative return).
* Buying when the spread is below -20: 1.03%.
* Buying when the spread is above 20: 0.52%.

Classic Bayesian persuasion models assume a receiver's beliefs are influenced strictly by quantitative correlations in a recommendation scheme, contrasting with behavioral economics findings that show human decision-making is also affected by how information is framed. This work introduces a theoretical framework that integrates natural language framing into the Bayesian persuasion model, utilizing Large Language Models (LLMs) as a noisy "belief oracle" to map framings to induced receiver prior beliefs. 

In this model, a sender can influence a receiver's beliefs—and subsequent utility-maximizing actions—by selecting a framing alongside a randomized signaling (or recommendation) scheme. The authors analyze two primary optimization variants for the sender:
1. **Framing-only (with a fixed recommendation scheme):** This approach proves severely challenging. The sender's utility is a discontinuous function of the induced belief, making it sensitive to small oracle errors, and finding the optimal framing is NP-hard even to approximate.
2. **Joint Framing and Recommendation:** This approach is much more tractable. The sender's utility is a continuous function, making it resilient to errors, and the problem admits a quasi-polynomial-time approximation scheme (QPTAS).

Guided by these theoretical results, the authors implement a practical hill-climbing method for the joint optimization problem. They combine LLMs (specifically GPT-4o-mini) to optimize framing and act as the belief oracle with analytical methods (using SciPy) to optimize the recommendation strategy. Empirical evaluations across two case studies (real estate and clothing retail) show the approach is highly effective when measured by LLM reactions. Validation with human subjects reveals less pronounced reactions with higher variance, though the model's predictions remain directionally correct and well-approximate the effect's magnitude. Ultimately, this work provides a scalable, algorithmic alternative to human-driven heuristics for persuasive communication.

Process modeling is vital in Materials Science and Engineering (MSE), yet existing ontologies face interoperability and reuse challenges due to the limited adoption of Ontology Design Patterns (ODPs). The authors first defined three core MSE process modeling requirements—Process Structure, Data and Resources, and Project Goals and Participant Roles—which were validated by nine domain experts. Using these requirements, ODPs were manually extracted from existing ontologies, including P-PLAN, Metadata4Ing (M4I), OPMW, WILD, General Process Ontology (GPO), and PMDcore. 

Additionally, the authors proposed a baseline method for automatically extracting ODPs. This approach uses sentence transformer models and cosine similarity to match textual ontology metadata with the defined requirements, followed by modular extraction using the ROBOT framework (specifically the STAR method with no intermediates). 

Evaluating the automated extraction against manually curated ground truths using precision, recall, and F1-score showed that P-PLAN achieved the highest F1-scores for Process and Resource ODPs, while PMDcore was the only ontology to support all three requirement categories. The automated method's limitations include biases from annotation quality, sensitivity to requirement phrasing, and the inability to identify patterns across multiple ontologies simultaneously. Future work will address these limitations by incorporating structural ontology features, controlled vocabularies, and ontology mappings, alongside developing a platform to publish the extracted patterns for the MSE community.

This passage discusses single-node and multi-node distributed system patterns, alongside functions and event-driven processing. 

The **adapter pattern** is a single-node pattern using a modular container to modify an application container's interface to conform to a predefined, consistent interface without changing the original container. This promotes reuse and decouples operations. It is commonly applied to:
*   **Monitoring:** Transforming diverse application metrics into a single format, such as using a Prometheus exporter for a Redis container.
*   **Logging:** Redirecting and normalizing heterogeneous log formats into a single structured stream using tools like `fluentd` for systems like Redis and Apache Storm.
*   **Health Monitoring:** Running separate containers containing custom health-check scripts (e.g., running queries against a MySQL database) to avoid modifying the base image.

In contrast, **multi-node distributed patterns** use loosely coupled microservices that communicate over network APIs. While microservices enable small teams, independent scaling, and agility, they complicate debugging and architecture, which distributed patterns help address:
*   **Replicated Load-Balanced Services:** Used for stateless services to ensure high availability and horizontal scaling. Traffic is distributed via a load balancer, which relies on readiness probes to know when containers can accept requests. Variations include session-tracked services (routing a user's requests to the same replica via IP hashing or cookies) and adding application-layer tiers like a Varnish caching layer (which can also handle rate-limiting for Denial-of-Service defense) and an `nginx` layer for SSL termination.
*   **Sharded Services:** Used for stateful services when data is too large for a single machine. Each shard serves a subset of requests, routed by a load-balancing root using a sharding function (typically a deterministic, uniform hash function with a modulo operator, or consistent hashing to minimize remapping during scaling). Sharded caches (e.g., deployed using `memcached` and `twemproxy` as an ambassador or shared routing service) maximize memory utilization compared to replicated caches. However, shard failures reduce the cache hit rate, increasing latency and backend load. Combining patterns into **replicated, sharded caches** provides fault tolerance and handles "hot shards" (disproportionate traffic to one shard) by dynamically scaling specific shards.
*   **Scatter/Gather Pattern:** Achieves time-based scalability by parallelizing computation. A root node simultaneously sends a request to multiple leaf nodes, which process parts of the request and return partial results for the root to combine. This can use replicated data or leaf sharding for large datasets (e.g., distributed document searches). However, performance gains are limited by per-node request overhead and the "straggler" problem, where overall latency is dictated by the slowest leaf node. Shards in a scatter/gather system can also be replicated to improve reliability and allow upgrades under load.

Finally, **Function-as-a-Service (FaaS)** supports temporary, request- or event-driven computation. 
*   **Benefits and Challenges:** FaaS simplifies deployment, scales automatically, and enforces modularity. However, extreme decoupling makes system-wide debugging and tracking dependencies difficult. Furthermore, FaaS is poorly suited for long-running background processing, applications requiring large amounts of data in memory (due to spin-up latency), and high-volume sustained traffic (where pay-per-request pricing becomes more expensive than virtual machines, though running open-source FaaS like `kubeless` on Kubernetes can mitigate this).
*   **FaaS Patterns:** FaaS is ideal for the **decorator pattern**, which transforms requests or responses (e.g., adding default values to an API call prior to processing), and for **handling asynchronous events** (e.g., triggering a two-factor authentication text message upon login) or building event-based pipelines.

Two-dimensional transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) possess tunable electronic and optical properties, which can be modified through defect engineering. While previous studies primarily used low-energy electron beams or ions, this work investigates high-energy (1 MeV) electron beam irradiation as a controlled method for defect engineering in chemical vapor deposition (CVD)-grown monolayer MoS2. Samples were irradiated with a flux of 3 × 10^6 electrons/s for 30, 60, and 120 seconds, and analyzed using Raman spectroscopy, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), Kelvin probe force microscopy (KPFM), photoluminescence (PL) spectroscopy, and first-principles calculations.

Raman spectra of irradiated samples showed peak shifts and increased longitudinal optical (LO(M)) and acoustic (LA(M)) mode intensities, indicating Mo-S bond dissociation, sulfur vacancy formation, and increased defect density. Room-temperature PL spectra exhibited excitonic peak blueshifts and intensity quenching. XPS confirmed that irradiation-induced sulfur vacancies facilitate ambient oxygen incorporation, selectively oxidizing Mo to form Mo5+ and Mo6+ states and Mo-O bonds. KPFM measurements showed a decrease in surface potential and a work function increase from 4.8 eV to 5.24 eV after 120 seconds of irradiation, indicating p-type doping caused by electronegative oxygen withdrawing electrons from the lattice.

Cryogenic (85 K) PL spectroscopy revealed a broad defect-related emission peak (D) at 200–300 meV below the A exciton, which resolved into deeper (D1 at ~1.64 eV) and shallower (D2 at ~1.73 eV) states at longer irradiation times. With prolonged exposure, the D peak's spectral weight increased while the A exciton's decreased, driven by non-radiative and defect-mediated recombination. Temperature-dependent PL showed that bound exciton emission weakens with heat, persisting up to 210–240 K. Fitting with the O’Donnell-Chen equation indicated strong electron-phonon coupling for defect-bound excitons (Huang-Rhys factor S of 4.5–5) compared to weaker coupling for A and B excitons. Excitation power-dependent PL demonstrated that defect states saturate at higher laser powers, though D exciton emission still prevailed over A exciton emission in heavily irradiated samples.

Circular polarization-resolved PL measurements showed that only the A exciton is polarized, and its degree of valley polarization dropped from 62% in the as-grown sample to 38% after 120 seconds of irradiation. This reduction is attributed to defect-mediated intervalley transitions and carrier trapping. Temperature-dependent valley polarization followed a non-monotonic trend consistent with the Maialle-Silva-Sham mechanism. First-principles calculations on a 4x4x1 MoS2 supercell confirmed that while bare sulfur vacancies create donor states near the conduction band, oxygen bonding and physisorption at these vacancies introduce shallow and deep acceptor levels near the valence band. This induces net p-type doping, explains the defect PL peak as a transition between the conduction band and acceptor levels, and reduces the Γ-K valley energy separation, enhancing valley depolarization.

The passage details the operation, programming, registers, and application of the Texas Instruments ADS868xW (ADS8681W, ADS8685W, ADS8689W) 16-bit successive approximation (SAR) analog-to-digital converter (ADC). 

**States and Power Modes:**
The device acquires analog input signals in the ACQ state and transitions to the CONV state on a rising edge of the CONVST/CS signal, or to the RESET state on an RST falling edge. After conversion, it returns to the ACQ state. To reduce power consumption at lower throughput rates, the device offers two programmable low-power modes: NAP mode and deep power-down (PD) mode, unlocked by writing 69h to register address 05h.

**Programming and Protocols:**
A data transfer frame begins on the CONVST/CS falling edge and ends on the rising edge. During the frame, the host provides SCLK clocks. Frames are classified as optimal (32 SCLKs), short (<32 SCLKs, where writes are ignored as NOPs but MSB reads are valid), or long (>32 SCLKs, where the last 32 bits form the command). A valid write requires at least 32 SCLKs. The device supports 1-byte or 2-byte (HWORD) operations, where HWORD commands ignore the LSB of the 9-bit address. Output data words can be programmed to include conversion results, fixed patterns, register data, and appended flags (Device Address, ADC Input Range, AVDD Alarm, Input Alarm, and Parity). 

The multiSPI interface uses four legacy SPI-compatible protocols (defaulting to SPI-00-S on power-up or reset) for writing and reading, using either a single SDO-x (1-bit default) or dual SDO-x (2-bit) bus width. Data reads also support a source-synchronous (SRC) protocol using an internal or external clock output on the RVS pin.

**Register Maps:**
The device contains nine 32-bit configuration registers (4 bytes each):
*   `DEVICE_ID_REG` (00h): Identifies up to 16 devices in daisy-chain mode.
*   `RST_PWRCTL_REG` (04h): Controls reset (POR or application), NAP, and PD modes.
*   `SDI_CTL_REG` (08h): Configures the SPI protocol.
*   `SDO_CTL_REG` (0Ch): Controls SDO data output modes, clock sources, and bus width.
*   `DATAOUT_CTL_REG` (10h): Controls output data values and appended flags/parity.
*   `RANGE_SEL_REG` (14h): Configures the internal reference and nine input voltage ranges.
*   `ALARM_REG` (20h): Contains active and tripped output flags for input and AVDD alarms.
*   `ALARM_H_TH_REG` (24h) & `ALARM_L_TH_REG` (28h): Control high/low thresholds and hysteresis for the input alarm.

**Application and Layout:**
The ADS868xW features an integrated analog front-end, programmable gain amplifier, ADC driver, and precision reference, supporting input amplitudes up to ±12.288V and settling to 1% accuracy in under 5µs. An example industrial PLC design pairs the ADS8681W with an 8-channel MUX36D08 differential multiplexer. The programmable input alarm thresholds and hysteresis help prevent false alarms from ambient noise, such as in NTC thermistor temperature-sensing applications. 

The device uses independent AVDD (analog) and DVDD (digital) power supplies. PCB layout guidelines recommend partitioning analog and digital sections, avoiding vias between pins and bypass capacitors, and decoupling AVDD, DVDD, REFCAP, and REFIO pins with specific ceramic capacitors (e.g., 1µF, 4.7µF, and 10µF) to improve the power-supply rejection ratio (PSRR). The document concludes with TI support resources, ESD cautions, revision history, and legal disclaimers.

Founded in 1851, Corning Incorporated is a science-based company with a history of innovation in glass and materials, including lightbulb glass, Pyrex, TV bulbs, and optical fiber. After spinning off its medical and consumer divisions in the 1990s to focus heavily on telecommunications, Corning suffered a severe collapse during the 2001-2002 telecom crash, losing $5.4 billion and laying off 12,000 employees. Instead of abandoning its core identity, returning CEO Jamie Houghton and COO Wendell Weeks increased R&D spending and improved risk management to rebuild the company. 

By 2008, Corning had recovered and operated four main segments: Display Technologies (accounting for 41% of revenue and 87% of net income in 2007), Telecommunications, Environmental Technologies, and Life Sciences. Corning combined these distinct business units with a centralized R&D facility at Sullivan Park, spending 10% of revenue on RD&E—64% funded by the businesses and 36% by corporate. Corning’s philosophy relied on "patient money" (long-term investment before profitability), learning from failure, and a five-stage-gate process to create "keystone" components. 

To manage innovation and balance risk across existing and developing businesses, Corning utilized two main governance councils. The Corning Technology Council (CTC), led by CTO Joe Miller, evaluated early Stage 1 and 2 projects. Promising late-Stage 2, 3, and 4 projects graduated to the Growth and Strategy Council (GSC). Centralized by Weeks in 2002 and led by the CEO, COO, and CTO, the GSC met monthly to review portfolios, provide strategic guidance, and allocate resources using zero-based budgeting. This prevented divisions from having absolute control over their growth portfolios and ensured unprofitable or hurting businesses still received necessary investment. The GSC proved instrumental in major wins, such as rapidly funding a diesel filter line for Volkswagen in 2005 and supporting Verizon's fiber-to-the-home deployment in 2003. 

Despite the GSC's success in fostering open dialogue and strategic alignment, it faced challenges. Some managers found the 18-to-20-person meetings intimidating. Furthermore, as Corning aimed to double its innovation rate to two to four new businesses a decade, executives questioned whether the centralized GSC could effectively scale, prioritize its time, maintain its frank culture, and evaluate entirely unfamiliar business models.

Developed at the University of Delaware by Coach Harold “Tubby” Raymond, the Wing-T is a versatile football offense that uses misdirection, unusual formations, and a diverse run game to slow down aggressive defenses. Rather than relying on a traditional dropback passing game or massive linemen, the Wing-T requires at least two solid running backs—including a strong fullback—an athletic quarterback, and smaller, quicker offensive linemen adept at pulling and trapping. 

The offense utilizes unique alignments such as the Wing, Wing-Slot, and Unbalanced formations to disguise its intentions. Its core running schemes include the Buck Sweep, the Down play, and the Trap. To complement the run game, the Wing-T features deceptive pass plays like the Waggle (designed to look like the Buck Sweep), the Single Receiver Option Route, and the Play Action Vertical Pass. 

While the traditional Wing-T is largely extinct in major college football, it remains popular and effective at the high school level. However, its principles still influence modern college football, with coaches like Gus Malzahn successfully combining Wing-T concepts with the modern spread offense at Auburn and UCF.

This MIT OpenCourseWare lecture covers the ordinary second-order wave equation, which can be written as a second-order equation or a first-order system with a symmetric matrix. Its eigenvalues are c and minus c, indicating a two-way wave effect where waves travel in both directions. While real-world problems involve variable coefficients, high-frequency oscillating forcing terms, and boundary conditions, the lecture focuses on model problems using pure exponentials to analyze growth factors.

In the continuous case, the equation yields two solutions where all frequencies travel at speed c or minus c along characteristic lines without dispersion. The lecture then introduces the semidiscrete method (or method of lines), where space is discrete and time remains continuous. Substituting pure exponentials reveals dispersion, meaning different frequencies travel at different speeds and create oscillating error. This derivation uses trigonometry and the sync function, showing that second differences provide second-order accuracy for a small delta x.

Finally, the lecture examines the fully discrete "leapfrog" method, which is discrete in both time and space. Because it is a multistep method with second differences, a g-squared term appears, requiring the quadratic formula to solve for two growth factors. Stability requires both factors to be less than or equal to 1. This depends on a quantity 'a' and reduces to the Courant-Friedrichs-Lewy condition: the method is stable if the Courant number 'r' is below 1, and unstable if 'r' is above 1. The next lecture will cover staggered grids.

Traditional Fabry–Perot (FP) resonators are too large for compact, scalable optical systems. While various microfabrication techniques exist to create smaller cavities, they involve performance trade-offs, and achieving high finesse at shorter, visible wavelengths requires extremely low surface roughness to minimize scattering loss.

This passage presents a simple, robust, and scalable method to fabricate visible-range microcavities using buckled dielectric membrane mirrors. The process begins by smoothing a silicon wafer via repeated wet oxide growth and HF removal, reducing surface roughness to 33–50 pm. A dielectric coating of SiO2 and Ta2O5 layers is then deposited. Finally, photolithography and a backside Bosch etch suspend the dielectric stack, which naturally buckles from built-in compressive strain. This yields rotationally symmetric mirrors with radii of curvature (ROCs) from 0.9 mm to 21 mm.

Characterized at 780.24 nm using a swept-ring-down method, the microcavities achieved a maximum finesse of 0.89 × 10⁶ and a maximum quality factor (Q) of 2.3 × 10⁹. As cavity length increases from 66 to 3750 µm, finesse drops monotonically due to diffractive losses, while Q increases, plateaus, and then drops. The measured finesse bounds the combined absorption and scattering loss to ≤ 2.20 ppm, corresponding to an upper-bound surface roughness of ≤ 90 pm. 

To demonstrate integrability, individual 1.7 mm mirror chips were etched from the wafer and manually glued together, creating compact cavity assemblies (45 µm and 1 mm lengths) that were tested with a cleaved fiber. These devices maintained high finesse and Q values, proving suitable for compact laser locking, high-efficiency filters, and quantum networking interfaces for neutral atom and ion trap systems.

This disclosure presents a computer-implemented method, system, and computer program product for executing customizable digital twin simulations of physical assets. A digital twin is a virtual representation that tracks changes to a physical asset over its lifespan using real-time data feeds from connected sensors, IoT devices, and recording systems. 

The system utilizes a digital twin module—which can be hosted on a networked computer system, in a cloud computing environment, or within containerized environments—comprising several specialized engines:
*   **Creation Engine:** Generates an initial base digital twin model of a physical asset and creates subsequent versions as the asset undergoes maintenance, modifications, or wear over time.
*   **Data Collection Engine:** Captures, organizes, and stores real-time performance datasets from the physical asset's sensors. These datasets are analyzed to detect asset changes, diagnose issues, and trigger the creation of new digital twin versions. Datasets may also be shared among a community of owners and manufacturers to improve predictive modeling.
*   **Version Management:** Maintains a timestamped timeline and logs detailing the differences between various versions of the digital twin models stored in a repository.
*   **Simulation Engine:** Executes performance simulations based on user-configured parameters. Users can interact with the system via a graphical user interface or augmented reality (AR) devices to design simulations using the current model, a previous version, or a hybrid model constructed by combining components from multiple digital twin versions. 
*   **Reporting Engine:** Displays, formats, and archives simulation results for the user.

To pinpoint performance changes or diagnose problems efficiently without simulating the entire physical asset, users can customize simulations in several ways:
1.  **Bypassing Components:** Users can select specific components of the model to bypass during a simulation to isolate the performance of remaining parts.
2.  **Substituting Components:** Users can replace bypassed or existing components with hypothetical alternatives across multiple simulations to predict the impact of part replacements or upgrades.
3.  **Overriding Values:** For simulations isolated to specific sections or utilizing hybrid models, users can verify intermediate simulation results or manually input overriding values to represent the output of upstream, non-simulated components, serving as entry criteria for the simulated components.

After the simulation engine outputs the results, users can review the data, revise the input parameters, or re-run the simulation as needed.

This passage describes a network security appliance and associated systems and methods for packet processing, rule distribution, and local device administration. 

Because network attacks like denial of service (DoS) can consume bandwidth and prevent remote administration, the described security appliance incorporates a local input/output interface, such as a multi-touch display. This interface allows administrators to control network functionality and configuration directly without logging in over a network. During an attack, the security device blocks the offending packets, sends notifications, and reserves memory and processing resources to give priority to the local interface. This allows users to mitigate attacks—such as by modifying filter rules, reprioritizing rules, or blocking sources—without manually rebooting or disconnecting the appliance.

The local interface also manages new or unrecognized devices (like IoT appliances) joining a local network. The security device automatically detects packets from unrecognized sources, buffers or blocks the traffic, and alerts the user. The user must physically interact with the local interface within a set timeframe to authorize the device and configure its filtering rules; otherwise, the packets are discarded.

To accelerate packet inspection and reduce latency compared to traditional B-tree database searches, the appliance can utilize geoprocessing-based analysis. Filter parameters (such as IP addresses, ports, and protocols) are mapped to multidimensional topographic regions or minimum bounding rectangles (MBRs). Incoming packets are compared to these regions using spatial algorithms and R-tree data structures, allowing multiple parameters to be searched simultaneously and much faster.

Additionally, to save memory, bandwidth, and processing power on individual appliances, a management server distributes security rules using a statistical model rather than sending an entire rules database to every device. Rules are divided into two categories: mandatory rules for known, active threats (distributed to 100% of appliances) and potential rules for inactive threats. Potential rules are distributed randomly to a subset of appliances based on likelihood scores or weights, using a random number generator or device-specific hashes. Appliances holding potential rules act as test machines; if an appliance detects an attack matching a potential rule, it notifies the management server, which can then upgrade the rule to mandatory for all appliances. Rule sets are refreshed periodically, often by transmitting only the differences (deltas) between old and new sets.

Finally, the passage details the hardware and software components of the security devices, client devices, and management servers, which include processors, memory, network interfaces, network stacks, packet processing engines, filter analyzers, and various operating systems and storage mediums.

The Supreme Court will hear arguments regarding a challenge to Colorado’s 2019 Minor Conversion Therapy Law, which bans mental health professionals from providing treatments intended to change a minor's sexual orientation or gender identity. 

Licensed counselor Kaley Chiles challenged the law, arguing it violates her free speech rights. After a district court and a divided 10th Circuit panel upheld the ban—ruling it regulates professional conduct that only incidentally involves speech, thus passing the lenient "rational basis" test—Chiles appealed to the Supreme Court. 

Chiles and supporting U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer argue that because her talk therapy uses only speech, the ban constitutes viewpoint discrimination and must face "strict scrutiny." They contend the law fails this stringent test because it lacks evidence of causing harm and is not narrowly tailored, as it allows non-licensed individuals to have the same conversations and permits counselors to have them with adults.

Conversely, Colorado argues the law narrowly regulates an unsafe, ineffective healthcare treatment, not speech, amidst a teen mental health crisis. The state warns that ruling for Chiles would destabilize longstanding healthcare regulations delivered through words. Colorado maintains that rational basis review applies, though it insists the law would also survive strict scrutiny.

Standardized testing mandates cause educators to alter curricula and narrow instruction to cater to specific exams. Through school choice programs and graduation requirements, several states force both public and private school students to take state-made exams, the SAT, or the ACT. Consequently, schools must align their priorities with these tests, even as exams like the SAT have lowered their standards in reading and math. 

Rather than banning standardized tests—which universities still find valuable for admissions—policymakers should offer testing choices. Alternatives like the Classic Learning Test (CLT), which uses classic texts to assess literacy and numeracy, allow schools to select assessments that fit their pedagogical styles. Because different tests can be reliably compared using scale alignments and correlated scoring, states can still compare student performance without relying on a single exam. Therefore, states should follow the examples of Arkansas and Florida by offering a menu of assessment options for school choice programs, graduation requirements, public college admissions, and scholarships to ensure education diversity and freedom.

In *National Sheet Metal Company v. A A A Highway Express Incorporated et al.*, decided March 4, 1937, the plaintiff sought damages for an automobile accident at a street intersection, alleging negligent operation by the defendants. The court affirmed the judgment in favor of the defendants, finding that conflicting evidence authorized the verdict and no error of law appeared. Specifically, the court found no error in the trial court's jury instructions regarding the defendants' alleged failure to sound a horn, both parties' lawful right to use the highway, the obligation to exercise ordinary care, alleged violations of State law and city ordinances, or comparative negligence. Furthermore, without specific allegations in the petition or special requests, the trial court did not err by omitting instructions on right-of-way laws or speed reduction at intersections. Finally, because the verdict favored the defendants, any alleged error concerning the measure of damages was deemed harmless. Judges Stephens, Sutton, and Felton concurred in the decision.
