This passage outlines hardware specifications, system functions, and peripheral timings for a Texas Instruments digital media processor. 

**Power and Resets:**
PLL and analog supplies require ferrite beads and small 0.1uF decoupling capacitors placed close to the pins, alongside bulk (10uF+) capacitors. System-level resets include Power-on Reset (POR), External Warm, Emulation Warm, Watchdog, Software Global Cold/Warm, Test (TRST), and Local resets. The device supports reset isolation for the PCI Express (PCIE) module and the Ethernet Switch (EMAC Switch). Most I/O pins enter a Hi-Z state during reset, and upon release, the ARM Cortex-A8 executes from the internal Boot ROM.

**Clocking and Interrupts:**
Device clocks are generated from reference clocks (DEV, AUX, SERDES_CLKN/P, CLKIN32, and AUD_CLKIN0/1/2) fed into 12 top-level and 4 embedded PLLs, which start in Bypass mode after reset. The DEV and AUX clocks (typically 20–30 MHz) use either an external crystal with internal oscillators or a 1.8-V LVCMOS input. Clock outputs (SYSCLKs) are routed to modules via the PRCM. Interrupts are managed by the ARM Cortex-A8 Interrupt Controller (handling up to 128 requests) and the C674x DSP interrupt controller (combining 128 events into 12 prioritized interrupts).

**Peripherals and Debugging:**
* **DCAN & EDMA:** Two DCAN interfaces support CAN 2.0 (A/B). The EDMA controller manages data transfers across 64 channels mapped to synchronization events.
* **Debugging:** Supports Advanced Event Triggering (AET), real-time Trace (at Cortex-A8 and System levels), and IEEE 1149.1 JTAG for boundary scan and emulation.
* **EMAC & MDIO:** The 3-port gigabit EMAC switch supports MII, GMII, RMII, and RGMII modes at 3.3V I/O. The MDIO module polls up to 32 addresses to manage external PHYs.
* **GPIO & GPMC/ELM:** Four GPIO modules provide up to 128 configurable I/O pins. The GPMC provides a glueless 8-/16-bit interface to external memories (NOR, NAND, SRAM), supported by the Error Locator Module (ELM) for NAND BCH error extraction.
* **Video (HDMI, HDVPSS, Video DAC):** Includes an HDMI 1.3a transmitter requiring specific TMDS PCB routing (100-Ω differential, 60-Ω single-ended impedance) and ESD protection. The HDVPSS handles video input capture and output processing. The analog Video DAC operates in Normal mode (internal amplifier) or TVOUT Bypass mode (external amplifier) for 75-Ω systems.
* **I2C:** Four I2C modules (v2.1 compliant) support 8-bit data transfers at 10–400 Kbps with 32-byte FIFOs. 

Extensive register maps, AC timing requirements, and switching characteristics are provided for these interfaces.

This passage details the technical specifications, electrical timing requirements, and peripheral interfaces for the Texas Instruments device. 

**Resets, Clocks, and Interrupts**
The device supports reset isolation for the PCI Express (PCIE) Subsystem and the Ethernet Switch (EMAC Switch), allowing them to reset independently or remain undisrupted during certain system resets. Each power domain has dedicated Warm and Cold Resets. During most resets, device I/O pins enter a Hi-Z state, except for Emulation, isolated EMAC Switch, and RSTOUT_WD_OUT pins. Upon reset release, the ARM Cortex-A8 executes Boot ROM code.
System clocks are generated from reference clocks—primarily the Device (DEV, typically 20 MHz) and Auxiliary (AUX, 20–30 MHz) clocks—which are sourced via internal oscillators with external crystals or external 1.8-V LVCMOS-compatible inputs. Additional inputs include a differential clock for the PCIE PHY, AUD_CLKIN0/1/2, and a 32768-Hz CLKIN32. Two selectable clock outputs (CLKOUT0/1) are provided. The device uses 12 top-level and 4 embedded PLLs, which initialize in Bypass mode after reset and feed the PRCM Module to generate SYSCLKs. 
Interrupts are serviced by the ARM Cortex-A8 Interrupt Controller (AINTC), handling up to 128 programmable requests, and the C674x DSP interrupt controller, which combines up to 128 device events into 12 prioritized interrupts.

**Peripherals and Debugging**
*   **DCAN:** Two interfaces support CAN protocol 2.0 parts A and B for real-time control.
*   **EDMA:** Handles data transfers between memory and slave peripherals using up to 64 channels mapped to synchronization events.
*   **Debugging:** Features Advanced Event Triggering (AET), real-time Trace (at Cortex-A8 and System levels), and an IEEE 1149.1 JTAG interface with an internal pulldown on the TRST pin.
*   **EMAC Switch & MDIO:** A 3-port gigabit switch (one internal, two external) supporting 10/100/1000 Mbps across MII, GMII, RMII, and RGMII modes at 3.3 V. It uses the CPPI protocol and an MDIO module to poll and control up to 32 PHY addresses.
*   **GPIO:** Four modules provide up to 128 configurable 1.8-V/3.3-V I/O pins capable of generating CPU interrupts.
*   **GPMC & ELM:** The General-Purpose Memory Controller interfaces with NOR, NAND, SRAM, and Pseudo-SRAM on an 8-/16-bit bus (up to 512 MBytes across 8 chip selects). The Error Locator Module (ELM) uses BCH algorithms to locate 4-, 8-, and 16-bit errors in NAND operations.
*   **Video & Imaging:** An HDMI 1.3a transmitter (supporting TMDS, DDC, and CEC) requires external 5V ESD protection and specific PCB routing (100 Ω differential, 60 Ω single-ended impedance). The High-Definition Video Processing Subsystem (HDVPSS) manages video inputs and outputs, featuring two display pipelines, three graphics layers, and analog video DACs (operating in Normal or TVOUT Bypass mode). The Imaging Subsystem (ISS) processes pixel data via Parallel (CAM) or Serial (CSI2) interfaces using an Image Signal Processor (ISP).
*   **I2C:** Four modules support Philips I2C v2.1 (10–400 Kbps) in master/slave modes with a 32-byte FIFO, lacking fail-safe I/O buffers.
*   **DDR2/DDR3:** A dedicated controller supports JEDEC-compliant 64Mb–4Gb SDRAM devices with 16- or 32-bit data paths, two PHYs, and dynamic memory interleaving, requiring strict adherence to TI PCB routing and termination rules.

Citizenship education and science education are interconnected, as both aim to cultivate informed, responsible, and scientifically literate individuals capable of addressing societal and global challenges, including the UN's Sustainable Development Goals. In Turkey, however, citizenship education is largely confined to social studies, leaving its relationship with science education tenuous and poorly defined, despite the 2018 Turkish science curriculum incorporating a Science, Technology, Society, and Environment (STSE) approach. 

This qualitative study examined the links between science and citizenship education in Turkey by analyzing the national science curriculum and interviewing eight secondary school science teachers. Thematic analysis revealed that both the curriculum and teachers conceptualize this connection through scientific literacy, society, the environment, values, and skills. While technology is emphasized in the curriculum, teachers did not strongly link it to citizenship. 

Teachers emphasized that scientific literacy is essential for active citizenship, equipping students with critical thinking, inquiry, observation, and problem-solving skills. They also connected science education to societal life—such as public health, safety, and socio-scientific issues (e.g., climate change, COVID-19)—and highlighted the cultivation of values like responsibility, respect, scientific integrity, and patriotism. Environmental awareness and conservation emerged as the most prominent links to active citizenship in both the curriculum and teacher interviews.

Despite recognizing a strong theoretical link between science and citizenship education, the interviewed teachers reported that practical implementation often falls short. Major barriers include an exam-centric education system that prioritizes test-taking over practical application, overcrowded classrooms, inadequate laboratory infrastructure, curriculum deficiencies, and communication challenges with refugee students. 

The authors conclude that education policymakers should explicitly integrate citizenship competencies, socio-scientific issues, and sustainability into the science curriculum, while providing teachers with the necessary training and support to foster scientifically literate, democratic citizens.

The Fourth Industrial Revolution (4IR) and Education 4.0 demand a shift from rote, memory-based education to personalized, skill-based learning and assessment. Aligned with India's National Education Policy (2020), Digital Game-Based Learning (DGBL) is emerging as an innovative pedagogy. Digital Games (DGs) make learning engaging, reduce extraneous cognitive load through multimodal environments, and help develop both cognitive and non-cognitive skills. 

In assessment, DGs offer a flexible alternative to detached traditional methods. A key technique is Stealth Assessment (SA), an automated process that measures and enhances learning in real-time during gameplay without the learner's awareness, thereby reducing test anxiety. SA relies on a multidisciplinary approach combining Evidence-Centered Design (ECD), Machine Learning (ML) algorithms, formative assessment, and feedback. As students play, ECD and ML algorithms collect and statistically analyze digital traces to evaluate competencies, provide immediate feedback, and create customized learning support systems. 

Despite these benefits, DGBL remains underused by teachers due to several challenges. Developing customized educational games is difficult because it requires integrating multiple disciplines, including education, psychology, technology, and neuroscience. Additionally, concerns exist regarding cognitive overload, improperly calibrated game difficulty, potential negative brain impacts (such as reduced gray matter), and the need for extensive research to establish the validity and reliability of DGBL.

Integrating Artificial Intelligence (AI) and educational robotics into early childhood and primary education personalizes learning, supports inclusive environments, and develops digital competencies and computational thinking. Because introducing these technologies requires new teaching competencies, this 2024 mixed-method study investigated the conceptions of future preschool and primary school teachers regarding robots. 

Researchers initially surveyed 143 fourth-year students at the University of Belgrade using a Draw-And-Answer-Test (DAAT), requiring participants to draw a robot and answer open-ended questions. Twenty-two students exhibited misconceptions, mostly depicting robots as standard electrical appliances, stick figures, virtual reality hardware, or avatars. The remaining 121 students (75 preschool, 46 primary) demonstrated accurate conceptions. Most (98) had real-life experience with robots—primarily at their faculty—with preschool education students having three times more in-person experience than primary education students. 

Respondents most commonly depicted animal-shaped robots (47.1%, like the Bee-Bot), typical robots (24.8%), mechanical objects (24%), and humanoids (4.1%). Most drawings (76) showed neutral emotions, while 44 showed positive emotions and one was negative. The most recognized robot functions were educational (52.9%) and assistive (31.4%). Experimental studies of neutrino oscillations rely on various sources, including supernova explosions, Big Bang relics, cosmic ray showers, the sun, particle accelerators, and nuclear reactors. These studies examine parameters such as length, energy, and sensitivity to specific mass ranges. 

Early solar neutrino experiments, like the Davis (Homestake) experiment, observed fewer electron neutrinos than theoretically expected. Later, the SNO experiment used neutral scattering to measure the total number of neutrinos, finding it matched theoretical expectations. This proved the neutrinos were not lost, but oscillating between flavors. 

Atmospheric neutrinos are produced by cosmic rays interacting with the atmosphere, causing pions and kaons to decay. Experiments showed that the expected ratio of muon to electron neutrinos was not observed because the muon-like neutrinos disappear due to oscillation. 

Accelerator-driven neutrino experiments, located at facilities like Fermilab, CERN, and in Japan (such as T2K), gained prominence in the 2000s. They use both near and far detectors to measure total flux and observe neutrino appearance or disappearance, providing clear evidence of oscillation. 

Finally, reactor neutrinos are produced via the nuclear fission of heavy isotopes like uranium and polonium. Experiments in countries like France, Japan, and China use inverse beta decay to study anti-electron neutrino disappearance, allowing researchers to directly observe neutrino oscillation and survival probability.

Governments are increasingly focusing on regulating artificial intelligence (AI), making AI policy a vital area of study. Although policy and compliance will significantly impact the AI development life cycle, AI policy discussions are largely absent from computer science (CS) curricula. To address this gap, this paper synthesizes AI regulatory developments in the United States and European Union and proposes a framework to integrate AI policy discussions into CS courses.

The US and EU are key state actors that heavily influence AI developers. In the US, comprehensive federal AI legislation does not yet exist, and efforts primarily consist of non-binding statements. Furthermore, US AI policy exhibits partisan divides at both state and federal levels. Democrats generally favor consumer protection and safety, as seen in President Biden’s 2023 Executive Order 14110. Conversely, Republicans emphasize economic competitiveness and national security, evidenced by President Trump’s 2025 rescission of EO 14110 and replacement with EO 14179, which focuses on maintaining global AI dominance. In contrast, the EU enacted the comprehensive EU AI Act in 2024. The Act categorizes AI systems by risk level: it prohibits unacceptable risk practices, subjects high-risk practices to management and oversight requirements, and imposes transparency and copyright compliance rules on general-purpose AI models.

Three main themes emerge from the US and EU landscapes:
1. The AI policy landscape is rapidly changing, particularly in the US, requiring developers to adapt to shifting regulatory demands.
2. Translating non-technical, abstract policy goals into concrete technical specifications is challenging, especially when technical solutions (such as uncircumventable watermarks) do not yet exist. This requires collaboration between policymakers and engineers.
3. Because the technology economy is global, regulations like the EU AI Act will likely have cross-border implications, potentially influencing US companies to adopt EU standards globally, similar to the "Brussels Effect" seen with the GDPR.

To integrate AI policy into computing courses, the authors propose a flexible framework built on a continuum of three perspectives—socio-political, translational, and technical—intersected with three dimensions: scope, power, and agency. The translational perspective bridges normative socio-political preferences and technical specifications. The dimensions examine what a policy requires (scope), who creates and benefits from the policy (power), and how practitioners can influence policy and navigate ethical dilemmas (agency). A grid of guiding questions across these perspectives and dimensions is provided to help students evaluate AI policies, consider underrepresented viewpoints, and translate abstract demands into technical interventions. Future work may involve developing targeted curricular activities for this framework and applying requirements engineering practices to bridge the gap between AI principles and practices.

This study develops and experimentally validates a unified, parameter-free multiscale framework linking atomic-scale solid-melt interface energetics to macroscopic GaN crystal growth kinetics. Using molecular dynamics simulations based on a machine learning interatomic potential at 1000 K, the researchers confirmed that liquid Ga atoms at the GaN-Ga melt interface form structurally ordered layers with localized charge redistribution, varying between Ga-polar and N-polar surfaces. 

Well-tempered metadynamics simulations were then applied to calculate the free energy landscapes for N adatom adsorption, lateral migration, and step-edge crossing. These calculations revealed a "Ga lubrication" mechanism: interfacial liquid Ga forms bonds that reduce N adatom lateral migration energy barriers (to approximately 0.56 eV on Ga-polar and 0.34 eV on N-polar interfaces) compared to a clean Ga-polar surface (~1.1 eV). However, N adatoms approaching step edges from upper terraces encounter higher Ehrlich-Schwoebel barriers (>0.6 eV), which can hinder step descent.

Integrating these energy barriers into kinetic Monte Carlo simulations demonstrated that while high N flux (10²⁸ m⁻²s⁻¹) causes rough, joint-island growth, lower N flux (10²⁴ m⁻²s⁻¹)—and practical molecular-beam epitaxy (MBE) conditions—operates in a diffusion-controlled, layer-by-layer regime. Consequently, the authors embedded the simulated free energies, N diffusivity, and N solubility limits into a continuous diffusion-controlled mathematical model based on a modified Fick's first law. This model predicted facet-specific growth rates between 0.01 and 0.04 nm/s for wurtzite and zinc blende GaN phases without using fitted parameters.

To validate the model, partially nitridated Ga/GaN particles were grown via MBE on amorphous SiNx substrates at 650 °C for 1 and 5 minutes. Characterization of over 200 particles using scanning and high-resolution transmission electron microscopy confirmed the predicted facet-dependent growth rates and morphological trends. The findings establish that for systems with near-zero solubility of key elements, like N in liquid Ga, the interfacial free-energy profile for adatom adsorption and migration dictates crystal growth kinetics. Stated limitations of the current framework include omitting trace impurities (such as O or H), potential machine learning interatomic potential training set constraints, simplifying assumptions in the one-dimensional steady-state diffusion equation, and experimental averaging over multiple facets.

The passage details the technical specifications, operational modes, programming, and application guidelines for the Texas Instruments ADS868xW (ADS8681W, ADS8685W, ADS8689W) 16-bit SAR ADC data acquisition devices.

**Analog Front-End and Reference:**
The device integrates a Programmable Gain Amplifier (PGA) that converts single-ended or differential inputs (bipolar or unipolar) and adjusts common-mode levels. Gain is configured via the `RANGE_SEL[3:0]` bits, utilizing trimmed resistors to minimize gain error. A second-order, antialiasing low-pass filter (LPF) with a typical 500kHz cutoff frequency follows the PGA, along with an integrated high-bandwidth ADC driver. The device operates with a factory-trimmed 4.096V internal reference (enabled by default) or an external reference with an internal buffer. The internal reference is temperature-compensated from –40°C to +125°C, though soldering thermal stress can shift the value. Specific decoupling capacitors are required on the REFIO and REFCAP pins. The ADC outputs data in a straight-binary format.

**Alarms:**
The device features active-high input and AVDD alarms, which can be output on a multifunction pin, read from internal registers, or appended to the data output. Each alarm has active and tripped flags. The input alarm monitors the ADC input against user-programmable high and low thresholds and a common hysteresis setting. The AVDD alarm monitors the analog supply against fixed thresholds of 4.7V and 5.3V.

**Interfaces, Modes, and Programming:**
Communication utilizes a multiSPI digital interface, acting as a 32-bit input-output shift register. Topologies include single-device configurations or multiple devices in a daisy-chain. The device operates in three states controlled by the `CONVST/CS` and `RST` pins: RESET (configurable as application reset or power-on reset), ACQ (signal acquisition), and CONV (conversion using an internal clock). 

Programming utilizes 32-bit optimal data transfer frames, though short and long frames are also processed. The device supports 1-byte or 2-byte (`HWORD`) read, write, set, and clear commands across nine configuration registers (`DEVICE_ID_REG`, `RST_PWRCTL_REG`, `SDI_CTL_REG`, `SDO_CTL_REG`, `DATAOUT_CTL_REG`, `RANGE_SEL_REG`, `ALARM_REG`, `ALARM_H_TH_REG`, and `ALARM_L_TH_REG`). Write operations use four legacy SPI protocols. Read operations support legacy SPI protocols (single or dual SDO) and source-synchronous (SRC) protocols using an internal or external clock. Output data words can be configured to append device addresses, range settings, alarm flags, and parity bits.

**Applications, Power, and Documentation:**
An example application combines the ADS8681W with an 8-channel MUX36D08 multiplexer for industrial PLC modules, achieving a 5µs settling time. Another application uses an NTC thermistor to demonstrate how programmable alarm hysteresis prevents false triggers from ambient noise. The device uses separate analog (AVDD) and digital (DVDD) supplies, requiring specific decoupling capacitors and PCB partitioning to optimize the power-supply rejection ratio (PSRR) and minimize noise. For power saving at lower throughput rates, the device offers programmable NAP and deep power-down (PD) modes. The passage concludes with related TI documentation, support resources, ESD cautions, a May 2025 revision history note, and legal disclaimers.

This study compared air-conduction (AC) and bone-conduction (BC) Auditory Brainstem Response (ABR)—the current diagnostic gold standard—and Auditory Steady-State Response (ASSR) thresholds in 50 sleeping infants (aged 0–6 months) with normal hearing (NH) and conductive hearing loss (CHL). Participants underwent 1000 Hz tympanometry, transient-evoked otoacoustic emissions (TEOAEs), ABR, and ASSR testing at 500 and 2000 Hz. Because no infants demonstrated CHL at 2000 Hz, analyses primarily focused on 500 Hz data. 

Results at 500 Hz showed that AC ABR and AC ASSR thresholds were significantly higher in the CHL group than in the NH group, while BC thresholds did not significantly differ between groups for either test. However, AC and BC thresholds between ABR and ASSR were poorly correlated, and ASSR thresholds had greater standard deviations. The mean 500 Hz air-bone gaps (ABGs) were significantly larger in the CHL group (ABR: 36 dB; ASSR: 21 dB) compared to the NH group (ABR: 15 dB; ASSR: 12 dB), though ABR and ASSR ABG sizes were poorly correlated. Furthermore, there was greater overlap in ASSR thresholds and ABGs between the NH and CHL groups compared to the ABR. 

Minimum normal intensities (the level at which >90% of NH infants responded) for ABR were 30 dB nHL for 2000 Hz (AC and BC), 35 dB nHL for 500 Hz AC, and 20 dB nHL for 500 Hz BC. For ASSR, minimum intensities were 40 dB HL for 2000 Hz (AC and BC), 40 dB HL for 500 Hz AC, and 30 dB HL for 500 Hz BC. 

When evaluating CHL detection, cutoff thresholds where the ASSR ABG had high sensitivity lacked high specificity. Overall, ASSR thresholds and ABG sizes had too much variability to reliably separate NH from mild low-frequency CHL. The authors conclude that ABR remains the superior diagnostic tool for Early Hearing Detection and Intervention (EHDI) programs, and ASSR requires further research across various degrees of hearing loss and frequencies before clinical implementation.

NVIDIA Turing GPUs introduce a Hybrid Rendering model that combines real-time ray tracing, rasterization, AI, and simulation. Real-time ray tracing is enabled by new hardware-based RT Cores in each SM, which autonomously accelerate Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH) traversal and ray/triangle intersection testing. This offloads the SM and, when combined with advanced denoising filtering, delivers up to 10 times faster ray tracing performance than the Pascal architecture. This capability enables physically accurate ray-traced shadows, ambient occlusion, and reflections in real time.

Turing also features NVIDIA NGX (Neural Graphics Acceleration), a deep learning technology stack utilizing Tensor Cores for AI-based graphics enhancements. NGX includes Deep Learning Super-Sampling (DLSS), which renders at lower input sample counts and uses a trained neural network to infer high-quality results with roughly half the shading work of Temporal Anti-Aliasing (TAA). Other NGX features include InPainting to replace removed image content, AI Slow-Mo for smooth frame interpolation, and AI Super Rez for upscaling images and video.

To optimize geometry and shading, Turing introduces several new features:
*   **Mesh Shading:** Uses cooperative Task and Mesh Shaders to process object lists in parallel, eliminating CPU draw call bottlenecks and enabling dynamic level-of-detail (LOD) management.
*   **Variable Rate Shading (VRS):** Allows developers to dynamically adjust the shading rate for every 16x16 pixel region independently of the visibility rate, supporting Content Adaptive Shading, Motion Adaptive Shading, and Foveated Rendering.
*   **Texture Space Shading (TSS):** Decouples visibility and appearance sampling by computing and storing shading values as texels in a separate texture space for reuse across frames or views.
*   **Multi-View Rendering (MVR):** Expands on Pascal’s Simultaneous Multi-Projection by supporting up to four views per pass in hardware, improving efficiency for complex stereo and canted VR displays.

Additional advancements include DX12 resource binding improvements and VR enhancements such as VirtualLink (USB Type-C) connectivity and RT Core-accelerated VRWorks Audio. 

Turing is implemented in the TU102, TU104 (used in the GeForce RTX 2080, Quadro RTX 5000, and Tesla T4), and TU106 (used in the GeForce RTX 2070) GPUs. Unlike TU102 and TU104, the TU106 does not support NVLink or SLI. Because hybrid rendering uses multiple operation types concurrently—including Tensor, FP32, RT, and parallel INT32 operations—NVIDIA introduced the RTX-OPS metric, which calculates usable performance by derating peak operations based on their representative workload distribution over a single frame time. The passage concludes with legal disclaimers, warranty limitations, and trademark notices from NVIDIA.

Inclusive education ensures equal opportunities for all children in mainstream settings by removing barriers to learning. Effective implementation requires well-defined legal frameworks and educational leaders who are aware of them. Because existing research in Ethiopia has focused primarily on physical and preparedness barriers rather than legal frameworks, this study assesses the global, regional, and national policies guiding inclusive education and evaluates the policy awareness of educational leaders in Addis Ababa’s resource centers.

Using a qualitative case study design, researchers purposively selected fifteen participants—school principals, itinerant teachers, general teachers, and Ministry of Education (MoE) Inclusion Department experts—across three Addis Ababa inclusive education resource centers. Data were collected via semi-structured interviews and document reviews, then analyzed thematically.

The document review identified several legal frameworks supporting inclusive education:
*   **Global:** The Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR), International Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination (ICERD), Convention on the Rights of the Child (CRC), Salamanca Statement, Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (CRPD), Marrakesh Treaty, and Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).
*   **Regional (Africa):** The African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights (ACHPR), African Charter on the Rights and Welfare of the Child (ACRWC), and the African Disability Protocol.
*   **National (Ethiopia):** The Constitution, Proclamation No. 1263/2021, Education and Training Policy (ETP 2023), Education Sector Development Plan VI (2020-2025), Special Needs/Inclusive Education Strategy (2022/23-2029/30), and the National Children’s Policy (2017). 

Findings regarding policy awareness revealed significant variations among participants:
*   **MoE Experts:** Demonstrated strong insight into global, regional, and national frameworks. However, it was noted that Ethiopia lacks a single, stand-alone national policy dedicated specifically to inclusive education.
*   **School Principals:** Showed a significant gap in awareness. While acknowledging the importance of accommodating students with disabilities, they lacked detailed knowledge of specific policies due to insufficient training and the demands of daily school routines.
*   **Itinerant Teachers:** Possessed a good understanding of the legal frameworks, largely due to their specialized academic backgrounds in special needs education. They noted that school principals and district leaders lacked this awareness because they are often subject-matter graduates without formal training in inclusive education.
*   **General Teachers:** Admitted to having no awareness of specific national or international legal frameworks. They viewed inclusive education merely as a matter of personal compassion, fairness, and humanitarian effort rather than a practice guided by formal policy.

Advancing quantum technologies requires modeling nanoscale light-matter interactions, yet a unified approach bridging quantum and classical descriptions is needed. Classical electromagnetic solvers cannot capture nonclassical features like entanglement, while quantum models describe idealized systems, cannot account for realistic macroscopic devices, and become computationally prohibitive for large systems. Semiclassical approximations also fail to accurately capture quantum features. 

To address the incompatibility between quantum simulations and classical Maxwell solvers, the authors introduce a stochastic Bloch-vector approach underpinned by stochastic differential equations (SDEs). Unlike conventional methods, this approach does not rely on wave-function unraveling, phase-space representations, or operator-valued noise. Instead, it overcomes the limitations of symmetric diffusion matrices by deriving a stochastic Bloch vector from a complex, non-symmetric diffusion matrix to capture asymmetric noise correlations from non-commuting quantum operators. This method links quantum emitter dynamics to spatio-temporally resolved classical electromagnetic fields and offers potential integration with Maxwell solvers. The approach is validated using a coherently driven two-level system and the Mollow spectrum, as well as comparisons to dedicated experiments.

Human rights education (HRE) in higher education is largely siloed in law schools, and existing teaching models do not fully address contemporary threats or the risk of compounding lived, intergenerational, or secondary trauma among students. Because many university learners—including refugees, LGBTQ+ students, and those with adverse childhood experiences—carry trauma histories, trauma-informed human rights education (TIHRE) is needed to mitigate adverse responses and empower students toward advocacy. 

Grounded in an interdisciplinary literature review and frameworks from the UN and SAMHSA, this article recommends three core practices for implementing TIHRE:

1. **Developing a Teaching Persona:** Educators should undergo "values clarification" to identify unconscious biases and unresolved traumas. They must cultivate an authentic, empathetic persona and build mutual trust, such as by learning students' names and backgrounds.
2. **Trauma-Sensitive Content Design:** Curricula should integrate the UN's tripartite framework (learning *about*, *through*, and *for* human rights) while avoiding graphic "trauma porn" or romanticized narratives. Educators can foster safety and agency by providing advance warnings of sensitive content, conducting wellbeing check-ins, utilizing student co-creation and project-based learning, and embedding structured reflective exercises like Gibbs’ Reflective Cycle.
3. **Dialogic Learning:** TIHRE should replace traditional power hierarchies with horizontal, discussion-based relationships that build critical thinking, community, and advocacy skills. Educators are encouraged to step back to allow student leadership and invite survivors and practitioners as guest speakers to bridge theory and real-world application. 

Ultimately, TIHRE aims to prioritize wellbeing, dignity, and agency, transforming learners and educators into catalysts for hope and human rights action.

This document standardizes the Guest-Hypervisor Communication Block (GHCB) memory area and protocols to enable a guest operating system (OS) to interoperate with hypervisors supporting Secure Encrypted Virtualization - Encrypted State (SEV-ES) or Secure Encrypted Virtualization – Secure Nested Paging (SEV-SNP). Because SEV-ES and SEV-SNP encrypt the guest's register state during world switches, the guest uses the 4 KB decrypted GHCB page to selectively share necessary register states with the hypervisor during Non-Automatic Exits (NAEs).

The specification details protocol versions and revisions (including Version 2 and Revisions 2.01 through 2.04), which introduce hypervisor feature advertisement via a 52-bit FEATURES bitmap. Prior to establishing the GHCB page or when decrypted memory cannot be written, the guest and hypervisor can communicate using the lower 12 bits of the GHCB MSR (0xc001_0130). This GHCB MSR protocol supports protocol negotiation, retrieving the SEV page table encryption bit, requesting CPUID values, AP reset holds, page state changes, running different VMPL levels, requesting termination, and registering or unregistering the GHCB guest physical address (GPA), which is required for SEV-SNP guests. The document also defines the SEV-SNP Secrets Page Guest Reserved Area (including 64-bit guest request message sequence numbers and the AP Jump Table address) and the EFI SEV-SNP Confidential Computing Blob configuration table used by firmware to pass the secrets and CPUID pages to the OS.

When an NAE occurs, hardware throws a VMM Communication Exception (#VC). The guest's #VC handler inspects the error code, populates the required fields and the VALID_BITMAP in the GHCB, and invokes the VMGEXIT instruction to generate an Automatic Exit (AE) for the hypervisor to process. The specification defines the standard VMGEXIT processing rules, error reporting via SW_EXITINFO1 and SW_EXITINFO2, and specific requirements for supported NAE events. These events include:
*   **IOIO_PROT, MSR_PROT, VMMCALL, and #NPF/MMIO Access:** Handling I/O instructions, MSR reads/writes, hypercalls, and memory-mapped I/O using shared decrypted buffers.
*   **Page State Change:** Allowing guests to request the hypervisor to make pages private or shared, or to provide PSMASH and UNSMASH hints for the RMP table.
*   **SNP Guest Requests:** Enabling SEV-SNP guests to communicate with the SEV-SNP firmware (SNP Guest Request), retrieve VCEK/VLEK certificate data (SNP Extended Guest Request), and bind to trusted PCIe devices while retrieving measurements, certificates, and TDISP attestation reports (SNP TIO Guest Request).
*   **AP Management and Multi-VMPL:** Retrieving the guest's APIC ID list, changing the vCPU's current VMPL level (SNP Run VMPL), and creating, updating, or destroying an AP's VMSA page at a specified VMPL level (SNP AP Creation).
*   **Secure AVIC:** Managing guest-owned APIC state using registered private backing pages per vCPU.
*   **Termination and Unsupported Events:** Allowing guests to request termination with specific reason codes or report unsupported NAE events.

Additionally, the document standardizes specific operational behaviors for SEV-ES and SEV-SNP guests:
*   **Guest Identification:** Hypervisors must provide specific CPUID properties so the guest can identify SEV-ES support and the encryption bit position.
*   **SMP Booting:** Because hypervisors cannot modify encrypted vCPU registers after initial measurement, APs cannot use the traditional INIT-SIPI-SIPI sequence to set the CS and IP registers. For SEV-ES and basic SEV-SNP, APs must use initial measured register values, park using the AP Reset Hold NAE or MSR protocol, and transition from UEFI to the OS using an AP jump table. Alternatively, SEV-SNP guests can use the SNP AP Creation NAE event to directly initialize or update AP VMSA pages, which also enables vCPU hotplug.
*   **Non-Maskable Interrupts (NMIs) and Debug Registers:** Hypervisors must intercept #DB (not IRET) and wait for an "NMI Complete" VMGEXIT before injecting another NMI. Hardware debug registers are virtualized via the VMSA if "DebugVirtualization" is supported; otherwise, the hypervisor must intercept DR7 accesses. System Management Mode (SMM) and nested virtualization are not supported.
*   **SNP Restricted Injection:** To safely isolate SEV-SNP guests, the Restricted Injection feature limits the host to notifying the guest of events via a #HV exception and a shared #HV doorbell page. The specification defines NAE events for configuring the doorbell page, sending IPIs (#HV Send IPI), and emulating APIC timers (#HV Timer). The doorbell page uses "PendingEvent" and "NoEoiRequired" fields to allow the host to present interrupt vectors and non-maskable events (like NMI or #MC) and to optimize End-of-Interrupt (EOI) cycles without requiring VM exits. To avoid interrupt shadow issues, guests must execute HLT with interrupts disabled and check for pending interrupts immediately upon resuming.

This study investigates whether and how the textual content ("soft" information) of earnings press releases predicts announcement-day stock returns, alongside numerical earnings surprises ("hard" information). The authors analyze a dataset of over 138,000 after-hours press releases issued between 2005 and 2023 (with 134,354 from 2006–2023 used for the main analysis). 

To extract numerical representations of the text, the study evaluates five natural language processing (NLP) methods: two bag-of-words topic models—a benchmark taxonomy (BKMX) and an online Latent Dirichlet Allocation (oLDA) model—and three BERT-based contextual embedding models (BERT-base-uncased, MPNET, and FinBERT). A rolling window framework using Lasso regression is applied annually to generate real-time return scores without look-ahead bias. 

Cross-sectional regressions and SHAP value analyses reveal that soft information is just as informative as earnings surprises in explaining announcement-day return variations, achieving a combined $R^2$ of up to 4.4%. Among the models, FinBERT is the most effective at extracting return-predictive soft information, outperforming earnings surprises in SHAP importance (52.12% vs. 47.88%). Furthermore, soft information does not explain stock returns the day prior to the announcement, indicating a low likelihood of average pre-release leakage.

For interpretability, the authors analyze topics using the BKMX taxonomy, oLDA, and GPT-4o to label and group tokens into metatopics. The topic analysis reveals a "self-serving bias" in corporate narratives: when companies achieve positive results, managers speak more positively about internal factors (such as financial adjustments, metrics, and performance), whereas below-expectation results are framed negatively around external factors (such as sector-specific news and macroeconomic conditions). 

Finally, the paper tests two practical applications:
1. **Market Efficiency:** A long-short trading strategy entering at 9:45 a.m. and exiting at the 4:00 p.m. close based on the agreement between hard and soft signals yields statistically significant negative abnormal returns close to zero. This indicates that overnight information is fully incorporated into stock prices by market open, supporting the Efficient Market Hypothesis.
2. **Advance Information ("Hacking"):** If press releases and earnings surprises are obtained prior to official publication (as occurred in documented cybersecurity breaches), combining the agreement of both hard and soft signals significantly enhances the ability to identify extreme stock performance. Specifically, the precision for predicting the top 10 best- and worst-performing stocks increases from a range of 0.25–0.36 (using either signal alone) to 0.44–0.52 (when combined).

Universal Interatomic Potentials (UIPs) are predominantly trained on bulk material datasets and tend to underestimate surface energies. This study systematically evaluates the effectiveness of machine learning potentials (MLPs) in predicting material surface properties using the MACE-MP-0a-small foundation model across three strategies: training from scratch on surface data (TS), using pre-trained UIPs without modification (zero-shot, ZS), and fine-tuning (FT). These methods were tested on unary (Au), binary (RuO2), and ternary (BiVO4) surface systems. 

Across all three systems, increasing the training dataset size reduced prediction errors, though overall performance declined as system complexity increased. FT models consistently outperformed TS and ZS models in energy and force predictions, achieving comparable or superior accuracy to TS models while requiring significantly fewer training configurations. In diatomic potential evaluations, TS models exhibited physically unrealistic behaviors, such as multiple local minima and incorrect short- or long-range interactions. In contrast, FT models produced physically reasonable potential shapes consistent with density functional theory (DFT) references. Furthermore, in the complex BiVO4 system, the FT model leveraged the foundation model's prior knowledge of high-force environments to achieve the lowest force prediction error (0.17 eV/Å) and effectively suppress high-force outliers compared to the TS model.

Despite these advantages, conventional FT modifies foundation model parameters and can cause catastrophic forgetting, where the model loses predictive performance on its original pre-training data and fails to generalize to other out-of-domain (OOD) systems. For instance, a model fine-tuned exclusively on Au surfaces showed poorer surface energy predictions for other noble metals (Ag, Cu, Pt, Ir) than the ZS model, alongside degraded accuracy on the original MPTrj bulk dataset.

To mitigate catastrophic forgetting, the study evaluated multi-head fine-tuning (MHFT), which trains concurrently on original bulk data and new surface data. When trained on Au surfaces and a subset of the MPTrj bulk dataset, MHFT retained bulk prediction competence and reduced the surface energy prediction error (RMSE of 16 meV/Å²) for Ag, Cu, Pt, and Ir to nearly half that of the ZS model (27 meV/Å²), far outperforming the FT model (88 meV/Å²). However, MHFT requires roughly 100 times more training time than FT, slightly degrades accuracy on the specific fine-tuned Au dataset compared to FT, and requires strict alignment of computational conditions and energy reference points between the pre-training and fine-tuning datasets.

The RSI indicator measures the speed and magnitude of price movements on a scale from 0 to 100. The MACD-histogram trading strategy is a mean-reversion system that identifies market momentum changes and reversal points. Visually representing the difference between the MACD and signal lines, the histogram indicates bullish or bearish momentum when bars cross above or below the zero line, respectively. For this strategy, traders enter on the close and exit on the first day the close is higher than the previous day's (vice versa for short positions, though long positions perform better). Across 77 liquid ETFs, the strategy generated 6,669 trades with mostly positive average gains. A backtest on the 2x leveraged Nasdaq 100 ETF (QLD) since 2007 yielded 85 trades, a 2.2% average gain, a 19% max drawdown, and 10.4% annual returns while invested only 5% of the time.

Poker is a complex game of incomplete information, with tournament formats like three-player Spin & Go presenting unique algorithmic challenges due to changing stack sizes and player counts. While past AI breakthroughs relied on Counterfactual Regret Minimization (CFR) and prior Large Language Model (LLM) attempts like PokerGPT were limited by low-stakes spectator data, this paper introduces SpinGPT, an LLM-based poker agent built on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. 

SpinGPT utilizes a two-stage training methodology. First, Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) using LoRA was conducted on 320,000 anonymized decisions from high-stakes Spin & Go games played by a professional. Hand histories were parsed into structured text prompts, and the model outputted specific actions and bet sizes. Second, to move beyond human imitation toward Game Theory Optimal (GTO) play, offline Reinforcement Learning (RL) using the ORPO algorithm was applied to a combined dataset of 50,000 human hands and 270,000 synthetic post-flop hands generated by the InstaGTO solver.

The models were evaluated on Professional and Solver test sets. The initial model, SpinGPT-SFT, achieved 80% exact accuracy, 84% tolerant accuracy, an 86% macro F1 score, and a 0.61 BB Mean Absolute Error (MAE) on the Professional set, making illegal moves in only 1.4% of cases. The final RL-refined SpinGPT model saw its Professional set imitation accuracy drop slightly to 79% (84% macro F1), reflecting behavioral adjustments toward solver feedback, while improving its bet-sizing MAE to 0.30 BB. On the Solver test set, SpinGPT achieved 72% exact accuracy, 78% tolerant accuracy, a 77% macro F1, and a 0.93 BB MAE.

In gameplay evaluations, SpinGPT-SFT was tested against the heads-up cash game benchmark agent Slumbot (200 BB stacks). Because SpinGPT-SFT was trained on shallower Spin & Go stacks (starting at 25 BB), a heuristic patch was applied to replace deep-stack all-in shoves with smaller bets or raises. With this patch, SpinGPT-SFT achieved a win rate of 13.4 ± 12.9 BB/100 over 30,000 hands. In a 10,000-hand head-to-head duplicate match at a 25 BB stack depth, the final SpinGPT model defeated SpinGPT-SFT with a win rate of 13.2 ± 7.24 BB/100, confirming the value of the RL phase.

Limitations include the lack of a final SpinGPT evaluation against Slumbot due to cost and format mismatches, as well as LLM numerical hallucinations (e.g., treating "5.11" as greater than "5.2"). Total compute was estimated at 5.2 kgCO2e. Future work could explore stronger base models, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) for GTO charts, chain-of-thought prompting, opponent adaptivity, natural-language explainability, and direct solver coupling.

This manuscript examines the value, potential, and epistemological and methodological considerations of quantitative criticalism in education research. Intended for scholars, students, and educators, the article challenges the notion that quantitative research is purely objective. Because researchers possess implicit biases and perspectives shaped by their lived experiences, the authors share their own positionalities—specifically regarding queer, white, cisgender, and Vietnamese-Chinese American identities—to demonstrate how social positioning influences scholarly inquiry.

Quantitative criticalism combines quantitative methods with critical epistemologies to advocate for social justice, dismantle oppressive systems, and recognize students holistically within broader structures rather than through deficit-based models. Practicing this approach requires embedding criticality throughout a project's entire lifespan, from developing research questions to analyzing data, while partnering with studied communities to drive transformational change.

However, merging critical frameworks with quantitative methods creates inherent tensions:
*   **Historical Roots:** Modern statistics are historically rooted in white supremacy, cisheteropatriarchy, and eugenics, requiring researchers to actively unsettle and rebuild the foundations of educational statistics.
*   **Threshold of Criticality:** Because criticality is a continuum and readers cannot fully know an author’s intentions, there is no clearly defined standard for what makes a study "critical enough."
*   **Methodological Limitations:** Survey designs often rely on reductive, essentialist demographic categories. Furthermore, small sample sizes for multiply minoritized populations can restrict statistical power, though underutilized nonparametric tests can help address this. Additionally, the post-positivist drive for broad generalizability often centers majority white experiences and masks nuances within marginalized groups.

To illustrate how scholars navigate these tensions, the authors review four studies utilizing three critical frameworks:
1.  **Critical Race Theory (CRT):** Sablan (2019) combined CRT and quantitative methods (QuantCrit) to operationalize Yosso’s community cultural wealth model into scales, creating space for asset-based counternarratives despite limited generalizability.
2.  **Queer Theory:** Garvey (2017) advocated for including "queer" as a survey response and testing for within-group differences. This highlights the tension between the necessity of categorizing data for quantitative analysis and queer theory's emphasis on identity fluidity.
3.  **Intersectionality:** Szymanski and Lewis (2016) used regression interaction effects to study how African American women cope with gendered racism, while Wilson and Urick (2022) used latent class analysis to study high school opportunity gaps. These studies demonstrate different methods—and limitations—for analyzing intersecting identities rather than treating social categories as independent variables.

Ultimately, the authors encourage researchers and methods instructors to build coalitions, reflect on their positionalities and intentions, and move beyond objectivist approaches to use quantitative methods as a vehicle for equity and collective liberation.

The NVIDIA Turing GPU architecture introduces several advancements in display, rendering, and AI technologies. Its new display engine supports 8K resolution at 60 Hz via DisplayPort 1.4a and USB-C, native HDR processing, tone mapping, and updated NVENC/NVDEC units for improved video encoding and decoding. For Virtual Reality (VR), Turing supports VirtualLink, allowing headsets to connect using a single USB-C cable, and utilizes NVLink in TU102 and TU104 GPUs for increased bandwidth in two-way SLI configurations. 

A primary feature of the Turing architecture is real-time ray tracing, which realistically simulates lighting, reflections, refractions, and shadows. Because ray tracing is computationally intensive, Turing uses a Hybrid Rendering model that combines traditional rasterization with ray tracing. This is powered by dedicated hardware called RT Cores within each Streaming Multiprocessor (SM). RT Cores offload the SM by autonomously accelerating Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH) tree traversal and ray-triangle intersection testing, allowing Turing to run ray tracing 10 times faster than the previous Pascal architecture. Performance is further optimized by AI and non-AI denoising filtering techniques, which reduce the number of rays required per pixel while enabling physically correct shadows, ambient occlusion, and reflections.

Turing also integrates NVIDIA NGX (Neural Graphics Acceleration), a deep learning technology stack that uses Turing Tensor Cores to run AI-based graphics functions. A key NGX feature is Deep Learning Super-Sampling (DLSS), which is trained on 64x supersampled reference images to produce high-quality anti-aliased images with roughly half the shading work of Temporal Anti-Aliasing (TAA). Other NGX features include InPainting for replacing removed image content, AI Slow-Mo for interpolating video frames, and AI Super Rez for upscaling images and video.

To further optimize workloads, Turing introduces several new shading capabilities:
* **Mesh Shading:** Uses cooperative Task and Mesh Shaders to eliminate CPU draw call bottlenecks, allowing for the real-time rendering of hundreds of thousands of complex objects and dynamic level-of-detail (LOD) adjustments.
* **Variable Rate Shading (VRS):** Allows developers to dynamically adjust shading rates for every 16x16 pixel region. VRS supports Content Adaptive Shading (lowering rates in low-detail areas), Motion Adaptive Shading (lowering rates for fast-moving objects), and Foveated Rendering (lowering rates in the viewer's peripheral vision).
* **Texture Space Shading (TSS):** Decouples visibility and appearance sampling by computing and storing shading values in texture space, allowing shaded texels to be reused across frames or stereo VR views.
* **Multi-View Rendering (MVR):** Expands on Pascal's Simultaneous Multi-Projection to support up to four views in a single pass, improving efficiency for wide field-of-view VR displays and shadow rendering.

These features are implemented across the TU102, TU104 (used in the GeForce RTX 2080, Quadro RTX 5000, and the data-center-focused Tesla T4), and TU106 (used in the GeForce RTX 2070, which omits NVLink and SLI support) GPUs. Because Hybrid Rendering distributes frame time across different hardware units—typically 20% for DNN/Tensor workloads and 80% for rendering (split 50/50 between ray tracing and rasterization, alongside concurrent integer execution)—NVIDIA introduced the RTX-OPS metric to accurately measure usable operations across Tensor Cores, CUDA Cores, RT Cores, and INT32 pipes. 

Finally, NVIDIA provides standard legal disclaimers stating the specifications are provided "as is" without warranties, are subject to change, and that NVIDIA products are not authorized for use in life-support or other critical equipment.

This study evaluated an automated system designed to monitor adherence to clinical practice guidelines in intensive care units (ICUs). To overcome scalability challenges caused by varying local data models, the system combines Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (FHIR) for computer-interpretable guideline representations with the Observational Medical Outcomes Partnership (OMOP) Common Data Model (CDM) for standardized patient data. 

Researchers selected six ICU guideline recommendations—primarily focused on COVID-19 and Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS) treatments—and encoded them in FHIR. Clinical data from five German university hospitals, totaling 82,015 ICU episodes from January 2020 to May 2023, were transformed into the OMOP CDM. A custom execution engine ingested the FHIR-encoded guidelines and queried the OMOP databases to evaluate daily guideline applicability and adherence. To validate the system, its performance was compared against seven ICU physicians across three hospitals, using reviews from two supervising physicians as the ground truth.

The automated system achieved 97.0% accuracy, significantly outperforming the human reviewers' 86.6% accuracy. It was also vastly more time-efficient, processing over 2,000 patient days per second compared to the 150 hours required by humans to review 18,115 patient days. Over 80% of discrepancies between the system and physicians were caused by human errors, such as overlooking high-volume data or inconsistently interpreting imprecise guidelines. The rare system errors primarily occurred because relevant information was recorded in unstructured free-text fields that were not transferred into the OMOP CDM. 

Overall guideline adherence rates varied by hospital and recommendation, mostly ranging between 10% and 60%. Low adherence was attributed to the novelty of COVID-19 guidelines, incomplete documentation, and the strictness of automated evaluation against imprecisely defined recommendations. Study limitations included retrospective validation, potential bias in ground truth labeling, and a small number of tested recommendations. Ultimately, the study demonstrates that combining FHIR and OMOP CDM provides a scalable, accurate, and efficient method for monitoring ICU guideline adherence.

A 2018 *Journal of Climate* paper by Nicholas Lewis and Judith Curry concludes that high future global warming estimates from most computer climate simulations (CMIP5) are inconsistent with observed warming since 1850. By analyzing observed temperatures, greenhouse gas effects, and extended IPCC AR5 forcing data up to 2016, the study suggests future warming will be 30% to 45% lower than central computer model projections. 

Using globally-complete temperature data, the authors derive a median equilibrium climate sensitivity (ECS) estimate of 1.66°C (1.66 K) and a transient climate response (TCR) estimate of 1.33°C (1.33 K). These are substantially lower than the comparable CMIP5 model estimates of 3.1°C for ECS and 1.9°C for TCR, and feature much lower upper uncertainty bounds than a predecessor study. Standard data without infilling yields even lower medians of 1.50 K for ECS and 1.20 K for TCR. 

Furthermore, the authors examine previous methodological criticisms—such as time-varying climate sensitivity, forcing-efficacy effects, sea-surface warming variability, and temperature estimation issues—and conclude that these factors are unfounded or cause minimal to no bias when using globally-complete temperature data.

This passage outlines the Statistical Analysis Plan (SAP) for the ZEA-DNK-02170 (Protocol ZP4207-17086) clinical trial, detailing pharmacodynamic, pharmacokinetic, and safety analyses, alongside data presentation and quality control specifications. 

Summary statistics and graphs will be generated for plasma glucose concentrations, pharmacodynamic metrics, and plasma dasiglucagon and GlucaGen concentrations by treatment group and time point. Time to plasma glucose recovery will be analyzed using summary tables, Kaplan-Meier survival curves, Cox proportional hazard models, and sensitivity analyses.

Safety analyses are based on the safety set and include:
*   **Extent of Exposure:** Summaries and listings of prior insulin administration, the hypoglycemia induction procedure, trial medication, and post-treatment rescue IV glucose infusions.
*   **Local Tolerability:** Injection site reactions assessed at 30, 120, and 300 minutes post-dose, summarized by time point, symptom, and grade.
*   **Adverse Events (AEs):** Summaries are restricted to treatment-emergent AEs (TEAEs), coded via MedDRA (v21.0+), and categorized by severity and causal relationship. Missing relationships default to "related," while missing severities are not imputed. Specific tables will cover AEs of special interest, injection site reactions, serious AEs, and deaths.
*   **Laboratory and Other Assessments:** Continuous and categorical tabulations, listings, and changes from baseline (screening V1 to follow-up V3) will be prepared for hematology, biochemistry, coagulation, and urinalysis. Pregnancy tests, alcohol breath tests, vital signs, physical exams, and 12-lead ECGs (including QTcF interval thresholds) will be summarized or listed. Immunogenicity (anti-drug antibodies [ADA]) will be analyzed descriptively by counting treatment-induced and treatment-boosted ADA patients.

The SAP notes minor changes from the protocol regarding the rewording of the primary efficacy analysis, added sensitivity analyses, and updated terminology for secondary efficacy variables.

Finally, the appendices establish rules for data presentation and SAS programming quality control (QC):
*   **Appendix A:** Defines formatting for tables, figures, and listings, rounding rules, date/time formats, handling of partial dates, and mathematical formulas for durations, unit conversions, BMI, and baseline changes.
*   **Appendix B:** Details SAS programming QC requirements, including program header standards, log reviews, output verification, Pinnacle 21 dataset validation, spot-checking, and documentation.
*   **Appendix C:** Provides a comprehensive index and mock templates for all planned tables, figures, and listings (TFLs) for demographics, efficacy, safety, and PK/PD parameters.

Arizona enacted the nation’s first targeted Empowerment Scholarship Account (ESA) voucher program in 2011 and expanded it to be universal in 2022. Total enrollment grew from 144 students in FY2012 to 87,602 by the third quarter of FY2025, with 64,133 enrolled in the universal category. Because Arizona provides little transparency and no accountability for participating private entities, the Grand Canyon Institute (GCI), a nonpartisan research organization, analyzed the program’s usage and financial impact. 

Voucher amounts equal 90% of charter school funding, typically under $8,000, though weighted awards for areas like autism can exceed $30,000. In FY2023, GCI estimated $304 million was spent overall. Only $173 million went to private school tuition—accounting for no more than 40% of total ESA students—indicating many parents use funds for homeschooling, extracurriculars, or items not clearly tied to educational curriculum. Of the private school spending, 51% ($97 million) went to religious schools (86% of which were Evangelical Christian and Catholic), 44% ($75 million) to special needs schools, and under 5% ($7.8 million) to secular schools. Furthermore, parents—especially of special needs students—have accumulated unspent funds in rollover accounts, which can eventually be used for college tuition. Unspent balances reached $175 million across 60,000 accounts by the end of FY2023 and an estimated $360 million by the end of FY2024. 

Zip code analysis reveals that ESA vouchers primarily enroll children from higher-income areas, though income differences across zip codes flattened somewhat between May 2023 and March 2025. While about 90% of new universal entrants in FY2025 previously attended district or charter schools—disproportionately impacting charters—nearly three-quarters of all current universal participants never attended public schools. 

Consequently, contrary to arguments that vouchers save money, GCI concludes the universal program is a net cost to the state’s general fund. While the state realizes modest savings when charter students transfer to vouchers, it incurs net costs when district students transfer (due to local property tax equalization formulas) and pays the entire voucher cost for students who never would have attended public schools. Factoring in student origins, kindergarten adjustments, and administrative shares, GCI estimates the universal ESA program had a net cost to the state of at least $330 million in FY2024 and approximately $350 million in FY2025.

Curriculum evaluation is a comprehensive process essential for revising and improving educational programs, and teachers' opinions are a crucial component of this evaluation. Previous studies indicate that the physical education and sports curriculum needs revision due to limited school opportunities, insufficient course hours, crowded classrooms, and a lack of equipment. This study aimed to determine the opinions of pre-service teachers regarding the secondary education (5-8) Physical Education and Sports Curriculum's achievements, content, learning-teaching processes, and measurement and evaluation practices. Using a scanning model and quantitative methods, a researcher-developed questionnaire was administered to 100 students from four departments at Bayburt University's Faculty of Sports Sciences. 

The results showed that novice teachers had generally positive views on the program's achievements, finding the outcomes understandable, properly structured, and suitable for students' levels, though 37 were undecided about the presence of scientific errors. Regarding program content, 80% agreed it was arranged in a meaningful order, but the majority were undecided about scientific errors, age appropriateness, and compatibility with other countries' programs, indicating a lack of information about the content. For learning-teaching processes, 56% stated processes were enriched with activities and 61% noted concrete materials were used. However, 60 disagreed that different methods and techniques were utilized, and most were undecided regarding the activities' compatibility with student development and other disciplines. In assessment and evaluation, 43 agreed that different forms were used, while 34 were undecided about the use of different methods and techniques. Because research on this subject is insufficient, the study recommends conducting more research, organizing informative seminars or congresses for prospective teachers, and including training program review courses in teacher training programs.

This patent application details methods for forming 3-dimensional vertical NOR-type (VNOR) memory string arrays using damascene local vertical bit lines. To improve the structural stability of word line stacks and prevent a stress-induced deformation called "ribboning," the method reduces the aspect ratio during patterning by etching local word lines in two steps. 

The fabrication process begins by depositing a multi-layer memory structure (such as alternating silicon nitride and silicon oxide layers) isolated from an underlying conductive layer of global interconnect lines. A first set of trenches is etched using masking structures and filled with a sacrificial dielectric layer. A second masking layer is then used to etch a second set of parallel trenches, forming narrow word line stacks. Any width variability caused by lithography misalignment during this two-step etching can be absorbed within the chip design by grouping left and right thin-film transistors separately. Next, the silicon nitride layers are selectively etched away to create cavities, which are filled with metal to form local word line strips. The second trenches are then filled with a sacrificial dielectric.

Elongated vias are etched through the sacrificial dielectric layers, and memory films—including a tunneling dielectric, charge storage, blocking dielectric, channel, optional liner, and sacrificial dielectric layer—are successively and conformally deposited inside them. Shafts are subsequently etched into the sacrificial dielectric and filled with heavily doped semiconductor material to form common source and drain regions (bit lines) for the thin-film storage transistors. The source and drain layers connect to bottom and/or top global interconnect lines, and a "staircase" structure is etched at the ends of the word line strips to connect them to selective circuitry in the semiconductor substrate or a companion integrated circuit.

Two alternative embodiments for forming and supporting the word line strips are also described. One embodiment forms dielectric pillars prior to word line strip formation to mechanically support the high aspect-ratio stacks during trench etching. Another embodiment uses two stacked masking layers with different pitches and dimensions to define the word line stacks and etch the two sets of trenches before performing the metal replacement process.

The RTX Blackwell Neural Rendering Architecture introduces advancements in ray tracing, AI, video, power efficiency, and hardware. 

**Mega Geometry & Ray Tracing:** Mega Geometry increases geometric detail for ray-traced applications and LOD systems like Nanite. It addresses cluster-based LOD updates via Cluster-level Acceleration Structures (CLAS) and manages high object counts using Partitioned Top-Level Acceleration Structures (PTLAS), minimizing CPU overhead and enabling real-time ray-traced subdivision surfaces. Supported on Turing and newer GPUs, Mega Geometry is enhanced by Blackwell’s 4th-gen RT Cores, which double ray-triangle intersection rates and introduce Linear Swept Spheres (LSS) to accelerate strand rendering while reducing VRAM. Shader Execution Reordering (SER) 2.0 doubles core reorder logic efficiency, and a dedicated RISC-V AI Management Processor (AMP) offloads GPU context scheduling from the CPU to reduce latency.

**Video, Display, & Power:** Blackwell adds hardware encode/decode support for YUV 4:2:2 video. It features the 9th-gen NVENC (improving AV1/HEVC quality and adding AV1 Ultra High Quality mode), the 6th-gen NVDEC (doubling H.264 decode speeds), and DisplayPort 2.1b supporting up to 80 Gbps. Max-Q power improvements include Advanced Power Gating (with GDDR7 memory clock gating and independent voltage rails), 1000x faster Accelerated Frequency Switching, and a Low Latency Sleep state entered 10x faster than Ada.

**DLSS 4 & Neural Shaders:** Powered by 5th-gen Tensor Cores, DLSS 4 introduces Multi Frame Generation—generating up to three additional frames per rendered frame—alongside hardware Flip Metering for precise pacing. DLSS 4 transitions from CNNs to transformer-based models for Super Resolution, Ray Reconstruction, and DLAA, ingesting 2x more parameters to improve temporal stability and detail. Furthermore, Blackwell introduces developer-created neural shaders using the Cooperative Vectors API, unlocking features like RTX Neural Materials, Neural Texture Compression (with Stochastic Texture Filtering), Neural Radiance Cache, RTX Skin (subsurface scattering), and generative AI-driven RTX Neural Faces.

**Hardware & Disclaimers:** The Blackwell GPU lineup includes the flagship GB202 (92.2B transistors, 24,576 CUDA cores, powering the RTX 5090), the high-end GB203 (45.6B transistors, 10,752 CUDA cores, powering the RTX 5080 and 5070 Ti), and the performance-segment GB205 (31B transistors, 6,400 CUDA cores, powering the RTX 5070). Finally, the document provides NVIDIA's legal disclaimers, noting that specifications are provided "AS IS" without warranties, Liability is limited, and the products are not authorized for life-critical applications.

To address the growing complexity of software development and automate service composition, researchers propose Digital Ecosystems. Unlike systems that use the term "ecosystem" merely for branding, true Digital Ecosystems are software systems engineered to exploit the robust, scalable, and self-organizing properties of biological ecosystems to solve complex, dynamic problems efficiently. 

Designing these systems requires incorporating evolutionary computing and balancing internal self-organization with user-defined constraints. Because user needs change, the system's fitness landscape is dynamic. Agents within the system must reproduce, vary, interact, move, and die. As Complex Adaptive Systems, Digital Ecosystems exhibit non-linear behavior, requiring designers to carefully balance solution diversity, adaptive efficiency, and system stability to prevent issues like premature convergence or mass extinctions.

In practice, the proposed Digital Ecosystem functions as a Multi-Agent System using a two-level optimization scheme. A decentralized peer-to-peer network of distributed agents feeds local evolutionary algorithms operating on single habitats (peers). Unlike traditional island-models of distributed evolutionary computing that use fixed topologies to solve a single problem, this approach uses a dynamically re-configurable network topology based on Hebbian learning. Connection probabilities between habitats strengthen or weaken based on the success of agent migration, ultimately mirroring the small-world network topology of the user base.

Furthermore, the system evaluates different, yet similar, user requests on separate islands, accelerating adaptation by sharing solutions across populations. Users submit requests as semantic descriptions to their local habitat. The habitat instantiates an evolving population seeded with local agents and previously evolved agent-sequences. Fitness is evaluated using a distance function between the request's semantic description and the agents' ontological descriptions. Once an optimal agent-sequence is evolved and executed by a user, it migrates to other connected habitats to assist with future requests. This Ecosystem-Oriented Architecture was tested in a simulation of 100 users in a business ecosystem, utilizing evolutionary computing and dynamic population sizes to evolve optimal agent-sequences for simulated user requests.

This lecture explores effective field theory (EFT) with fine tuning, specifically within the context of non-relativistic two-nucleon EFT. Fine tuning occurs when an operator that appears irrelevant through naive dimensional power counting is actually relevant in calculations. This requires expanding around an interacting fixed point rather than a trivial one. 

In non-relativistic elastic scattering, the theory relies on contact interactions, and all loop diagrams are bubble diagrams that form a geometric series. Summing these loops easily proves the quantum mechanical effective range expansion without needing to specify a potential. However, when matching to experimental data, the nucleon scattering length ($a$) is unnaturally large, indicating a fine tuning that invalidates naive dimensional power counting and the standard MS-bar scheme, which misses power law divergences.

To properly treat the $C_0$ operator as relevant to all orders, the lecture introduces two alternative renormalization schemes: off-shell momentum subtraction and the Power Divergence Subtraction (PDS) scheme (which subtracts poles at $D=3$). Both schemes track the power law divergences and yield a beta function with three fixed points ($a = 0, \pm\infty$) and a pole corresponding to a bound state, the deuteron. At the $a = \pm\infty$ fixed points, the theory is scale-invariant and exhibits conformal and SU(4) spin-isospin symmetries. 

Using the renormalization group equations from these schemes, the enhancement from the fine-tuned $C_0$ operator can be systematically propagated to determine the correct, enhanced power counting for higher-order operators (like $C_2$ and $C_4$). While the resulting amplitudes are ultimately scale-independent, this re-organized power counting allows for precise, practical predictions in areas like deuteron physics.

Shieldalloy Metallurgical Corporation petitioned the United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit to challenge the Nuclear Regulatory Commission's (NRC) transfer of regulatory authority over in-state nuclear materials to New Jersey. For a decade, Shieldalloy had worked with the NRC on a decommissioning plan involving the on-site disposal of radioactive byproducts at its Newfield, New Jersey facility. Under the Atomic Energy Act, the NRC may transfer authority to a state if the state's program is compatible with the NRC's and adequate to protect public health and safety. 

During the public comment period for the proposed transfer, Shieldalloy argued that New Jersey's program was incompatible with the federal scheme. Specifically, Shieldalloy contended that the transfer violated the NRC's "criterion 25"—which requires arrangements to prevent the interruption of pending license applications—and requested that the NRC exclude the Newfield site from the transfer. The NRC rejected Shieldalloy's protests and transferred the authority. Shortly thereafter, New Jersey notified Shieldalloy that its pending decommissioning plan failed to meet state requirements. 

The Court of Appeals agreed with Shieldalloy that the NRC's transfer of authority was arbitrary and capricious. The court found the NRC's responses to Shieldalloy's comments regarding criterion 25 and the potential retention of jurisdiction to be incomplete and dismissive. Despite having previously approved a partial transfer excluding a specific subcategory of materials in Oklahoma, the NRC failed to adequately explain why a partial transfer was not a viable alternative for Shieldalloy's discrete subcategory of waste. Furthermore, the NRC failed to explain how Shieldalloy's decommissioning process could proceed without interruption given New Jersey's consistent hostility toward the termination proceedings. 

Because the NRC failed to provide a sufficient explanation for its actions regarding criterion 25 and the retention of jurisdiction, the court declined to evaluate Shieldalloy's remaining compatibility challenges. The court granted Shieldalloy's petition, vacated the NRC's transfer of authority to New Jersey, and remanded the case for further proceedings.

Cover 0 is a high-risk, high-reward defensive strategy that blitzes every player not assigned to man-to-man coverage to quickly pressure the quarterback. However, this leaves defenders isolated and the middle of the field open. Offenses can beat Cover 0 if their protection holds and they utilize a disciplined quarterback, elite perimeter play-makers, and immediate, quick-hitting routes like slants, shallow crosses, and pick plays. Specific offensive plays designed to exploit Cover 0 include Double Slants, the Full-Slide Fade-Out/RB Seam Gadget, the Trips Bunch Jerk Route, the Slant-Rub, and the Jerry Rice Motion Slant-Flat.

Depression and anxiety disorders affect over 300 million people globally. While speech and linguistic features offer insights into these conditions, identifying objective digital biomarkers, aligning Large Language Model (LLM) outputs, and distinguishing between the two disorders remain challenging. 

To address these gaps, researchers collected over 15,000 minutes of clinical interview audio recordings from 1,160 Mandarin-fluent outpatients (aged 12–80) at the Shanghai Mental Health Center between August 2023 and January 2024. Diagnoses were established using the Chinese version of the ICD-10, and all data and Electronic Medical Records (EMRs) were de-identified. 

After transcribing the anonymized recordings, researchers collaborated with psychiatrists to design a corpus of clinical indicators using EMRs and assessment scales. A pre-trained LLM, enhanced via supervised fine-tuning with psychiatrists' annotations, was used to identify symptoms and rate assessment scale components from the transcripts. Researchers also extracted linguistic and acoustic features from the transcripts and speech. By fusing these modalities, they constructed an ensemble machine-learning pipeline that predicts outpatient diagnostic groups and symptoms with moderately high accuracy, demonstrating that LLM-extracted cues and behavioral markers can effectively aid psychiatric diagnosis and assessment.
