This passage outlines the editorial practices, declassification process, and scope of *Foreign Relations, 1981–1988, Volume IV*, which documents the Reagan administration’s policies and bilateral relations with the Soviet Union from January 1983 to March 1985. The volume uses editorial notes and first-hand accounts to supplement the official record, and its compilation and declassification are overseen by the Advisory Committee on Historical Diplomatic Documentation. A declassification review conducted between 2015 and 2019 resulted in withholding one document in full and making excisions in 33 others. 

Part of a broader subseries examining the Reagan era and U.S.-Soviet relations, this specific volume focuses on the implementation of a four-part agenda—arms control, human rights, regional issues, and bilateral relations—codified in National Security Decision Directive 75. It details how U.S. officials developed and promoted these policies with Soviet counterparts, despite the absence of high-level meetings between President Reagan and Soviet leaders Yuri Andropov or Konstantin Chernenko.

This passage discloses systems and methods for localizing the position and orientation of objects within virtual reality (VR) and augmented reality (AR) systems. Accurate, low-latency tracking of a user's head pose and real-world objects (like handheld controllers or totems) is necessary to properly render virtual content and prevent motion sickness. 

The disclosed display system includes a head-mounted AR display, sensors, processors, and local and cloud computing modules that utilize a "passable world model" database. In some embodiments, the device uses stacked waveguides to present virtual content, decodes QR codes from camera images to retrieve virtual content from a network location, and enables multi-user content sharing via activation gateways.

To achieve precise localization, the system adapts electromagnetic (EM) tracking by placing a compact EM field emitter in a handheld controller and small EM sensor coils on the headset or belt pack. By comparing induced currents in the coils and integrating inertial measurement unit (IMU) data, the system calculates the relative position and orientation between components. Power and mass are optimized by operating the EM system at a reduced duty cycle (e.g., 10%), integrating coils directly into the headset frame, using lightweight ferrite cores, and employing time division multiplexing, summing amplifiers, and dynamic frequency tuning. Audio speaker interference is mitigated using a noise-cancelling circuit, and system calibration is achieved via ultrasonic signals, optical fiducials, or virtual targets.

The system also utilizes sensor fusion, combining EM and IMU data with optical and depth sensors (including passive stereo, active stereo, structured light, modulated time-of-flight, and LIDAR). Outward-facing cameras perform Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) to track head pose against 3D map points. For embedded processors, vision-based pose calculation is divided into five stages: pre-tracking (using IMU "pose prior" data to pre-fetch map points), tracking (feature matching), low-latency mapping (triangulating new points), latency-tolerant mapping (bundle adjustment), and post-mapping cleanup, while using semantic segmentation to remove moving objects.

Generative models, specifically Boltzmann Generators (BGs), offer a promising alternative to molecular dynamics (MD) and Monte Carlo simulations for generating statistically independent equilibrium samples of many-particle systems in "one shot." However, scaling previous "global" BGs to large condensed-phase systems has been impractical due to high training costs and low sampling efficiencies, limiting studies to around 500 particles.

This work introduces a scalable, "local" BG architecture for large crystalline materials by basing the generative process on local environments rather than full configurations. The approach combines graph neural networks with augmented coupling flows, which introduce auxiliary variables modeled as a noised copy of the physical system. This enables energy-based training without requiring target distribution samples. By fixing the number of neighbors and modeling displacements from the ideal crystal lattice, the architecture achieves linear scaling and size transferability, allowing models trained on small systems to be evaluated on much larger ones.

Experiments on crystalline phases using Lennard-Jones (LJ) and Stillinger-Weber (SW) potentials (including monatomic water, silicon, and germanium) demonstrate that local BGs trained on small systems (e.g., 128 to 256 particles) accurately transfer to systems exceeding 1000 particles (up to 1728). The local BGs reproduce radial distribution functions and energy histograms matching MD simulations. Compared to global architectures, local BGs drastically reduce training times (e.g., four GPU days versus over 330) while achieving significantly higher effective sample sizes (ESS) and lower variance.

Using targeted free energy perturbation and Legendre transformations, the local BGs provide accurate Helmholtz and Gibbs free energy estimates for large systems, closely matching reference MD with multistate Bennett acceptance ratio (MD+MBAR) results while requiring far fewer energy evaluations on large systems. Furthermore, training costs are amortized by conditioning the flows on simulation box shapes, temperatures, and interaction potential parameters (such as the SW three-body interaction strength), enabling accurate phase diagram predictions across varying thermodynamic states and cutoff radii. While size-transferability was excellent for most tested structures, the silicon $\beta$-tin structure proved more challenging for large-system free energy accuracy. Future directions include extending the method to liquid phases and broader chemical spaces.

At a ceremony at the American University, the speaker addresses the urgent need for genuine world peace, noting that total war makes no sense in the nuclear age. While weapons spending currently maintains peace, the speaker urges Americans to reexamine their attitudes in four areas:

1. **Peace:** Rather than viewing peace as impossible, humanity must pursue it as a practical, dynamic process based on evolving institutions, concrete actions, and mutual tolerance. 
2. **The Soviet Union:** Despite baseless Soviet propaganda and America's repugnance toward communism, Americans must not view conflict as inevitable. Both nations abhor war, bear heavy burdens in the arms race, and would be the primary targets of total war. Thus, both share a deep interest in peace and halting the arms race.

The NVIDIA Turing GPU architecture introduces a Hybrid Rendering model that combines real-time ray tracing, traditional rasterization, AI, and simulation. Key to its hardware-based ray tracing acceleration are the new RT Cores included in each Streaming Multiprocessor (SM). RT Cores autonomously accelerate Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH) traversal and ray-triangle intersection testing, offloading the SM so it can handle other graphics and compute work. Working alongside advanced denoising algorithms and RTX-compatible APIs, RT Cores enable Turing to run ray tracing 10 times faster than the Pascal architecture, delivering over 10 Giga Rays/Sec and producing realistic shadows, ambient occlusion, and reflections.

Turing also features NVIDIA NGX (Neural Graphics Acceleration), a deep learning technology stack utilizing Tensor Cores and Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) to enhance graphics and rendering. NGX only works on Turing and later architectures and is managed via GeForce Experience or Quadro Experience. Key NGX features include:
*   **Deep Learning Super-Sampling (DLSS):** Trained on 64x supersampled reference images, DLSS renders at a lower input sample count to infer a high-quality result with roughly half the shading work of Temporal Anti-Aliasing (TAA). A "DLSS 2X" mode is also available for higher quality.
*   **InPainting:** Removes unwanted objects from images and synthesizes new content to fill the gap.
*   **AI Slow-Mo:** Inserts interpolated frames into video streams for smooth slow-motion.
*   **AI Super Rez:** Upscales image or video resolution by 2x, 4x, or 8x by intelligently creating new pixels.

Turing introduces several advanced shading and rendering technologies to improve efficiency:
*   **Mesh Shading:** Uses cooperative thread models via new Task and Mesh shader stages to eliminate CPU draw call bottlenecks, manage levels of detail (LOD), and render hundreds of thousands of complex objects in real time.
*   **Variable Rate Shading (VRS):** Allows developers to dynamically adjust the shading rate for every 16x16 pixel region independently of the visibility rate. VRS powers Content Adaptive Shading (lowering rates in low-detail areas), Motion Adaptive Shading (lowering rates for fast-moving objects), and Foveated Rendering (lowering rates in the viewer's peripheral vision).
*   **Texture Space Shading (TSS):** Decouples visibility and appearance sampling by computing and storing shading values as texels in texture space. These texels can be reused across frames or views, improving temporal stability and VR efficiency.
*   **Multi-View Rendering (MVR):** Expands on Pascal's Simultaneous Multi-Projection to support up to four views in a single pass, optimizing stereo rendering and wide field-of-view (FOV) VR displays.

For Virtual Reality, Turing integrates MVR, Foveated Rendering, RT Core-accelerated VRWorks Audio for 3D sound, and hardware support for USB Type-C and VirtualLink, which powers headsets through a single cable. Additionally, Turing supports DX12 Tier 3 resource binding and Tier 2 resource heaps.

The Turing lineup includes the TU102, TU104, and TU106 GPUs. The TU104 chip features 13.6 billion transistors, 3,072 CUDA Cores, 368 Tensor Cores, 48 RT Cores, and NVLink support; it powers the GeForce RTX 2080, Quadro RTX 5000, and the data-center-focused Tesla T4 (which uses a 40 SM configuration). The TU106 chip, used in the GeForce RTX 2070, contains 10.8 billion transistors, 2,304 CUDA Cores, 288 Tensor Cores, and 36 RT Cores, but lacks NVLink and SLI support. 

To measure hybrid rendering performance across Turing's multiple processing units, NVIDIA introduced the RTX-OPS metric. Based on a representative frame time distribution, RTX-OPS weights peak operations by their usage: 80% for FP32 CUDA cores, 40% for RT cores, 28% for concurrent INT32 pipes, and 20% for Tensor operations. Finally, the document provides standard legal disclaimers, noting that NVIDIA provides specifications "as is" without warranties, limits its liability, prohibits use in life-support or military systems, and lists relevant third-party and NVIDIA trademarks.

This disclosure presents technologies for configuring and reducing resource consumption in time-aware networks (TANs) and time-sensitive applications (TSAs). It focuses on providing low-latency and scalable gate control for Time-Sensitive Networking (TSN), enabling multiple TSAs to share a single physical network link, and supporting time-aware, energy-efficient communication across various deployment scenarios, such as IoT and industrial automation.

In TSN, time synchronization across interconnected time-aware systems is achieved using Precision Time Protocol (PTP) and generalized PTP (gPTP) domains, managed by a grandmaster (GM) clock selected via a best master clock algorithm (BMCA). Traffic scheduling relies on transmission selection algorithms and time-triggered gates associated with traffic class (TC) queues. These gates open and close according to a predefined schedule in a Gate Control List (GCL). 

In traditional TSN Network Interface Controllers (NICs), implementing the GCL in dedicated on-chip SRAM requires significant silicon area, consumes high power, and involves complex, slow programming via indirect addressing. To resolve these issues, an improved TSN NIC architecture moves the GCL (divided into odd and even banks) to the host memory and utilizes a smaller prefetch buffer and GCL registers within the NIC's MAC layer. The MAC uses a dedicated channel (such as an (R)DMA channel) to prefetch GCL entries in bursts and parses them ahead of time to fetch required data payloads before the corresponding queues open. The MAC executes operations from one memory bank while gate control logic updates the other. This architecture achieves sub-nanosecond resolutions, reduces cycle times via direct memory programming, and saves silicon area and power.

Additionally, the disclosure addresses the complexity of configuring "complex end stations" that host multiple sending applications ("talkers") sharing a single physical network interface. Using the Stream Reservation Protocol (SRP), talkers and receiving "listeners" declare attributes to reserve network resources and guarantee Quality of Service (QoS). To simplify dynamic configuration and prevent interference between applications, a complex end station is presented to centralized network management during device discovery as a virtual bridge/switch connected to multiple simple virtual end stations (each hosting a single talker). The centralized management computes a viable configuration for the virtual switch, which the complex end station then applies to its physical network interface and workload scheduling. A Gate Control Engine (GCE) manages the hardware mechanisms controlling the transmission gates based on the GCL.

University at Albany chemists have synthesized a new boron-rich compound, manganese diboride, which could make space flights more efficient by requiring less fuel storage space. Compared to the aluminum currently used in solid rocket boosters, manganese diboride is over 20% more energetic by weight and about 150% more energetic by volume. Despite its high energy, the compound is stable and only combusts when it meets an ignition agent like kerosene. 

To produce it, researchers pressed manganese and boron powders into a pellet, heated it to 3,000°C using an arc melter, and rapidly cooled it. This process forces a central manganese atom to bond to too many other atoms, creating a crowded structure. Computer models revealed that the compound's high potential energy is stored in a structural skew, or "deformation," within its interlocking hexagonal lattice. Beyond rocket propulsion, the underlying boron-based structure has potential applications in building more durable automotive catalytic converters and serving as a catalyst to break down plastics.

The ProShares UltraPro QQQ (TQQQ) is an exchange-traded fund tracking the Nasdaq-100 index. Unlike stock trading, which involves buying and selling company shares, TQQQ option trading involves buying and selling European or American style call and put options. Call options give the right to buy at a specific price (used when expecting price increases), while put options give the right to sell (used for expected decreases or hedging). Common strategies include buying calls or puts and writing covered calls or puts. 

Because options use leverage, they offer higher potential returns than traditional investments, alongside benefits like hedging and capitalizing on short-term market movements. However, they are complex, speculative, and carry a high risk of large losses due to unexpected security movements, option term changes, and market sentiment shifts. 

To manage risk, traders should use stop-loss orders, diversify, choose liquid options, never invest more than they can afford to lose, and backtest strategies before committing money. Traders can analyze options using quantified strategies, fundamental and technical analysis, and the Black-Scholes model to estimate fair value. 

When selecting options and deciding when to enter or exit trades, investors must consider their goals, risk tolerance, market conditions, volatility, and expiration timeframes. Minimum capital requirements and trading costs—such as commissions, contract fees, and slippage—vary by broker. Additionally, profits are generally subject to capital gains tax in the resident country, and traders must adhere to specific regulations regarding capital, leverage, margin calls, stop-loss orders, and hedging.

A gap in trading refers to price levels that have little to no trading between the close and the next day's open. Gaps occur across all time frames and asset classes—most frequently overnight on daily charts—due to news and imbalances accruing during non-trading hours. Common labels for gaps include common, exhaustion, runaway, and breakaway gaps.

While gap trading strategies have been popular for decades, their profitability has diminished due to increased computer power and trader competition. To find working strategies today, traders must apply more criteria and filters, which increases the risk of curve-fitting. Gaps can be traded via day trading or swing trading by either fading or following the gap.

A gap is considered "filled" when the price moves back to its pre-gap level. A 25-year test of S&P 500 E-mini continuous futures data shows that smaller gaps fill on the same day much more frequently than larger gaps (about 60% for 0.1% gaps versus roughly 30% for 1% gaps). Bearish gaps are slightly more likely to fill due to the stock market's upward bias. 

Predicting gaps beforehand is nearly impossible, and successfully backtesting strategies requires reliable data, as free sources often contain erroneous highs and lows. While simple day trading backtests on S&P 500 gaps yield poor or negative returns, a swing trading strategy holding trades overnight—exiting on the same day only if the gap fills and closes higher than the previous day—produces an average gain of 0.48% per trade.

The Mid Screen is the most used offensive tactic, involving a "Big" screening against a "Little." Two proven strategies to defend against it are the Basic NBA Show & Recover and the All Out SOS Disruption. 

Most NBA teams prefer the Show & Recover method over switching to prevent the screener from posting up against a smaller defender. This involves three phases: the defender stepping out hard to force the ballhandler wide, recovering back to the post once the original defender re-establishes position, and a final match-up utilizing pass denials and weakside help.

Alternatively, All Out SOS Disruption forces the offense into a "free lance" situation by initiating defensive action before the first screen occurs. Its three phases involve double-teaming the ballhandler at the baseline checkpoint, rotating according to the near player concept when the ball is passed out of the trap, and setting a final alignment that utilizes pass denials, low post fronting, and trap rotations.

This study investigated whether exogenous oxytocin (OT) primarily enhances behavioral and neural responses to gentle stroking touch targeting C-touch (CT) fibers or medium pressure massage targeting non-CT fibers, and whether these effects depend on the administration route. In a double-blind, placebo-controlled design, 171 healthy Chinese adults received 24 IU of intranasal OT, oral OT, or a placebo before experiencing both touch conditions on their calves. Researchers measured behavioral ratings, plasma OT concentrations, physiological arousal (ECG and SCR), and cortical brain activity via functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS). 

Results showed that while participants rated the medium pressure massage as more pleasant, intense, and arousing overall, both intranasal and oral OT selectively increased pleasantness ratings only for the gentle stroking touch. Neither OT treatment affected physiological arousal, perceived intensity, or willingness to pay. Neurally, both OT treatments prolonged and enhanced oxyhemoglobin concentration changes in the bilateral medial orbitofrontal cortex (mOFC), mediolateral OFC (mlOFC), and posterior superior temporal sulcus (pSTS) exclusively during the gentle stroking touch. Classification analyses of neural time courses successfully discriminated between the OT groups and the placebo group, but could not distinguish between the intranasal and oral OT groups. 

Furthermore, both intranasal and oral administrations significantly increased plasma OT concentrations compared to the placebo, though intranasal OT produced a larger initial increase. Mediation analyses revealed that post-treatment plasma OT concentration changes completely mediated the enhanced pleasantness ratings for gentle stroking touch in both OT groups. Overall, the findings demonstrate that intranasal and oral OT equivalently and selectively facilitate hedonic behavioral and neural responses to CT-targeted social touch, and that these effects are primarily mediated via peripheral increases in plasma OT concentrations rather than direct entry into the brain.

Interpreting single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data traditionally relies on manual annotation or computational methods that map gene expression embeddings to predefined, static categories. To overcome these limitations, the authors introduce Cell2Text, a multimodal generative framework that converts scRNA-seq profiles into natural language descriptions of cellular identity, tissue origin, disease associations, and active pathways. 

Cell2Text's architecture consists of three main components:
1. **Cell Encoder:** A frozen, pretrained Geneformer model that extracts individual, contextualized embeddings for up to 4,096 genes per cell rather than pooling them into a single vector.
2. **Adapter Module:** A trainable two-layer feedforward network that projects and normalizes the gene embeddings into the language model's semantic space.
3. **Natural Language Decoder:** Instruction-tuned Large Language Models (Meta-Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct and Gemma3-4B-it), which are adapted to the task using either full fine-tuning or Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA).

To train and evaluate the framework, the authors constructed a dataset of 1,000,000 cells from the CELLxGENE Census across 7,331 donors, 783 cell types, 347 tissues, and 128 diseases. Ground-truth text descriptions were generated by combining metadata with OBO Cell Ontology definitions and the top two active biological pathways identified via pySCENIC and MSigDB Hallmark pathways.

In experiments, Cell2Text generated text with high lexical overlap (BLEU and ROUGE) and strong semantic fidelity, achieving BioBERT F1-scores over 93.9% for fully tuned models. When regular expressions were used to extract classification labels from the generated text, the fully tuned Cell2Text models outperformed supervised baselines (Geneformer with a linear classification head and Geneformer with LightGBM) across cell type, tissue, and disease prediction tasks. Notably, Cell2Text-Gemma-4B achieved 77.83% accuracy in cell type classification, beating the linear head baseline by over 10%. 

Furthermore, the authors introduced a Personalized PageRank similarity metric based on the Cell Ontology graph to evaluate the biological relatedness of incorrect predictions. Cell2Text-Gemma-4B achieved the highest similarity score (85.62%), indicating that its misclassifications are ontologically close to the true labels. In multi-label pathway activity classification, Cell2Text surpassed the linear head baseline and performed competitively against an ensemble of 34 LightGBM classifiers, demonstrating that training models for text generation yields rich cellular representations.

This passage describes a smart gateway platform for industrial automation systems designed to optimize artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning, and statistical data analytics. Conventional big data approaches stream large volumes of unstructured, uncorrelated raw data from industrial devices into storage, requiring extensive processing time, storage capacity, and human verification to identify useful correlations and avoid spurious results. To address these issues, the smart gateway platform leverages encoded domain expertise to narrow the data space and apply useful constraints prior to analysis.

The platform includes a device interface, a model configuration component, a data modeling component, a gateway analytics component, an analytics interface, a user interface, a processor, and memory. The memory stores a library of model templates classified hierarchically by industry, machine type, and specific business objectives (e.g., minimizing machine downtime, optimizing energy efficiency, or maximizing product output). Each template encodes collective domain expertise by generically defining the subset of data inputs, correlations, and causalities relevant to a specific business objective. 

Through the user interface, a user selects a model template corresponding to a desired business objective and maps the template's generic data inputs to actual data sources discovered on the plant network, such as standard data tags or pre-contextualized smart tags (which include State, Rate, Odometer, and Event data types). This mapping yields a customized analytic model. If a required data input is missing from the user's facility, the guided mapping process prompts the user, indicating the need to install the appropriate sensor.

The platform collects only the mapped data items from disparate plant-floor devices and operational technology (OT) or information technology (IT) software systems (e.g., data historians, maintenance spreadsheets, work order and inventory databases). The data modeling component then synchronizes, normalizes, and aggregates this raw and smart data into a common representation. It contextualizes the data by adding modeling metadata based on the model's predefined relationships. This includes adding AI fields that identify key variables, correlated variables, mathematical relationships, and the class of analytic problem to be solved. Data can also be modeled according to plant hierarchies or object-oriented asset hierarchies (such as a pump type hierarchy), and used to calculate new Overall Equipment Effectiveness (OEE) metrics or trigger alarms.

The resulting structured and contextualized data is fed to an analytic system. Because the data is pre-modeled and constrained to relevant subsets, the analytic system can more quickly determine root causes, generate actionable insights, and predict operational issues without extensive data cleansing. Analytic results can be delivered to client devices as visual presentations or used to automatically generate control outputs that alter industrial device operations (e.g., modifying a motor drive's speed setpoint). 

Finally, the platform supports a scalable, multi-level analytics architecture spanning the device, system (e.g., on the gateway itself or an edge device), and enterprise or cloud levels. Real-time analytics and automated countermeasures for single devices or entire production lines are generally executed in the OT environment (device and system levels), while non-real-time analytics for visualization dashboards are executed in the IT or cloud domain. Analytic tasks and results can be scaled upward or downward across these levels based on time-sensitivity and relevance.

Robots navigating unstructured environments rely on generated world maps for motion planning. However, sensor noise, occlusions, and state estimation errors cause inconsistencies between successive maps, leading to oscillating trajectories in deterministic planners like the Kinodynamic Efficiently Adaptive State Lattice (KEASL). To address this without model training or parameter tuning, this work introduces a multi-hypothesis planning approach that computes edge costs using multiple temporally sampled environment maps. The most recent map acts as the primary hypothesis requiring a collision-free final solution, while prior maps guide the search.

Four methods were explored to search this multi-world-hypothesis space:
1. **Valid in Every Hypothesis (VEH):** A baseline method that only expands edges valid in all hypotheses, resulting in overly conservative plans.
2. **Per-Edge Hypothesis (PEH):** Allows expansions valid in at least one world and uses a sub-search "Rerouter" to route around obstacles in other hypotheses to average the cost. Its high computational cost made it impractical for field experiments.
3. **Goal-Edge Hypothesis (GEH):** Defers considering multiple worlds until an edge reaches the goal, then reroutes from the first point of divergence to the goal and averages the cost. This concentrates expansions near the goal, limiting long-range planning efficiency.
4. **Goal-Edge Graph Revision Hypothesis (GEGRH):** Improves GEH by adding a graph-revision step after goal-edge cost updates, focusing expansions at the divergence points rather than the goal.

The methods were evaluated using ARA* on 221 planning problems collected from an Unmanned Ground Vehicle (UGV), testing two and three successive environment maps against traditional Single-Hypothesis (SH) planning. Because PEH was too slow and GEGRH superseded GEH, analysis focused on VEH and GEGRH. 

Results showed that while both multi-hypothesis methods required more planning time and produced longer path durations than SH due to increased caution and computation, GEGRH outperformed VEH. Compared to VEH, GEGRH reduced planning time by 15.4% (two hypotheses) and 29.27% (three hypotheses), and reduced path duration by 6.64% and 18.72%, respectively. Case studies demonstrated that GEGRH generally finds more direct routes by evaluating the risk of rerouting through uncertain choke points, though VEH occasionally outperforms it when GEGRH's rerouting sub-search hits the one-second time limit, yielding a suboptimal path. Future work includes incorporating more hypotheses, non-binary map data, alternative cost functions, and hypothesis certainty estimates.

1. Determine if a contract exists with committed parties, specific payment terms, commercial substance, and probable collection.
2. Identify single or bundled performance obligations.
3. Determine the transaction price, factoring in variable components, time delays, or the fair value of non-cash payments.

This passage describes ecologically sustainable methods, chemical formulations, and apparatus for manufacturing vacuum-molded, fiber-based packaging and containers to replace single-use plastics. Traditional molded fiber products lack the necessary barriers and structural features required for certain food and beverage applications. The invention addresses these limitations by combining specific geometric features with optimized chemical slurries and modified manufacturing tools.

The manufacturing process utilizes a closed-loop vacuum forming system where a wire mesh-covered mold is immersed into a fiber-based slurry (comprising water and base fibers like softwood, bagasse, bamboo, old corrugated containers, or newsprint). A vacuum draws the slurry onto the mesh, and excess slurry is recirculated while a sampling module monitors and maintains steady-state chemical additive levels. The formed part is then cured using either a dry process (heated air) or a wet press process (heat and pressure). Grinding the pulp fibers refines the slurry, improving bonding and strength. 

Depending on the application, specific chemical additives are mixed into the slurry or applied as topical coatings:
*   **Produce Containers:** Utilize old corrugated containers and newsprint fibers with moisture barriers like alkyl ketene dimer (AKD), plus liquid starches, dry strength additives (e.g., Topcat L95, Hercobond), and wet strength additives (e.g., Kymene 577) to maintain hoop strength. 
*   **Microwavable/Oven Containers:** Require moisture, oil, and water vapor barriers to prevent condensation and leakage. They use a softwood/bagasse base with AKD, fluorine-containing polymers (e.g., UNIDYNE TG 8111) for oil resistance, organic retention aids (e.g., Nalco 7527), and inorganic salts (e.g., Hercobond 6950). Vapor barriers are achieved by reducing porosity via fiber grinding or applying a topical spray coating (e.g., Daikin S2066).
*   **Meat Containers:** Use softwood, bagasse, and/or bamboo fibers with AKD for moisture resistance, optional oil barriers, and dry strength additives to preserve rigidity over an extended shelf life.
*   **Beverage Lids:** Use softwood, bagasse, and/or bamboo fibers combined with AKD, Hercobond 6950, and Kymene to maintain rigidity and moisture resistance. 

Structurally, the containers incorporate geometric features to enhance rigidity, such as rolled edges, overhanging skirts, indented side shelves, varying draft angles, and various sidewall and bottom rib configurations. 

The invention also introduces modified vacuum tooling:
1.  **Vent Hole Tooling:** A directional water impingement cleaning system uses re-directed spray nozzles on a manifold to horizontally spray and remove excess pulp around vertical mold inserts. This creates larger, extended vent holes in produce containers without altering the underlying molds.
2.  **Lid Tooling:** Beverage lids require a zero or negative draft lock ring to snap onto cups, which typically locks the part onto conventional molds. The modified mold assembly includes a pneumatically actuated retractable piston. When extended, the piston forces the lid's lock ring to momentarily expand and unlock from the mold.

Finally, these chemistries and structural features can be adapted for non-food utility containers and shipping kits, such as a flat-screen TV packaging kit containing covers, a screen protector, corrugated pulp corner pieces, and a pallet strap.

This lecture covers the properties and applications of Poisson processes. It begins with a review of previous concepts: a Poisson process is an arrival process characterized by independent and identically distributed (IID), memoryless, exponentially-distributed interarrival times. It can be represented by arrival epochs, interarrival times, or a counting process $N(t)$. The increments of a Poisson process are stationary and independent, and the sum of independent Poisson random variables is also a Poisson random variable whose mean is the sum of the individual means. Alternate definitions of the process rely on stationary and independent increments alongside either the Poisson probability mass function (PMF) or specific small incremental conditions.

The lecture then introduces combining and splitting Poisson processes. Combining two independent Poisson processes of rates $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2$ yields a new Poisson process with a rate of $\lambda_1 + \lambda_2$. Furthermore, the sum of many small independent arrival processes tends to be Poisson even if the individual processes are not. Conversely, splitting a Poisson process using an independent Bernoulli process results in two independent Poisson processes. Combining and splitting can be used together to solve complex problems, such as finding the probability of service completion without interruption in a last-come, first-served queue. 

For non-homogeneous Poisson processes, where the arrival rate $\lambda(t)$ varies over time (such as in modulated optical transmission), the counting process formulas, as well as combining and splitting properties, still hold using the average arrival rate over an interval. However, the interarrival times are no longer exponential.

Next, the lecture examines arrival epochs conditioned on a specific number of arrivals, $N(t) = n$. For $N(t) = 1$, the conditional probability density of the arrival is uniform ($1/t$) and independent of $\lambda$. For $N(t) = n$, the joint density is $n! / t^n$. This is identically distributed to the order statistics of $n$ IID uniform random variables over the interval $0$ to $t$. Using these order statistics, the expected value of the first arrival epoch is found to be $t / (n + 1)$, and the interarrival intervals share the same uniform density properties.

Finally, the professor introduces a paradox: while the mean interarrival time of a Poisson process is $1/\lambda$, if an observer arrives at an arbitrary time $t$, the mean interval between the previous arrival and the next arrival is larger than $1/\lambda$. This happens because a randomly chosen point in time is proportionally more likely to fall within a larger interval than a smaller one.

The passage describes a novel packet processing pipeline that enhances match-action packet header processing in reconfigurable hardware switches. The switch includes an ingress pipeline, a queuing system (such as a centralized data buffer), and an egress pipeline. Both pipelines contain a parser, a match-action unit (MAU), and a deparser. 

When a packet is received, the parser separates the packet header data from the payload and determines which header fields might be processed by the MAU. Using an extractor state machine, the parser populates a primary packet header vector (PPHV) with participating header fields that may be used by the MAU, and populates a secondary packet header vector (SPHV) with non-participating header fields that will not be processed by the MAU. Both the PPHV and SPHV consist of sets of registers that store the fields. Separating these fields improves switch efficiency by avoiding the waste of MAU resources on unused data, simplifying switch wiring, and allowing the parser to parse deeper into packets without sending additional data to the MAU.

The parser delivers the PPHV to the MAU, which contains multiple reconfigurable match-action stages. Each stage includes crossbars (Xbar), exact match tables (implemented with SRAM), ternary match tables (implemented with TCAM), and a Very Long Instruction Word (VLIW) action engine. The MAU stages match the PPHV header fields against the tables and apply actions, such as modifying header data, assigning the packet to an output port or queue, sending it to a controller, or dropping it. Meanwhile, the parser sends the SPHV and the packet payload directly to the deparser, bypassing the MAU. 

After MAU processing, the deparser reassembles the packet by combining the processed PPHV data from the MAU with the unprocessed SPHV data and payload received directly from the parser. An ingress deparser sends the reassembled packet to the queuing system to be forwarded to the egress pipeline, while an egress deparser sends the packet out of the switch.

The parser and MAU operate based on configuration data from the control plane. A compiler receives code defining switch operations (such as P4 code) and generates a parse graph along with control and table flow graphs. Based on the flow graphs, the compiler determines which header fields participate in the MAU stages, annotates the parse graph accordingly, and generates configuration data for both the MAU and the parser. A configurator module then distributes this configuration data to the switch's parser and MAU. The parser's extractor state machine uses the configuration data (implemented as TCAM entries representing the parse graph) and values from current packet header fields (such as the EtherType or protocol fields) to iteratively extract header fields into the PPHV or SPHV until reaching the payload.

The buy-and-hold strategy, also known as position trading or long-term investing, is a passive approach where investors purchase stocks, mutual funds, or ETFs and keep them for years or decades, ignoring short-term market fluctuations. This aligns with the Efficient Market Hypothesis and contrasts with active trading, which attempts to time the market. 

Because most individual stocks have poor lifetime returns, building a diversified portfolio or investing in index-tracking ETFs is recommended to reduce risk. However, investors can also apply growth or value investing styles to individual stocks with strong fundamentals. 

Studies show that buy-and-hold investors generally outperform active traders over long horizons. Benefits of the strategy include:
* Lower trading costs and fees.
* Favorable long-term capital gains tax rates and tax deferral.
* Reduced "manager risk" (human error).
* Less stress and time commitment.
* Shareholder privileges like dividends and voting rights.

Critics argue that buy-and-hold investors miss optimal selling times and suffer setbacks during market downturns. A backtest comparison showed that while holding the SPY ETF from 1993 yielded a 9.7% annual return, an active portfolio of trading strategies in SPY and QQQ experienced substantially fewer drawdowns. Ultimately, while active trading offers a smoother ride, passive buy-and-hold is the best option for most people to create wealth.

Malnutrition, including wasting, stunting, and undernutrition, is a critical issue globally and in Pakistan, increasing the risk of disease and death in children under five. This multicenter cross-sectional study aimed to identify the determinants of these conditions among children in southern Punjab, Pakistan. 

Researchers enrolled 185 children aged 6–59 months with severe wasting or stunting at Community Management of Acute Malnutrition centers across four villages. Data on sociodemographic characteristics, nutrition, and medical history were collected through parental interviews and medical records, alongside standardized anthropometric measurements. Data were analyzed using independent t-tests and multivariate linear regression models.

Of the 185 participants, 56.2% were female, 69.2% had a family monthly income of ≤15,000 PKR, 80.5% were not exclusively breastfed, and 89.2% experienced poor complementary feeding practices. Statistical analyses revealed that family monthly income and complementary feeding practices were significant determinants of wasting. Tuberculosis contact history and exclusive breastfeeding practices were significantly associated with stunting. Furthermore, monthly income and exclusive breastfeeding practices were significantly associated with undernutrition. Other factors discussed as impacting nutritional status include maternal education, birth intervals, and having a larger household size or more siblings. 

In conclusion, wasting, stunting, and undernutrition among children under five in Pakistan are associated with exclusive breastfeeding, complementary feeding practices, household size, family income, and infection history. Addressing child malnutrition requires concerted efforts from all societal sectors and the incorporation of dietary awareness into child nutrition programs.

Patterns for distributed systems offer three main values: learning from others' mistakes, establishing a shared vocabulary, and building reusable components. Containers serve as the foundational building blocks for these patterns, and splitting applications on a single machine into multiple co-located containers (such as a Kubernetes pod) provides resource isolation, clear team ownership, and separation of concerns. 

There are three primary single-node patterns:
* **The Sidecar Pattern:** A sidecar container shares resources (like filesystems or networks) with the main application container to augment and extend its functionality. Examples include adding HTTPS to legacy services, dynamic configuration synchronization, process monitoring (`topz`), and building a simple Git-based PaaS. For modularity and reusability, sidecars require parameterization, a stable API, and clear documentation (e.g., via Dockerfiles).
* **The Ambassador Pattern:** An ambassador container acts as a proxy that brokers interactions between the application container on localhost and the external world. It is used to route requests to a sharded storage backend (such as Redis), handle service discovery and brokering across different environments, and perform experimentation or request splitting (e.g., sending 10% of traffic to an experimental version via nginx).
* **The Adapter Pattern:** An adapter container modifies the heterogeneous interface of an application container so it conforms to a predefined, consistent interface expected by external tools. Common use cases include adapting metrics for monitoring aggregators like Prometheus, normalizing varied logging formats using tools like fluentd, and executing rich health-check scripts for databases like MySQL.

Beyond single-node patterns, multi-node distributed patterns use loosely coupled microservices that communicate over networks via formal APIs. While microservices enable small teams to work independently and scale components individually, they are harder to debug and architect than monoliths, making distributed patterns essential.

Two key multi-node patterns are:
* **Replicated Load-Balanced Services:** Used for stateless applications, this pattern places multiple identical server replicas behind a load balancer for redundancy, high availability, and horizontal scaling. These services require readiness probes to indicate when a container is initialized to receive traffic, and they can use IP hashing or cookies for session tracking. The pattern can be expanded with additional replicated layers, such as a Varnish caching proxy tier to improve performance and provide rate-limiting (denial-of-service defense), and an nginx tier to handle SSL termination.
* **Sharded Services:** Used for stateful services when data is too large for a single machine, sharding splits data across multiple machines, where each shard serves a specific subset of requests. A sharded cache (such as memcached) maximizes memory utilization compared to a replicated cache. Because a shard failure results in cache misses that increase latency and load on the backend, systems can combine patterns to create replicated, sharded caches for greater resilience. Traffic can be routed to shards via a client-side ambassador or a shared routing service using a sharding function. This function relies on a hashing function and the modulo operator, requiring determinism (identical inputs always map to the same output) and uniformity (requests distribute evenly across shards).

A Death Cross in trading occurs when a short-term moving average, typically the 50-day, crosses below a long-term moving average, typically the 200-day. While this lagging indicator often sparks media speculation about bear markets, a 60-year backtest of the S&P 500 reveals it only signals lower returns in the short term (under 30 days). For longer periods, returns are generally positive and align with long-term averages. Consequently, relying solely on a Death Cross can cause investors to prematurely exit positions and miss bull markets, as occurred in March 2020. 

However, the Death Cross is useful as a defensive tool to reduce drawdowns. Buying at a Death Cross and selling at a Golden Cross (when the short-term average crosses above the long-term average) yields a poor 0.4% annual return. Conversely, buying a Golden Cross and selling at a Death Cross yields a 7% CAGR. While slightly below buy-and-hold returns, this combined strategy reduces market exposure by 30% and significantly lowers maximum drawdowns.

This patent document details medical systems, devices, and methods for delivering and optimizing neural modulation, such as Spinal Cord Stimulation (SCS), to alleviate pain. An implantable neuromodulation system typically comprises an implantable pulse generator (IPG) or an external trial stimulator (ETS) connected to electrode arrays on leads placed near targeted neural tissue. External devices, including a clinician's programmer and a patient's remote control, communicate wirelessly with the stimulator to initialize, adjust, and control modulation parameters. Modulation therapies can be perceptible (causing paresthesia) or sub-perception (using specific frequency ranges, duty cycles, or selective tissue targeting so the patient does not feel the stimulation). 

Because numerous electrodes and complex electrical pulse capabilities create millions of potential modulation parameter sets—and because sub-perception therapies can take hours or days to wash-in or wash-out—an automated, closed-loop machine learning or search system is used to identify optimal stimulation patterns without requiring constant clinician interaction. 

The optimization system uses a processor and memory to access three main types of inputs:
1. **Patient Input:** Subjective data and pain metrics, including visual analog scales (VAS), numerical rating scales (NRS), satisfaction scores, global impression of change, and self-reported activity. Patients can also rank or sort programs using a graphical user interface.
2. **Clinician/User Input:** Selected parameter sets, specific dimensions to evaluate (e.g., spatial location, frequency, pulse width, burst patterns, duty cycle), and search configuration options (e.g., parameter test ranges, evaluation times, survival thresholds, and search objectives).
3. **Automatic Input:** Objective data and physiological metrics collected from patient devices or wearable sensors, such as activity and posture from an accelerometer, heart rate or heart rate variability from a heart rate monitor, EEG, fMRI, and field potentials from an IPG.

The system feeds these inputs into a search method to evaluate candidate parameter sets in the time, space, and informational domains. Example search methods include:
* **Sorting Algorithms:** Programs are scheduled, scored by the patient, and sorted. Programs failing to meet a predefined survival threshold score are discarded.
* **Gradient Descent/Ascent:** The system optimizes a specific parameter dimension (e.g., frequency) by testing adjacent values in steps and moving toward a local optimal score.
* **Sensitivity Analysis:** A regression model is built from stimulation variables and outcome variables to identify a coefficient matrix. This separates "sensitive" parameter sets (kept to guide therapeutic programming) from "insensitive" sets (dropped or used to introduce parameter variation).

The search methods can also optimize spatial parameters (such as electrode fractionalization and current steering using virtual multipoles) within bounded search spaces. To manage noise in patient feedback caused by daily variables, the system may average multiple scores, re-verify programs, or corroborate subjective feedback with objective physiological data. Once optimal programs are identified, the system programs the neuromodulator. To prevent the patient's nervous system from adapting to a fixed stimulation pattern (neurological conditioning), the IPG can be configured to regularly or irregularly cycle through multiple effective programs. These optimization methodologies can be executed across various networked or standalone processor-based machines, including the IPG, remote control, programmer, or cloud servers.

The provided passage from the Physical Layer Simplified Specification Version 6.00 details the operational states, commands, and protocols for SD Memory Cards. 

**Data Transfer, Read, and Write Operations:**
* **Tuning and State Transitions:** The host uses CMD19 for tuning (completing 40 executions within 150ms) and operates at fOD frequency during Card Identification Mode before switching to fPP for Data Transfer Mode. CMD7 selects a card for the Transfer State or deselects cards to the Stand-by or Disconnect states. 
* **Bus Width and Block Length:** ACMD6 selects between a 1-bit (default) and 4-bit bus width (rejected if the card is locked). For 2GByte, SDHC, and SDXC cards, the block length for memory access is fixed or capped at 512 bytes, whereas SDSC cards use byte addressing with lengths set by CMD16. SDHC and SDXC cards use block addressing and disable partial or misaligned access.
* **Read/Write Protocols:** Data transfers are synchronous to the clock and protected by CRC bits. Read (CMD17, CMD18) and write (CMD24, CMD25) operations can be aborted using the stop command (CMD12). Cards may buffer block writes, holding the DAT0 line low to indicate a busy (Programming) state. Hosts can speed up multiple block writes by pre-erasing blocks via ACMD23. While a card is programming, parameter set and read commands are not allowed, and resetting the card (CMD0/CMD15) will terminate programming and may destroy data.

**Erase Operations:**
* **Standard Erase, Discard, and FULE:** Erasing requires the sequence CMD32 (start), CMD33 (end), and CMD38 (erase). Out-of-sequence commands trigger ERASE_SEQ_ERROR or ERASE_RESET bits. SDHC and SDXC cards also support DISCARD (CMD38 argument 00000001h, 250ms timeout) to de-allocate blocks, and Full User Area Logical Erase (FULE, CMD38 argument 00000002h, 1s timeout) to logically erase the entire user area.

**Write Protection and Card Ownership Protection (COP):**
* **Protection Methods:** Cards support mechanical switches (host responsibility), internal write protection, and password protection (CMD42). 
* **Passwords (PWD and FEP):** A 128-bit password (PWD) locks the card, restricting it to basic commands. Type 3 cards support Card Ownership Protection (COP) using a Force Erase Password (FEP). When FEP is set, standard "Force Erase" (which erases all data and the PWD) and "Clear PWD" are disabled. Instead, "COP Unlock" (CMD42[1Fh]) is required after power-on, and erasing requires "FEP Force Erase" with the correct FEP.

**Application and Switch Commands:**
* **Application-Specific (CMD55) and Interface (CMD8) Commands:** CMD55 precedes an ACMD; undefined ACMDs are treated as regular commands. CMD8 initializes Version 2.00+ cards in the Idle state by verifying host supply voltage before ACMD41 is issued.
* **Switch Function (CMD6):** Mandatory for Version 1.10+ cards, CMD6 checks (Mode 0) or switches (Mode 1) card functions across six groups, returning a 512-bit status block. Defined groups include Access Mode (e.g., 25 MB/sec High-Speed mode), Command System (extending CMD34-37, CMD50, CMD57), Driver Strength (UHS-I), and Power Limit (default 0.72W, adjustable up to 1.44W for UHS-I and 1.80W for UHS-II based on VDD1/VDD2 consumption).

**Clock Control, CRC, and Timeouts:**
* **Clock Control:** The host can adjust or stop the bus clock to manage data flow or save energy, provided it supplies at least 8 clock cycles after the last bus transaction and a clock edge to clear busy signals.
* **CRC and Error Handling:** Commands, responses (except R3), and registers use CRC7; data payloads use CRC16. Failed CRC checks or illegal commands cause the card to withhold responses and set error bits (COM_CRC_ERROR or ILLEGAL_COMMAND) without changing states.
* **Timeouts:** Read timeouts are 100ms (or 100x typical access time for SDSC). Write busy timeouts are up to 250ms for SDSC/SDHC, while SDXC cards may indicate write busy up to 500ms under specific conditions.

Because this doubling persists even after adjusting for age and weight, the study indicates that osteoarthritis is not simply a "wear-and-tear" disease caused by aging and obesity. Instead, researchers hypothesize that modern physical inactivity may be a primary factor, as exercise strengthens supporting muscles and thickens cartilage to help joints withstand stress. While activity does not guarantee prevention and may not be advisable for severely damaged joints, the findings suggest that changing modern lifestyle factors could help counteract the rise of arthritis.

This preprint examines how human contact network structures impact pathogen spread, using COVID-19 as an example. Because interpersonal interactions form complex networks across households, schools, and workplaces, individual risk-tolerance decisions affect the broader population. 

The authors constructed synthetic networks of approximately 3,000 individuals based on 2019 US American Community Survey data. Networks layered household, classroom, workplace, and background community interactions, assigning individuals age and vulnerability statuses. The study compared demographic structures using data from Florida (higher average age, smaller households) and Texas (lower average age, larger households). It also tested three risk-tolerance scenarios: full participation in work and school, vulnerable individuals avoiding work and school interactions, and entire households with vulnerable members avoiding these interactions. 

Pathogen spread was simulated using a discrete-time, chain binomial SEIR model (tracking susceptible, exposed, symptomatic/asymptomatic infectious, recovered, and deceased classes) parameterized for the original Wuhan COVID-19 strain. In the model, vulnerable individuals experienced longer recovery times and higher mortality.

The study found that:
* Behavioral changes by vulnerable individuals in isolation are insufficient to reduce their infection risk.
* Population structure can have varied, counter-acting effects on epidemic outcomes.
* Co-worker interactions generally contribute more to disease spread than school classmate interactions.

Prostate cancer (PCa) is a prevalent male malignancy with rising incidence. Because advanced PCa often resists current treatments, identifying novel, genetically validated drug targets is critical. This study utilized Mendelian randomization (MR) to identify therapeutic targets for PCa by analyzing druggable genes from the eQTLGen Consortium alongside PCa genome-wide association study (GWAS) data from the UK Biobank (discovery cohort) and FinnGen Consortium (replication cohort). 

In the discovery phase, 151 genes were causally associated with PCa risk. Replication validated 12 genes lacking pleiotropy and heterogeneity. Five genes (HOXA9, MPHOSPH6, SLC45A3, PBX2, and HLA-A) positively correlated with PCa risk, while seven (PPARGC1A, FLOT2, TKT, CARNS1, GPBAR1, CSF1R, and TRAV21) negatively correlated. Gene Ontology (GO) and KEGG enrichment analyses revealed these genes participate in various metabolic processes and cancer pathways, and a protein-protein interaction (PPI) network was constructed. 

Using the DSigDB database, the top five candidate intervention drugs identified were Tauroursodeoxycholic acid, Adehl, GDP366, Decanoic acid, and GW612286X. Molecular docking via AutoDock evaluated interactions between these drugs and targets (PPARGC1A, GPBAR1, and CSF1R), yielding seven binding results, with GPBAR1 and Tauroursodeoxycholic acid showing the highest affinity (binding energy of -11.1). While using two genetic databases reduces false positives, the study is limited by excluding environmental and lifestyle factors, necessitating further experimental validation and clinical trials to confirm drug safety and efficacy.

Originally inspired by management thinker Peter Drucker and British politician David Howell, an "ownership society" involves privatization and individuals managing their own lives and finances without government interference. Key reforms include addressing bank insolvency and consolidating public sector banks, abolishing most LPG and kerosene subsidies for middle- and upper-class households, and using the UDAY program to transfer electricity board responsibilities to state governments rather than providing central bailouts. Ultimately, achieving a true ownership society requires eliminating government handouts and implementing mass privatization.

Researchers measured COVID-19 antibody levels and recorded medical problems in participants receiving BNT162b1, BNT162b2, BNT162b2SA, or a placebo across study Phases 1 and 2/3. 

Immune responses against the original COVID-19 strain one month after a BNT162b2 booster, and against the Beta variant one month after a BNT162b2SA booster or two primary doses of BNT162b2SA, were as good as responses against the original strain one month after two doses of BNT162b2.

In Phase 1, a few participants experienced a temporary drop in lymphocyte counts after Dose 1 of BNT162b1 or BNT162b2, which mostly returned to normal within 6 to 8 days. All tested Phase 1 doses (10, 20, and 30 µg) were well tolerated except for 100 µg of BNT162b1, which was stopped after Dose 1 due to reactions. BNT162b2 at 30 µg was selected for Phase 2/3.

Across all phases, injection site reactions (most commonly pain) and systemic events (most commonly tiredness and headache) within 7 days of vaccination were mostly mild to moderate, well tolerated, and temporary. Other medical problems within one month of Dose 2 or boosters were also mostly mild or moderate. Less than 1% of Phase 2/3 participants left the study due to medical problems.

Few participants experienced serious medical problems within 1 to 6 months after Dose 2 or boosters. Most were considered unrelated to the vaccines. However, in the 16 and older age group in Phase 2/3, researchers believed a few temporary serious medical problems may have been vaccine-related, including limb numbness/tingling, a portal vein blood clot, and a mini-stroke after two doses, plus two cases after a 30 µg booster. 

No participants died in Phase 1, and no participants who received only BNT162b2SA died in Phase 3. During Phase 2/3, 170 participants across the BNT162b2 and placebo groups died from various causes; researchers do not believe these deaths were caused by BNT162b2.

Traditional echocardiographic parameters like left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) often fail to detect early cardiac dysfunction in coronary heart disease (CHD) patients, while newer echocardiographic technologies are complex and difficult to adopt widely. This study investigated the association between a simpler echocardiographic index, first-phase left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF-1), and the severity of coronary artery stenosis, as well as changes in LVEF-1 before and after percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI). 

Researchers enrolled 207 chest pain patients undergoing their first coronary angiography between June 2021 and June 2023. Patients were classified into mild (73), moderate (39), and severe (95) stenosis groups. Clinical, blood, angiographic, and echocardiographic data were collected, with 82 severe group patients re-examined four days post-PCI.

Results showed no statistically significant difference in traditional LVEF among the groups. However, LVEF-1 decreased as stenosis severity increased. LVEF-1 negatively correlated with gender, smoking, blood pressure, glucose, LDL, BNP, and the Gensini score. Furthermore, LVEF-1 was an independent predictor of moderate (≥50%) and severe (≥70%) coronary artery stenosis, demonstrating a significantly higher diagnostic value (AUC) than other evaluated parameters, including global longitudinal peak systolic strain (GLS). 

Following PCI, patients exhibited a significant increase in LVEF-1 and GLS, and a decrease in the E/e' ratio, while LVEF showed no significant early postoperative changes. The Gensini score and stent diameter—rather than total stent length—were identified as independent factors positively influencing post-PCI LVEF-1 improvement. 

Despite study limitations such as a small sample size, multi-center measurement variations, and a lack of coronary functional testing, the findings conclude that LVEF-1 is a sensitive, valuable clinical indicator for assessing CHD severity and early cardiac recovery following PCI.

Digital leaders foster a transparent data culture where accessible, governed data drives collaborative decision-making, innovation, and flexibility. Supported by leadership and standardized APIs (used by 88% of leaders versus 27% of laggards), they establish clear, measurable goals that align the organization vertically and horizontally. For instance, a transformed retail company implemented real-time sales reporting three times daily to enable data-driven decisions across business units. However, even leaders occasionally struggle with inconsistent data literacy or over-analyzing simple decisions.

Conversely, digital laggards restrict data to departmental silos, hoarding it for power and relying on individual tenure or a "culture of genius" rather than objective metrics. They set unrealistic, unmeasured goals, defaulting to rigid, qualitative processes that stifle innovation and create organizational misalignment, as entrenched habits and insufficient resources prevent them from matching behaviors to ambitions. 

Nevertheless, laggards can successfully transform by shifting their core beliefs and practices. As organizations evolve, they typically begin in one of four patterns based on their culture and technical sophistication: "data novices" (lacking enabling culture and systems), "insight ready" (possessing a risk-accepting culture but lacking advanced technical capabilities), "tech enabled" (having technology and data but lacking an experimental culture), and "data reliant" (over-relying on data at the expense of critical thinking). Companies can build on their specific category's strengths to achieve a strong data culture.

Investing in stocks and bonds is an alternative way to grow net worth, and combining them can yield high returns in rising markets while limiting losses in downturns. 

Buying stocks provides a company stake, potential price increases, dividends, and benefits from share buybacks. Although stocks are historically the best-performing asset class, most perform poorly over their lifetimes, carrying capital loss risks even over ten-year periods. Therefore, diversifying across companies, industries, and stock types is recommended.

Buying bonds means lending money to a company or government agency for a fixed period, usually with fixed interest payments. Interest rates depend on maturity length and bond quality. Bonds are less risky than stocks because bondholders are paid before shareholders in a bankruptcy. Sovereign bonds mostly mitigate risk during market crashes, whereas corporate bonds may be unsafe in recessions due to credit risk and sentiment. 

While stocks have historically been the better investment, there is no definitive answer as to which is best; it depends on factors like time frame and proximity to retirement. A 60% stock and 40% bond allocation lowers returns compared to 100% stocks, but reduces volatility and drawdowns. 

Additionally, the seasonal "Sell in May and go away" or "Investing only in Winter" strategy involves investing in the US, Japan, and Europe from November to April, and shifting to Australia, South Africa, and Latin America from May to October. Backtesting equally weighted regional ETFs showed this strategy did not perform as expected.

The TPS7H500x-SP series is a family of radiation-hardness-assured, fixed-frequency, peak current mode PWM controllers used for space-grade DC-DC converters (such as buck, flyback, forward, push-pull, and full-bridge topologies) with switching frequencies up to 2 MHz. Operating from a 4 V to 14 V input supply, the devices require a minimum 0.1 µF input bypass capacitor. 

Key operational features and programmability across the series include:
* **Dead Time and Blank Time:** The TPS7H5003-SP has a fixed 50-ns typical dead time and leading edge blank time. Other devices allow programming via external resistors (10 kΩ to 300 kΩ) on the PS, SP, and LEB pins (leaving PS/SP floating sets an 8-ns typical dead time; LEB cannot be left floating).
* **Pulse Skipping:** Implemented to prevent minimum on-time issues during high-frequency operation. It occurs when the COMP pin is below 0.3 V at the rising clock edge and the previous duty cycle was under 25%.
* **Duty Cycle:** The DCL pin configures maximum duty cycles (50%, 75%, or 100%) on the TPS7H5001-SP, TPS7H5002-SP, and TPS7H5003-SP, whereas the TPS7H5004-SP only supports a 50% limit.
* **Current Sense and Hiccup Mode:** The CS_ILIM pin senses primary-side current and sets the current limit. Exceeding 1.05 V triggers cycle-by-cycle current limiting and charges the HICC pin capacitor (minimum 3.3 nF recommended) to manage delay and restart times.
* **Protections:** The FAULT pin enables external fault shutdown when voltage exceeds 0.6 V for 0.4 µs to 1.4 µs. Internal thermal shutdown stops switching above 175°C and restarts below 160°C.
* **Compensation:** Subharmonic oscillation above a 50% duty cycle is mitigated by setting slope compensation via a resistor on the RSC pin. The internal transconductance error amplifier supports Type 2A or Type 2B frequency compensation connected to the COMP pin.

The passage also details a 500-kHz synchronous push-pull converter design example using the TPS7H5001-SP and GaN FETs to produce a 5 V output. The example outlines calculations for component selection, including resistors, a 33-nF soft-start capacitor, a transformer, an RCD clamp, a 0.47-μH output inductor, 2.3 mF of output capacitance (accounting for single event transients), and an optional secondary filter. 

To ensure design reliability, PCB layout guidelines recommend minimizing high di/dt and dv/dt switching loops, separating analog ground (AVSS) from power ground until a single connection point, placing bypass and compensation components close to the controller, and routing noise-sensitive traces away from magnetics and high dv/dt signals. Finally, the document provides related Texas Instruments documentation links, a revision history from 2023 to 2024, mechanical and packaging notes, and legal disclaimers.

This patent application discloses muscle-targeting compositions, specifically engineered recombinant adeno-associated virus (rAAV) vectors, capsids, particles, and related systems. Conventional rAAVs with natural capsid variants primarily infect the liver and have limited transduction efficiency in other tissues, requiring large doses that can cause liver toxicity and manufacturing challenges. Additionally, transduction efficiency varies across species. 

To address these limitations, the invention provides targeting moieties effective to target muscle cells, coupled to or associated with a cargo. These targeting moieties comprise one or more short peptide n-mer motifs (1–20 amino acids long), which include RGD motifs (such as XmRGDXn or RGDXn) and non-RGD n-mer motifs. The n-mer motifs can be inserted into viral capsid proteins—such as AAV1, AAV2, AAV3, AAV4, AAV5, AAV6, AAV7, AAV8, AAV9, AAV rh.74, or AAV rh.10—so the motif is external to the capsid surface, conferring muscle-specific tropism, increased potency, and reduced immunogenicity. In certain embodiments, the motif is inserted between amino acids 588 and 589 of an AAV9 capsid polypeptide or analogous positions in other AAVs.

The disclosed compositions, vector systems, cells, kits, and pharmaceutical formulations are designed to deliver cargo to treat or prevent muscle diseases or disorders, including autoimmune diseases, cancers, muscular dystrophies (e.g., Duchenne, Becker, Limb-Girdle, Myotonic, FSHD), neuromuscular diseases, sugar/glycogen storage diseases, expanded repeat diseases, dominant negative diseases, cardiomyopathies, viral diseases, and progeroid diseases. The cargo may include morpholinos, antisense oligonucleotides, therapeutic transgenes, peptides, mini- or micro-dystrophin genes, or CRISPR-Cas system molecules, and may be capable of inducing exon skipping in a gene. Methods for generating diverse capsid libraries and selecting potent variants across species using mRNA-based selection and muscle-specific promoters (such as CK8 and MHCK7) are also provided, alongside extensive sequence listings of the identified capsid variants.

Researchers Willis Klein and Jennifer Bartz of McGill University, along with Suzanne Wood of the University of Toronto, have developed a new theoretical model to explain gaslighting. Moving away from outdated psychodynamic theories, their framework views gaslighting as a learning process based on prediction error minimization (PEM), which is how the mind processes information to predict the future and adjust expectations. 

According to the model, manipulators exploit close relationships and trust by behaving in surprising ways that violate expectations. They then repeatedly blame the target's grasp of reality for this surprise, eventually making the victim feel "epistemically incompetent." Because humans rely on close others to form their sense of reality, the researchers suggest that anyone can fall victim to gaslighting if they trust the wrong person. Klein noted that future research might explore whether traits like attachment styles or past trauma affect susceptibility, and hopes the model will help validate components of the phenomenon to better support victims.

This study investigated whether circulating indole 3-acetate (3-IAA) is associated with chemotherapy response and overall survival in patients with non-metastatic pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), aiming to validate previous findings by Tintelnot et al. in metastatic PDAC. Researchers analyzed pre-chemotherapy blood samples from 124 individuals with borderline resectable (n=68) or locally advanced (n=56) PDAC enrolled in the NORPACT2 study between 2018 and 2021. A subset of 35 participants also provided a second sample 2–4 months after starting treatment. 

The median pre-treatment 3-IAA concentration was 290 ng/mL, which correlated positively with age, but not with tumor diameter or serum CA19-9. Results showed no statistically significant differences in pre-treatment 3-IAA concentrations regarding chemotherapy response (defined by CT scan or CA19-9 decline), subsequent surgical resection, or one-year survival status. The median overall survival was 499 days, and statistical models revealed no significant association between pre-treatment 3-IAA levels and overall survival, even after censoring for surgical resection or adjusting for age, ECOG status, CA19-9, and tumor classification. 

The authors conclude that serum 3-IAA is not associated with chemotherapy response or survival in borderline resectable or locally advanced PDAC. Potential reasons for this discrepancy with prior research include assay differences and biological differences between metastatic and non-metastatic cancers. Future validation and clinical trials should focus on metastatic PDAC cohorts.

This study addresses a gap in Turkish academic literature by developing an AI model for Citation Intent Classification (CIC), which is challenging due to Turkish's complex morphology and domain-specific conventions. The authors introduce the first large-scale, publicly available Turkish CIC dataset, consisting of 2,650 labeled citation sentences extracted from 723 Computer Science research articles using the CEX module. The dataset uses a five-category Web of Science scheme (Background, Basis, Support, Differ, and Discuss) and was annotated via a hybrid approach combining human experts and AI-assisted In-Context Learning (ICL). 

In experiments using GPT-4o, Gemini 2.5 Flash, and Gemini 2.5 Pro, model performance was highly sensitive to manual prompt engineering, with revised prompts reaching up to 85.0% accuracy. Automating prompt optimization with the DSPy framework and a Chain of Thought module increased accuracy to 86.5%. Varying few-shot examples showed that more examples did not uniformly improve results; Gemini-2.5-Flash peaked at 89.1% (1-shot), while GPT-4o degraded as examples were added. To ensure stability and mitigate LLM inconsistencies, ensemble strategies were tested. While majority voting achieved 90.2% accuracy and a Logistic Regression meta-model reached 91.0%, a stacked generalization ensemble using an XGBoost meta-model achieved the highest accuracy of 91.3%. 

A major challenge identified was severe class imbalance, as the dominant "Background" class caused models to overfit and struggle with underrepresented or semantically close classes like "Differ," "Basis," and "Support." Future work aims to address this imbalance through hierarchical classifiers, synthetic data generation, and incorporating broader contextual information.

Applying deep learning to neuroimaging faces two primary challenges: small dataset sizes due to expensive brain scan acquisition, and domain shift (DS) caused by technical variations in imaging protocols, hardware, or differing subject populations across studies. To resolve these issues, this paper proposes a transfer learning (TL) pipeline that reuses features from deep neural networks across datasets.

The authors utilize Simple Fully Connected Neural Networks (SFCNs), which consist of a feature extractor and a classifier, to predict age and sex from structural 3D MRI scans. The models are pre-trained on a large dataset from the UK Biobank (UKB) containing scans from approximately 40,000 subjects. The pre-trained models are then evaluated and fine-tuned on three smaller target datasets—OASIS-3, IXI, and ABIDE—which vary significantly in age distributions, sex proportions, and MRI scanner hardware. The proposed transfer learning pipeline involves pre-training the model on UKB, reshaping and retraining the classifier on the target dataset while keeping the feature extractor fixed (if output dimensions differ), and finally fine-tuning the entire model on the target dataset. 

Results show that directly applying UKB-trained models to other datasets leads to a decline in performance due to domain shift, though accuracy remains higher than random selection. Visualization of the extracted features reveals that they are highly task-specific; a model pre-trained on age does not spatially separate sex, and vice versa. Consequently, fine-tuning a model pre-trained on the same task outperforms using one pre-trained on a different task. Furthermore, while spatial separation of features is preserved in OASIS and IXI, ABIDE features show high confusion, likely because ABIDE subjects are much younger than UKB subjects. Therefore, fine-tuning the full model (including the feature extractor) is particularly necessary and beneficial for ABIDE, though it can cause slight overfitting in datasets like OASIS where features are already well-ordered.

Overall, the proposed transfer learning method significantly outperforms classical elastic net regression and training from scratch across tasks and datasets (except for ABIDE sex prediction, where negative transfer occurs due to domain differences). By testing against scaled random initialization, the authors confirm that performance gains are driven by actual feature reuse rather than initial weight scaling. Additionally, transfer learning speeds up training convergence and performs well in scarce data regimes, though fine-tuning only the final classifier layer may prevent overfitting when training samples are extremely limited. Ultimately, the authors suggest that the UKB can serve as an effective general pre-training dataset for neuroimaging, though challenges remain in transferring knowledge to direct disease prediction and harmonizing highly inhomogeneous datasets.
